research.summary:
How Boeing has valued staying in a market versus leaving it, from its own launch and no-launch decisions since 1993.

1. **Boeing has never left its core narrowbody market. It has left small segments using a plain forward-looking business case.**
   - Segments it left: the 717 (about $0.38B of charges), the 757 (production ended 2004), the very-large-aircraft segment (gave up the 747X in 2001) and the 747-8 (kept going through about $4.2B of losses, then ended).
   - Its rule for stopping a program is that remaining revenue must outweigh remaining cost (B-0153).
   - The 757 exit is the clearest cost of leaving a segment. The A321 went on to take roughly 70-85% of the top end of the narrowbody market. Boeing then spent 2014-2019 studying the NMA ($15-20B estimated) to get back in, and shelved it.

2. **When narrowbody share has been at risk, Boeing defended it with the cheapest product that was good enough.**
   - In 1993 the Next Generation 737 came about five years after the A320 entered service.
   - In 2011 Boeing re-engined the 737 (the MAX) for about 10-15% of what a new airplane would cost. Its stated rule: "if ... we are putting meaningful market share at risk by waiting to do a new airplane, we would re-engine instead" (B-0422).
   - What a customer defection cost: in April 2011 McNerney said a 3-4 year product gap would not cost Boeing customers. In July 2011 American Airlines, a Boeing-exclusive customer, put 260 of 460 aircraft with Airbus. Boeing "got half of it" (B-0803).
   - The defensive path had hidden costs. MAX costs were $18.6B by January 2020, and Goldman Sachs counts $45.6B of one-time and abnormal Commercial Airplanes costs over 2019-2025.

3. **Boeing's stated minimum share is about 40%.**
   - In 2012 Albaugh said Boeing did "not want them to get to 60% and us, 40%" because Airbus would then gain learning-curve and pricing advantages (B-0638).
   - In 2022 Calhoun accepted a stable 40% (B-1936).
   - Today Boeing holds about 34% of the single-aisle backlog against Airbus's 55% (AIN, January 2026).

4. **Boeing already counts terms the game leaves out.**
   - Services and lifecycle value were added on top of the airplane's own net present value in the NMA case (B-1457).
   - Boeing values the whole market and 50-60-year franchises, not just the first contract, in defense bids such as the KC-46, T-X and MQ-25 (BX-1033, BX-1545).
   - It spent about $5B to keep the 737 workforce and supply chain intact through the grounding (B-1618, B-1794). That is a revealed value for keeping the capability.
   - Each 737 rate cut moved fixed cost onto the remaining aircraft: about $1B when the rate fell to 42 a month, and $1.1-3.7B a year of unabsorbed overhead over 2019-2023.

5. **Today's leadership is business-case first but expects to stay in.**
   - Since 2016 Boeing has said it will not chase share (B-1131, B-1980).
   - Ortberg sets three conditions for a launch: the market, the technology and Boeing itself must be ready, with debt paid down first.
   - In March 2026 the CFO said "there will be a day where we have to enter into a new program".
   - In July 2026 Ortberg called the next airplane the chance to change Boeing's share of industry profit, and said funding should be ready by about 2030, with the new airplane in service by the end of the 2030s.
   - No source shows Boeing treating leaving the narrowbody market as an option.

**Suggested franchise terms for the game:**
- **Terminal value past the 20-year window.** Boeing calls a new airplane a 50-year product (B-2278).
- **Services income on the fleet in service,** using Boeing Global Services' roughly 18% margin as a proxy.
- **A margin penalty below 40% share.**
- **An overhead absorption charge on the widebody business** of about $1-4B a year as narrowbody volume falls.
- **A floor on the value of keeping the capability** of at least $5B.
- **A defection hazard:** a 3-4 year product gap can lose about half of a loyal account.

Rolls-Royce's 2012 exit from the narrowbody engine market, and its 2023 plan to re-enter only through a partner, show how slow and costly getting back in is.

- WebFetch could not reach boeing.mediaroom.com or www.sec.gov. Those two hosts need to be allowed in the session's network settings. Quotes from Boeing press releases and SEC filings in this output come from search-result excerpts, not fetched pages.
- "Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf" holds Rolls-Royce transcripts, not Boeing's. Boeing's 2026 calls are in "Transcript Digest (4).pdf".

findings.topic: 737 Next Generation (1993): late derivative defense
findings.claim: Boeing answered the A320 with a derivative, not a new airplane, about five years after the A320 entered service in 1988. Southwest launched the program in November 1993 with 63 737-700s. Airbus still reached roughly half of the segment from a standing start. Incumbency did not stop the entrant reaching about 50%.
findings.source: Leeham News, 'A320 v 737: the sales winner is' (2014-11-17), https://leehamnews.com/2014/11/17/a320-v-737-the-sales-winner-is/; Wikipedia, Boeing 737 Next Generation, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737_Next_Generation; Boeing release 1997-12-17, https://boeing.mediaroom.com/1997-12-17-First-Boeing-737-700-Goes-to-Southwest-Airlines
findings.quote: Coming from nowhere, with no customer base, Airbus captured 47.5% of the firm orders (Leeham, A320 family from launch through Sep 2014)
findings.unit: % of firm orders won by A320 family vs 737
findings.use_in_model: Precedent for the share path after a late response. A defensive derivative keeps the incumbent near 50% but does not restore dominance. Calibrates what Boeing can hope to hold if the fps enters service several years after NGSA (roughly 50/50 at best). Shows the incumbent advantage is worth only a few points of share, not a lock.

findings.topic: Value Boeing put on customer lock-in (1997 exclusive deals)
findings.claim: Boeing had signed 20-year exclusive supplier agreements with American, Delta and Continental. As a condition of EC clearance for the McDonnell Douglas merger, it agreed not to enforce them and not to sign new exclusive deals until 1 August 2007. That it signed such deals at all shows Boeing valued locking in a whole fleet for decades.
findings.source: McDonnell Douglas/Boeing SEC Form 8-K, July 1997, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000063917/000006391797000021/0000063917-97-000021.txt (quoted from a search-result excerpt; sec.gov blocked for fetch); CNN Money 1997-06-25, https://money.cnn.com/1997/06/25/companies/boeing/; Boeing release 1997-07-23 (boeing.mediaroom.com)
findings.quote: Boeing further agreed not to enforce the exclusivity provisions in its existing agreements with American Airlines, Delta Airlines and Continental Airlines.
findings.use_in_model: Supports a customer lock-in term: an incumbent customer is worth its whole replacement cycle, not one order. The EC remedy shows regulators also judged lock-in material. When AA (one of these accounts) split in 2011 (see the AA finding), Boeing lost half of a value it had once tried to secure for 20 years.

findings.topic: 717 exit (2005): leaving a sub-scale segment
findings.claim: Boeing ended the 717 (ex-MD-95, inherited in the 1997 merger) on a plain demand test and booked about $380M of pre-tax charges. About 155-156 aircraft were built. It made no attempt to defend the 100-seat segment for franchise reasons and later accepted leaving it to Embraer and the A220 (B-1666).
findings.source: Boeing Form 8-K Ex. 99.1 (Jan 2005), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000012927/000119312505008279/dex991.htm, and Boeing 10-Q 2005 (quotes from search-result excerpts; sec.gov blocked for fetch); NBC News 2005, https://www.nbcnews.com/news/amp/wbna6825716; repo B-1666 (FQ1 2020 call, Calhoun)
findings.quote: the overall market for the airplane does not support continuing 717 production beyond delivering on our current commitments (Alan Mulally, BCA CEO)
findings.unit: USD million pre-tax charges ($280M in Q4 2004)
findings.use_in_model: Gives a small exit-cost lump (about $0.4B) for a niche. Boeing applies a plain forward-looking business case to small segments. Do not apply this 'cheap exit' to the narrowbody: it is the largest segment and carries the overhead, services and supply-chain terms below (inference).

findings.topic: 757 exit (2003-04): the clearest cost of ceding a segment
findings.claim: Boeing ended the 757 (1,050 built) and argued the 737NG and 7E7 covered the space. Airbus kept the A321 and later dominated the top of the narrowbody market. The A321neo outsold the MAX 9/10 by 71% to 29% (Avolon, 2017) and later by about 4:1 (Cirium). Boeing spent 2014-2019 on the NMA to try to re-enter that space and never launched it.
findings.source: Boeing release 2003-10-16, https://boeing.mediaroom.com/2003-10-16-Boeing-to-Complete-Production-of-757 (quote from search-result excerpt); Flightglobal 'Boeing axes 757', https://flightglobal.com/boeing-axes-757/51210.article; AIN 2017-08-31 (Avolon), https://oldain.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2017-08-31/avolon-sees-clear-winners-losers-737-max-lineup; Cirium, https://www.cirium.com/thoughtcloud/ascend-by-cirium-weekly-need-a-bigger-plane
findings.quote: market reality for the 757 as well as the growth in range and seating capacity of our market-leading Next-Generation 737 family (Mulally)
findings.unit: % of A321neo vs MAX 9/10 orders (2,065 orders, Aug 2017)
findings.use_in_model: Best Boeing precedent for what Do Nothing or exit costs. After the exit, the rival took about 70-80% of the ceded segment, and getting back in cost a new airplane that never closed its business case. Supports making share loss after exit near-total and sticky. Treat re-entry as costing about a full clean sheet.

findings.topic: 747X and the very-large-aircraft segment ceded to the A380 (2001)
findings.claim: Boeing dropped the 747X stretch in 2001 because airline response was lukewarm, explicitly leaving the super-jumbo segment to the A380. Its demand forecast was far below Airbus's 1,235 very-large passenger aircraft (2000 forecast). The A380 ended in 2021, which bore out Boeing's choice. Ceding was right because the segment was small.
findings.source: Everett Herald/AP (Sept 2001), 'Mulally's challenge', https://www.heraldnet.com/?p=434920; Flightglobal, https://www.flightglobal.com/the-big-issue/907.article; Flightglobal 'Cancelled 747X leaves cargo void', https://www.flightglobal.com/cancelled-747x-leaves-cargo-void/37182.article
findings.quote: Mulally abruptly decided to abandon the 747X, a planned super-jumbo jet that was receiving lukewarm response from airlines ... leaves the super-size airplane market to Airbus's A380 (AP)
findings.unit: Airbus 2000 forecast of very-large passenger aircraft (Boeing far lower)
findings.use_in_model: Shows Boeing ties the value of a segment to its size. Ceding a niche can raise net present value, so a franchise premium should scale with segment size and overhead share (inference). The narrowbody is the opposite case: the largest segment, carrying most of Boeing's fixed cost.

findings.topic: Sonic Cruiser to 7E7/787 (2001-03): following what customers will pay for
findings.claim: Boeing announced the Sonic Cruiser in March 2001, three months after the A380 launch, and cancelled it on 20 December 2002 after airlines chose efficiency over speed (post-9/11, rising fuel). The 7E7 (787), announced January 2003, promised 17-20% less fuel than existing aircraft. Boeing reshaped its next airplane to the customer value proposition rather than to a show of market presence.
findings.source: Wikipedia, Boeing Sonic Cruiser, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Sonic_Cruiser; NPR 2002-12-21, https://www.npr.org/2002/12/21/887162/boeing-drops-plans-for-high-speed-jet; Flightglobal, https://flightglobal.com/sonic-cruiser-a-different-boeing/74989.article
findings.quote: The proposed 7E7 would consume ... 17–20% less fuel than conventional aircraft (Wikipedia summary)
findings.use_in_model: Product-definition risk: the franchise is defended only by an airplane airlines value (efficiency). Supports gating fps capture on a step-change gain, consistent with Calhoun's 25-30% bar (B-2082) and Boeing's 20%+ replacement-demand rule (B-0679).

findings.topic: 787 launch economics: clean-sheet cost and payback
findings.claim: The 787, launched April 2004 with 50 aircraft from ANA, was pitched as Boeing's best program economics ever (B-0024, 2006). It went about 3 years late on a roughly 5-year plan (B-0409). Development cost is reported above $32B, and deferred production costs reached about $28.7B. McNerney later said its financial characteristics 'were not fun' and Boeing did not want another (B-1009). This is why Boeing chose derivatives through the 2010s (B-0901).
findings.source: repo wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-0024 (FQ3 2006 call p.3061), B-0409 (May 2011 investor conf. p.2580s), B-1009 (FQ4 2014 call, Feb 2015); The Air Current, https://theaircurrent.com/aircraft-production/boeings-787-profitability-program-accounting/; Seattle Times figure via KNKX 2015, https://www.knkx.org/business/2015-08-12/boeing-bosses-are-looking-for-ways-to-reduce-787-costs
findings.quote: We love the airplane. And customers like it. But the financial characteristics were not fun. (McNerney, B-1009)
findings.unit: USD billion deferred production + inventory costs (2016); development >$32B (press estimate)
findings.use_in_model: Calibrates the clean-sheet overrun distribution behind the game's $60-65B fps bill and debt penalty. The 2004 plan was about $10B; out-turn development was above $32B (press estimate). Also shows a clean sheet can still become a long-lived franchise (787 now a profit driver), which argues for a value term beyond 20 years.

findings.topic: 747-8: Boeing's half-the-segment break-even rule and its stop test
findings.claim: Boeing's 747-8 case assumed about half of a roughly 740-aircraft very-large-aircraft market. Reach-forward losses then totalled about $4.2B: $685M (2008), $1,352M (2009), $885M (2015) and $1,258M (2016). Boeing kept the line going at 0.5 a month rather than kill it, then ended the 747 in 2023. Its stated test for continuing is forward-looking (remaining revenue over remaining cost), not franchise-based.
findings.quote: if we achieve half the market that you described, there will be no problem with profitability on this program. (McNerney, B-0222); Is it enough to kill the program? I don't think so. (B-0192)
findings.unit: USD billion cumulative 747 reach-forward losses (computed from the four charges)
findings.use_in_model: Use 50% of the segment as Boeing's planning share for a new program's business case. Use the forward-looking stop test (B-0153) as the default; franchise terms are additions Boeing has made only for its core and strategic programs, not niches.

findings.topic: 737 MAX 2011: Boeing's explicit share-at-risk decision rule
findings.claim: Boeing said its standing rule was to re-engine rather than wait for a clean sheet if waiting put meaningful share at risk. In 2015 it justified the MAX as protecting 'years of near-term market share strength' that a later clean sheet would have put at risk. In 2011 Boeing valued near-term share above better economics later.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-0422 (FQ2 2011 call, 2011-07-27, p.2551, McNerney); B-1038 (Investor Day 2015-05-12, p.1765, McNerney); B-0413 (FQ2 2011 p.2557)
findings.quote: It has always been our view that if it looked like we are putting meaningful market share at risk by waiting to do a new airplane, we would re-engine instead. (B-0422)
findings.use_in_model: Direct Boeing evidence that share at risk enters launch decisions beyond the program's own net present value. Supports adding a franchise-erosion penalty when Boeing's product falls behind (e.g., NGSA in service and fps not yet). The 2011 response was the cheapest adequate one, not a clean sheet.

findings.topic: Cost of a customer defection: American Airlines 2011
findings.claim: In April-May 2011 McNerney said a 3-4 year gap would not lose Boeing customers, and Albaugh relied on 'very high' switching costs. In July 2011 American, a Boeing-exclusive account, ordered 260 A320-family aircraft and 200 737s (about $38-40B list in total), its first Airbus order since the 1980s. Airbus used its balance sheet and leasing to get in (B-2399).
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-0338 (FQ1 2011 call p.2636), B-2395 (Investor conf. 2011-05-24 p.2602), B-2399 (FQ2 2011 p.2557); AMR Form 8-K Ex. 99.2, 2011-07-20, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000006201/000119312511191877/dex992.htm; NPR 2011-07-20, https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2011/07/20/138535143/american-airlines-places-largest-aircraft-order-in-aviation-history
findings.quote: the NEO will not seriously erode our customer base if there's a new airplane out there, three or four years after they introduce a re-engine ... my personal view is that we're not going to lose customers for a few years (McNerney, B-0338)
findings.unit: aircraft (56.5%) placed with Airbus by a Boeing-exclusive customer
findings.use_in_model: Calibrates a defection hazard. A product gap of about 3-5 years was enough for a 20-year Boeing account to put more than half of a fleet renewal with the rival. Model incumbent capture of replacement demand as falling sharply when Boeing's product is 3+ years behind; switching costs did not protect.

findings.topic: After defection, the split stays (MAX vs NEO catch-up)
findings.claim: BCA's CEO admitted Boeing salvaged only half of American and was still catching up on the NEO two years later. From 2014 Boeing accepted a roughly 50-50 split rather than buy share with price.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-0803 (Investor conf. 2013-05-22 p.2158, Ray Conner); B-0935 / BX-0481 (Morgan Stanley conf. 2014-09-16 p.1920, Conner)
findings.quote: Well, would I have loved to have taken all the share? Absolutely. But we got half of it...And the NEO, I think got a little bit of a jump on us, frankly, and we're still playing a little bit of catch up (B-0803)
findings.unit: % of the AA narrowbody renewal kept by Boeing
findings.use_in_model: Model share losses from a product gap as persistent (hysteresis). A customer that splits does not revert when Boeing's product catches up. The fps recovers share only gradually from the level it inherits at entry into service.

findings.topic: Price of holding the franchise in 2011: re-engine vs clean sheet
findings.claim: Boeing's CFO agreed re-engine R&D was about 10-15% of a new airplane's. A 737 re-engine was put at $2-3B (Mike Bair, 2010), against $10-12B analysts widely estimated for an all-new narrowbody in 2011. Albaugh said non-recurring cost uncertainty and doubts about building 60 composite airplanes a month killed the clean sheet.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-0432 (FQ2 2011 call p.2556, Bell), B-0493 (GS conf. 2011-11-03 p.2484, Albaugh), B-0532 (Credit Suisse conf. 2011-11-30 p.2455); Flightglobal, https://www.flightglobal.com/boeing-disputes-737-max-development-cost-report/103825.article; Wikipedia, Boeing 737 MAX, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737_MAX
findings.quote: R&D on something like this is something like 10% to 15% of a new aircraft, is that fair? -- That's probably about right. (Bell, B-0432)
findings.use_in_model: Gives a cheap defensive derivative option (about 10-15% of clean-sheet cost) that the game should price against fps. In the MAX phase-out world no further derivative is assumed, so its absence is itself a choice to give up the defense. The game's $60-65B fps is about 5-6x the 2011 nominal clean-sheet estimate (inference).

findings.topic: Boeing's own sizing of the 737 franchise at MAX launch
findings.claim: At board approval on 30 August 2011 (496 commitments from five airlines), Boeing forecast more than 23,000 airplanes worth nearly $2 trillion over 20 years in the 737 segment. Bloomberg reported Boeing was counting on the MAX to take about half, roughly $1 trillion of list-price revenue.
findings.source: Bloomberg 2011-08-30, 'Boeing Bets on New 737 MAX to Win $1 Trillion in Jet Orders', https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2011-08-30/boeing-approves-upgrading-737-after-496-order-commitments-1-; CAPA, https://centreforaviation.com/news/boeing-launches-737-max-with-496-commitments-117931
findings.quote: Boeing Bets on New 737 MAX to Win $1 Trillion in Jet Orders (headline; 'about half of a $2 trillion market' is a paraphrase from the search excerpt)
findings.unit: USD billion list-price revenue (about 50% of a ~$2T, 20-year segment)
findings.use_in_model: Order of magnitude for what Do Nothing gives up per 20 years at 50% share. List price overstates realized price, so apply the game's price x margin. Use to sanity-check the fps narrowbody operating-profit stream and any terminal value.

findings.topic: Hidden cost of the defensive-derivative path (MAX crisis)
findings.claim: Boeing put MAX grounding costs at about $18.6B in January 2020: $8.3B customer compensation, $6.3B higher production cost and about $4B abnormal costs. Goldman Sachs counts $45.6B of one-time and abnormal Commercial Airplanes costs and $17.0B of 737/787 cash concessions over 2019-2025. The House T&I final report (Sept 2020) has sections on 'Competitive Pressure' from the A320neo and on 'Production Pressure'.
findings.source: Reuters via aviationnews.eu 2020-01-29, https://aviationnews.eu/news/2020/01/boeing-posts-first-annual-loss-in-two-decades-as-737-max-costs-near-19-billion/; KVIA/CNN 2020-03-10, https://kvia.com/news/business-technology/2020/03/10/the-cost-of-the-boeing-737-max-crisis-18-7-billion-and-counting/; repo B-1650 (10-K FY2019 p.517); repo wargame/profiles/boeing/analyst_models_2026.md (GS BA BCA margin r87, GS BA FCF build r23); House T&I report, https://democrats-transportation.house.gov/imo/media/doc/final_boeing_737_max_report.pdf
findings.quote: Boeing Co on Wednesday swung to its first annual loss since 1997 as 737 MAX costs doubled to nearly $19 billion (Reuters)
findings.use_in_model: Tail-risk term: defending the franchise with a stretched derivative under competitive pressure carried a cost that dwarfed its $2-3B development bill. The causal link from the re-engine choice to the crisis is inference, supported by the House report's competitive-pressure framing. Do not credit franchise defense without a quality and certification risk haircut.

findings.topic: Value of keeping narrowbody capability (line kept warm)
findings.claim: During the 2019-20 grounding Boeing chose to keep its 737 workforce and production infrastructure rather than shed them, expensing about $4B of abnormal costs, later about $5B. That is a revealed price for retaining the capability.
findings.quote: This includes costs related to our decision to maintain the 737 production infrastructure, including labor during the suspension and low rate production. ... this decision is part of our efforts to sustain the gains in the production system and supply chain quality and health (B-1618)
findings.unit: USD billion abnormal production costs accepted to keep the 737 line intact
findings.use_in_model: Lower bound for the missing option or capability value. Boeing paid about $5B over about 2 years to avoid losing narrowbody workforce and supply-chain capability. Exiting by 2060 forfeits that capability, so re-entry would cost at least this plus a clean sheet (inference).

findings.topic: Overhead absorption: narrowbody volume carries fixed cost
findings.claim: Cutting the 737 to 42 a month added about $1B of program cost because fixed costs for the 3,100-aircraft accounting block were spread over a longer period. Goldman Sachs shows $1.1-3.7B a year of unabsorbed overhead at BCA in 2019-2023. The 747-8 rate deferral likewise 'drove higher allocations of fixed costs'.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-1543 (FQ1 2019 call p.1042, Greg Smith), B-0247 (10-K FY2009 p.1729); repo wargame/profiles/boeing/analyst_models_2026.md line 70 (GS BA BCA margin r88)
findings.quote: We also booked approximately $1 billion of additional costs due to the adjustment to the production rate to 42 a month. The additional costs are due to the lower production rate causing fixed costs for the 3,100 aircraft in the block to be amortized over a longer period of time. (B-1543)
findings.unit: USD billion per year unabsorbed overhead (GS); about $1B per 10/month rate step (Boeing)
findings.use_in_model: Add an overhead-absorption term. As 737 volume phases out from 2045 to 2060 with no fps, shared BCA fixed cost (Renton/Everett support, engineering, supply-chain management) moves onto the widebodies. Scale about $1-4B a year to the narrowbody's volume share. The size of the term in a full exit is inference.

findings.topic: Boeing's stated minimum narrowbody share: about 40%
findings.claim: In 2012 BCA's CEO named 40% as the share Boeing must not fall to. The stated mechanism: the leader comes down the learning curve faster and gains pricing power, 'a slippery slope'.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-0638 (Investor Conference 2012-05-15, p.2369, Jim Albaugh)
findings.quote: We're 48%, they're 52%. Pretty darn close to 50-50. We get paid a premium for our airplane. We like that. We do not want them to get to 60% and us, 40%... they come down the learning curve faster than we do, they have pricing power in the marketplace. It's a slippery slope
findings.use_in_model: Use 40% as a threshold for a share-floor penalty. Below it, apply a growing price and margin penalty to Boeing's remaining narrowbody deliveries (Airbus pricing power plus a slower learning curve). In the MAX phase-out world, Do Nothing drives share to 0 by 2060, far past this floor.

findings.topic: 2021-22 revision: stability at about 40%, not 50/50
findings.claim: Calhoun dropped 50/50 as an objective and said a stable 40% without China was acceptable. In 2021 he said Boeing would not try to win back share lost in the grounding, only hold its 'rightful share'. He called chasing Tier 1 status something that 'gets you in trouble'.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-1936 and B-1980 (Investor Day 2022-11-02 p.448, Calhoun); B-1798 (FQ1 2021 call p.727, Calhoun)
findings.quote: Whether we get to 50-50 I want to just highlight for all of you is not an objective of ours. I want to get to stable. If stable is at 40 without China, then that's what we want to do. (B-1936)
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's current floor is still about 40%, matching the game's 40% status-quo share (objectives.md). Supports making the share penalty bite only below 40%, with no premium for share above it (no 'trophy' value).

findings.topic: Where share stands now and analysts' view of Do Nothing
findings.claim: Through November 2025 Airbus held 55% of the 125-240-seat single-aisle backlog and Boeing 34%. By total program orders the A320neo family has 54% and the MAX 33%. BofA's Ron Epstein (analyst estimate) put Boeing's narrowbody share at risk of falling below 40% if no new plane arrives before 2035. Analysts put a new narrowbody at $20-30B of R&D and capex over 8-10 years.
findings.source: AIN 2026-01-07, https://backend.ainonline.com/aviation-news/aerospace/2026-01-07/airbus-dominates-single-aisle-sales-boeing-wins-widebodies; Forbes (2024), 'Why Boeing needs a new plane — soon', https://www.forbes.com.au/news/leadership/why-boeing-needs-a-new-plane-soon/
findings.quote: Airbus has a 55% market share of the backlog for the 125- to 240-seat single-aisle aircraft ... Boeing ... has a 34% share (AIN); Failing to roll out a new plane before 2035 means Boeing's share of the narrowbody market could slide under 40%, Ron Epstein of Bank of America has estimated. (Forbes)
findings.unit: % Boeing share of single-aisle backlog (vs 55% Airbus)
findings.use_in_model: Starting point for the share path: Boeing is already below its stated 40% floor in backlog terms. Use the Epstein estimate (an analyst estimate) as an outside check on the share decline under Do Nothing. Use the $20-30B analyst range as a cross-check against the game's $60-65B fps bill.

findings.topic: 2014-2016 doctrine: margin and business case over share
findings.claim: From 2014 Boeing's leaders said repeatedly that new airplanes and rate decisions rest on the business case, not on regaining share from Airbus. This held even as the A321neo opened a backlog lead.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-1131 / BX-1010 (Barclays conf. 2016-02-17 p.1689, Muilenburg); B-1169 (Investor Day 2016-05-11 p.1622); B-0935 (Morgan Stanley conf. 2014-09-16 p.1920, Conner); B-1100 (FQ4 2015 call p.1712)
findings.quote: if we see a real market demand evolve that leads to a business case for a modified or a new airplane, we'll make that based on business case analysis. It will not be based on market share. We are not in business just to chase market share. (B-1131)
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's public doctrine is net-present-value first, so franchise effects should enter as explicit, sized cash terms (services, overhead, share-floor pricing, capability), not as a goal ranked above value. Contrast with the 2011 rule (B-0422): share becomes decisive only when the loss is large and near.

findings.topic: NMA/797 (2015-2020): walking away from a 4,000-5,000-aircraft segment
findings.claim: Boeing sized the middle of the market at 4,000-5,000 aircraft (220-270 seats, about 5,000 nm). It said no business case closed in 2015, set the hurdle as twin-aisle comfort at narrowbody economics, and said it would stay with current products if the case did not close. Development was estimated at $15-20B (Reuters). Calhoun shelved it in January 2020 to 'start with a clean sheet of paper again'.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-1412 (Bernstein conf. 2018-05 p.1223), B-1019 (2015-02), B-1436 (2018-07), B-1613 (FQ4 2019 call 2020-01-29, Smith); Reuters via Oman Observer, https://www.omanobserver.om/ampArticle/17723; AFP via Arab News, https://www.arabnews.pk/node/1617406; Bloomberg 2019-01-29, https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-01-29/boeing-ba-to-decide-on-spending-15-billion-on-797-jetliner
findings.quote: what we're hearing from customers is we need something that has the comfort and twin-aisle benefit of widebodies but has narrowbody economics, and that's, frankly, the challenge of closing the business case... And if we don't, we'll continue down the path with our current product lines. (Muilenburg, B-1436)
findings.unit: aircraft (NMA market size per Boeing); $15-20B development (Reuters estimate)
findings.use_in_model: Precedent that Boeing will forgo a large adjacent segment when the airplane's own case fails. The outcome was A321neo dominance of the top of the narrowbody market. Use it as a Do Nothing case study: the cost appeared as lost share in the adjacent 737 segment, not inside the NMA's own net present value.

findings.topic: Boeing counts services and lifecycle value on top of the airplane's NPV
findings.claim: In the NMA case Boeing explicitly widened its business case beyond the airplane's own net present value to include lifecycle value from services and vertical integration. It also looked past the initial contract quantity to the broader market and 'what it would take to win'.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-1457 / BX-1147 (Morgan Stanley conf. 2018-09-12 p.1178, Muilenburg); B-1424 (Bernstein conf. 2018-05-31 p.1228); B-1462 (FQ3 2018 call p.1156, Greg Smith)
findings.quote: Not only are we looking at the net present value of the airplane itself in our traditional business case analysis, but also with the investments we're making in services and verticals. How does that create lifecycle value that could be factored into the business case? (B-1457)
findings.use_in_model: Direct Boeing precedent for adding an aftermarket/services NPV term to the fps valuation, which the game currently omits. Apply the same treatment to Do Nothing: the fleet in service shrinks after 2060, so its services annuity shrinks too.

findings.topic: Franchise valuation in Boeing's defense bids: whole market, 50-60 years
findings.claim: Boeing accepted zero-margin or loss-making development bids by valuing the whole long-run franchise rather than the first contract. KC-46: at least 179 aircraft against a market of about 400, a '50-, 60-year widebody franchise'. T-X and MQ-25 carried $691M pre-tax / $541M after-tax up-front charges based on 'considerable market potential'.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl BX-1033 (Investor Day 2016-05-11 p.1629, Muilenburg); B-0918 / BX-1411 (FQ2 2014 call p.1932, Greg Smith); BX-1545 (FQ3 2018 call p.1150, Greg Smith); B-1458
findings.quote: we're going to build at least 179. We think the market's more like 400. ... So this is a 50-, 60-year widebody franchise. And that's the way we think about it in terms of our company strategy. (BX-1033)
findings.unit: years of franchise life Boeing used in bid valuation
findings.use_in_model: Supports a terminal or franchise value beyond the game's 20-year post-entry window. Boeing values programs over 50-60 years. Caveat: these bids later produced large charges (e.g., B-0918), so haircut franchise terms for execution risk.

findings.topic: Installed base drives follow-on orders
findings.claim: BCA said Boeing had more than 250 737 customers, about 200 of them yet to choose their long-term fleet, which gave it a unique chance at the follow-on business. In 2011 Albaugh described the 737 and 777 as Boeing's two 'franchise programs' that fund development and price fights, against Airbus's one.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-1166 (Investor Day 2016-05-11 p.1615, Ray Conner); B-2397 (Investor conf. 2011-05-24 p.2605, Jim Albaugh); B-1137 (2016-03 p.1668, Tinseth: replacement 2.5-3% of installed fleet a year)
findings.quote: we have more than 250 737 customers... About 200 of those customers have yet to make a decision about what they're going to do long term, and I think that provides us a very unique opportunity to compete for the follow-on business (B-1166)
findings.unit: 737 customers / customers yet to decide long term
findings.use_in_model: Model incumbency as a higher capture rate of replacement demand from Boeing's installed base. Tinseth: replacement runs at 2.5-3% of the installed fleet a year. The capture advantage decays once Boeing has no new narrowbody to offer (see the AA defection finding).

findings.topic: Services margin and scale (aftermarket term calibration)
findings.claim: Boeing Global Services earned 18.3% on $5.6B revenue in Q3 2026 and 18.1% on $5.3B in Q2 2026, while BCA lost money. In 2017 the CFO said Boeing had only a 7-9% share of a $2.5T services market. In March 2026 the CFO said BGS is not MRO-heavy but sells parts, including third-party parts.
findings.source: repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest (4).pdf p.7 (FQ3 2026 call 2026-10-27) and p.39 (FQ2 2026 call 2026-07-28), p.100-101 (conference 2026-03-17, Malave); repo evidence.jsonl BX-1481 (2017-02-23 p.1483, Greg Smith); B-1966 (Investor Day 2022-11-02 p.437)
findings.quote: Revenue was up 4% to $5.6 billion. ... Operating margin of 18.3% was up from prior year on favorable volume and mix (FQ3 2026, p.7)
findings.use_in_model: Use about 18% as the margin on services revenue tied to Boeing's fleet in service (BGS mixes commercial and government work, so the commercial-only margin is inference). The services term should follow Boeing narrowbodies in service, which keeps paying for decades after production ends but shrinks to zero without a successor.

findings.topic: Today's leadership: three launch conditions, debt first
findings.claim: Ortberg makes a new airplane conditional on market readiness, Boeing's financial and capacity readiness, and technology readiness, with debt cut to a solid investment grade first. In 2025 he said none of the three was met. The CFO called a new airplane a 50-year product not to be rushed. Ortberg also named FAA certification reform as a precondition.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-2217 / BX-1247 (FQ3 2024 call p.137), BX-1296 (Bernstein conf. 2025-05-29 p.60), B-2316 (FQ2 2025 call p.46), BX-1305 (Morgan Stanley conf. 2025-09-11 p.30), BX-1309 (p.31), B-2278 (BofA conf. 2025-03-19 p.97, Brian West)
findings.quote: One is, when is the market ready? And two, when are we ready, both financially and from a capacity perspective? And third is, when is the technology ready? And I would say the answer is not now on all 3 of those work streams. (Ortberg, BX-1296)
findings.use_in_model: Supports the game's debt penalty and the gating of launch timing. Boeing's own view of 'value' includes balance-sheet capacity as a constraint. Franchise terms should not override a cash-constrained launch date. Frame them as raising the value of being ready to launch at the right time, not of launching now.

findings.topic: 2026 statements: Boeing expects to enter, and sees the next airplane as a value-chain reset
findings.claim: In March 2026 the CFO said Boeing will have to launch a new program but not soon, with none of the three conditions near. In July 2026 Ortberg said Boeing's share of industry profit on existing airplanes is fixed by the supply-chain structure, so the next airplane is the chance to change it, possibly through new partnerships or ventures. In October 2026 he said nothing had changed and any needed investment is in the cash outlook.
findings.source: repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest (4).pdf p.100 (Company Conference 2026-03-17, Jesus Malave), p.46 (FQ2 2026 call 2026-07-28, Ortberg), p.16 (FQ3 2026 call 2026-10-27, Ortberg)
findings.quote: I would say that there will be a day where we have to enter into a new program. That day is not today, and it's not any time near. (Malave, p.100); So it points to the next airplane as the opportunity to change that. (Ortberg, p.46)
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's leaders treat a successor as inevitable ('have to'). No source shows them treating a 2060 exit as an option. Ortberg's value-chain remark supports letting the fps margin exceed the MAX margin (a scenario parameter, inference), and possibly a JV or partner form that cuts the bill.

findings.topic: July 2026 timing: fund by about 2030, in service by the end of the 2030s
findings.claim: Ortberg said Boeing expects to be able to fund a 737 replacement by the end of the decade after 'another couple of years' of balance-sheet repair. He expects the airplane in service by the end of the next decade and said 'The market is not quite ready for the new airplane.' Airbus has said it plans to launch a narrowbody successor in 2030, in service in the second half of the 2030s.
findings.source: Irish Times (FT) 2026-07-20, https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/07/20/boeing-says-it-will-be-ready-to-fund-new-plane-programme-by-2030/; Bloomberg Law 2026-07-20, https://news.bloomberglaw.com/international-trade/boeing-says-next-generation-jet-likely-coming-end-of-next-decade (both read via search excerpts; FT wording on 'exact timing of the competitor' not verified)
findings.quote: The market is not quite ready for the new airplane. (Ortberg to Bloomberg TV); Boeing expects to have the financial firepower to launch a programme to replace its bestselling 737 Max by the end of the decade (FT/Irish Times)
findings.unit: year Boeing expects to be able to fund a launch
findings.use_in_model: Base timing scenario for the fps: launch about 2030, entry into service about 2038-2040, roughly simultaneous with NGSA. Under this timing the defection hazard (3+ years behind) is avoided, so most of the franchise terms are worth defending.

findings.topic: Calhoun era: technology bar for the next airplane
findings.claim: Calhoun committed to doing a new airplane but not in a hurry. He set the bar at 25-30% better than today's airplanes, refused to answer the A321XLR or an A220 stretch, and in 2022 said he would not back a new airplane until an engine with at least 20% better fuel burn arrived next decade.
findings.source: repo evidence.jsonl B-1620 (FQ4 2019 call p.902), B-1814 (2021-06), B-2070 / B-2082 (FQ2 2023 call p.306); Leeham News 2022-06-06, https://leehamnews.com/2022/06/06/boeings-steps-toward-its-next-new-airplane/
findings.quote: The next airplane, in my view, with respect to development has to be a meaningful change, 25%, 30% better than what flies today. (B-2082)
findings.use_in_model: Technology gate for fps capture. If fps gains are under about 20-25%, model replacement demand from Boeing's own installed base as weak (customers stay on the MAX or switch). The franchise value of fps depends on clearing this bar.

findings.topic: Analog (other company, in repo): Rolls-Royce narrowbody exit and attempted re-entry
findings.claim: Rolls-Royce left the narrowbody engine market in 2012, selling its 32.5% IAE stake for GBP 1.5bn. It kept parts supply and about $1 per flying hour on about 5,000 V2500 engines. By 2023 it said it was 'well positioned to reenter the narrow-body market' only through a partnership. Exiting turned the installed base into cash, and re-entry took more than a decade and needed a partner. (This file is Rolls-Royce's transcript digest, not Boeing's.)
findings.source: repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf p.1169 (RR FH1 2012 call 2012-07-26, Mark Morris), p.1050 (RR investor call 2014-06-19), p.91 (RR Investor Day 2023-11-28)
findings.quote: we have 5,000 engines at the point at which we exited IAE that generate a $1 per flying hour going forward (p.1050); In Civil Aerospace, we believe we are well positioned to reenter the narrow-body market. By choosing a partnership approach for the next program (p.91)
findings.unit: GBP billion received for the IAE stake (2012)
findings.use_in_model: Calibrates the missing option value of re-entry. After exit, re-entry is slow (more than 10 years) and partner-dependent, so the option is worth little unless the capability is kept. Also supports a small residual services annuity on the legacy fleet after exit, which shrinks as that fleet retires.

research.summary:
Exits and near-exits from commercial aircraft markets: 27 findings, drawn from repo evidence (B-/BX-/R-/P-/A- ids), the RR earnings-call digest ("Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf", which holds Rolls-Royce calls; the "(4)" digest holds Boeing's 2026 calls) and web search. WebFetch could not reach boeing.mediaroom.com or ftc.gov (host not allowed). Per the tool's instruction I stopped fetching after that, so every web figure comes from search-result snippets of the cited URLs, not from a full read of the document. Weak sources are flagged with low confidence.

What the record shows:
(1) No airframer that fully left large commercial aircraft has ever come back: Convair/GD 1962, Lockheed 1981, Fokker 1996, Douglas 1997, Saab 1997, BAE 2001, Fairchild Dornier 2002, Bombardier 2020. Successor revivals such as the Fokker relaunch attempts and the 2004 Fairchild Dornier restart failed. Rolls-Royce is the only exiter trying to return. It left in 2012, and in 2026 it is still looking for a partner, has spent more than £1bn, needs about £3bn more, and expects no entry before 2035. In the model, the value of an option to re-enter after Boeing's 2060 exit should be about zero.
(2) Once a company stops launching new products, its market share collapses quickly and long before production ends. MDC averaged a 12% share over ten years but took only 3-4% of 1996 orders. It declined a $3bn MD-XX and agreed to merge two months later. In the 757 segment, the A321neo won 71% of orders against 29% for the MAX 9/10. Do Nothing therefore needs a share-decay path, not just a phase-out schedule.
(3) Exiting has a direct cost of roughly 1-3 years of the segment's losses: Boeing's $1.4bn Douglas charge, Saab's SKr4bn provision against SKr3bn of losses, BAE's £250m plus £150m, and Bombardier's retained guarantees.
(4) The installed-base aftermarket outlives the exit by 15-30 years and can be sold. RR sold its IAE stake for $1.5bn plus flight-hour payments of about $300m a year to 2027, booking about £700m of one-off profit. Mitsubishi paid $550m plus about $200m of liabilities for CRJ support, about $0.9M per aircraft in service. Fokker Services survived Fokker. In 2020 the PW4000/PW2000 still provided 20-25% of P&W's aftermarket.
(5) A franchise that never reached scale was worth close to nothing on sale: Bombardier spent about $6bn on the CSeries, then sold control for C$1. New entrants spend $6-72bn and often fail (SpaceJet about ¥1tn, C919 $49-72bn of state support). That puts a floor under the cost of re-entry.
(6) Being in only one segment raised Rolls-Royce's exposure to the 2020 long-haul shock, which ended in a £2bn rights issue. Its executives call narrowbody 71% of volume and 50% of value and say it brings 'customer intimacy'.
(7) Boeing's own practice is to value franchises beyond the first programme (KC-46 as a '50-60 year franchise'; T-X/MQ-25 bids 'not just the initial' contract) and to stay in segments despite large charges (747-8). That supports adding franchise terms to the game's 20-year window.

Terms to add to the model:
(a) Do Nothing: a share-decay hazard on MAX capture, plus a one-off exit charge.
(b) Both branches: the installed-base aftermarket tail, decaying over about 20-25 years after the last delivery. This tail adds value even to Do Nothing beyond 2060.
(c) Re-entry option after a full exit: set to about 0.
(d) A diversification or risk benefit for staying in both segments.
(e) The sale value of the support business at exit, roughly the present value of the tail.

findings.topic: McDonnell Douglas share collapse
findings.claim: Before the merger, MDC averaged about 12% of the large commercial jet market over ten years. By 1996 it took only 3-4% of new orders, against Boeing about 64% and Airbus about 32%. In narrowbodies its share was larger, about 11% (1997 commentary). The share collapsed once Douglas stopped launching new aircraft (MD-12 never sold; MD-XX dropped in 1996).
findings.source: EC decision IV/M.877 Boeing/McDonnell Douglas, 30 Jul 1997 (https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/decisions/m877_19970730_600_fr.pdf); Boeing response to the EC Statement of Objections, 21 May 1997 (https://boeing.mediaroom.com/1997-05-21-Boeing-Responds-to-European-Commission-Statement-of-Objections-to-Merger); FlightGlobal 'Goodnight MDC' (https://flightglobal.com/goodnight-mdc/1805.article); DIW 97-37 (https://www.diw.de/documents/publikationen/73/diw_01.c.964853.de/97-37.pdf)
findings.use_in_model: Calibrate a share-decay hazard for Do Nothing: once the market believes no new product is coming, order share falls to about a third of its historical level within about 4-5 years, well before production ends. Apply it to MAX campaign capture from the year Do Nothing becomes visible, not only through the 2045-60 phase-out.
findings.quote: En moyenne, les parts de marché détenues par Boeing et MDC dans l'EEE au cours des dix dernières années ont atteint 54 % et 12 % respectivement. (EC). Boeing 1997: 'the market share for McDonnell Douglas commercial airplanes had fallen to only four percent of new orders' in 1996.

findings.topic: McDonnell Douglas: declining the next product
findings.claim: In late October 1996 MDC's board cancelled the MD-XX (an MD-11 derivative). The WSJ put the cost at $2bn of development plus $1bn to upgrade Long Beach. MDC said the risks of the $3bn project 'did not merit the required investment' and that it was not leaving the airline business. About seven weeks later (15 Dec 1996) it agreed to be acquired by Boeing.
findings.source: Virginian-Pilot, 29 Oct 1996 (https://scholar.lib.vt.edu/VA-news/VA-Pilot/issues/1996/vp961029/10290269.htm); FlightGlobal 'MDC board terminates MD-XX' (https://flightglobal.com/mdc-board-terminates-md-xx/4438.article); Tampa Bay Times, 16 Dec 1996 (https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1996/12/16/boeing-buys-mcdonnell-douglas/)
findings.use_in_model: A direct precedent for Do Nothing. The company declined a modest next product while saying it would stay in the market, and the independent franchise ended within months. Model the franchise loss as triggered by the decision, not by the end of production.
findings.quote: the risks involved in launching the $3 billion MD-XX project did not merit the required investment

findings.topic: McDonnell Douglas: customers stop counting the exiter
findings.claim: The FTC cleared the merger because Douglas Aircraft was 'no longer a meaningful competitive force'. Airlines testified that Douglas could no longer exert a competitive influence, and the FTC pointed to the 'absence of any prospect of significant commercial sales, combined with a dismal financial forecast'.
findings.source: FTC statement on Boeing/McDonnell Douglas, 1 Jul 1997 (https://www.ftc.gov/node/51578, reached through search only; the host was blocked for fetching); Australian Competition Law case summary (https://australiancompetitionlaw.org/intmergerlaw/cases/boeing.html)
findings.use_in_model: Losing customer relationships is a separate franchise loss: once airlines conclude an OEM has no future product, they stop treating it as a credible bidder, so its pricing power and campaign capture fall. In Do Nothing, scale MAX margin or capture down over time, rather than holding margin flat to 2060.
findings.quote: McDonnell Douglas, looking to the future, no longer constitutes a meaningful competitive force in the commercial aircraft market

findings.topic: McDonnell Douglas: deal value and exit write-off
findings.claim: Boeing paid about $13.3bn in stock (0.65 Boeing shares per MDC share). In January 1998 it took a special $1.4bn pretax Q4 1997 charge on Douglas commercial products, mainly inventory write-downs plus customer-financing adjustments. It limited the MD-80/MD-90 to about mid-1999 and the MD-11 mainly to freighters (final deliveries 2001).
findings.source: Boeing news release, 21 Jan 1998, 'Boeing Announces Special Fourth Quarter Earnings Charge For Douglas Products' (https://boeing.mediaroom.com/1998-01-21-Boeing-Announces-Special-Fourth-Quarter-Earnings-Charge-For-Douglas-Products, from search snippet); Boeing 8-K FY1996 (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000012927/000095015796000483/0000950157-96-000483.txt/seq-2); Boeing Capital 10-K (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/711513/000071151399000008/0000711513-99-000008.txt)
findings.use_in_model: A one-off exit charge for a third-place airframer of about $1.4bn in 1997 dollars, about $2.8bn in 2026 dollars at a CPI factor of about 2.0 (inference). Most of the $13.3bn presumably bought MDC's defence business (inference): the commercial franchise was valued near zero once it had no product pipeline.

findings.topic: Boeing's own segment exit: 717 and the 100-150 seat market
findings.claim: Boeing kept the MD-95 as the 717 after the merger. It announced the end of production in January 2005 and built the last of 156 aircraft in May 2006. Airbus sized the sub-150-seat market at about 6,000 aircraft over 20 years, and it later entered that segment by taking the CSeries for C$1. In 2020 Boeing left the segment uncontested and called it a contest between Embraer and the A220 that would not 'move the market'.
findings.source: Boeing 717 history (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_717); repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-2480 (FQ3 2017 call, p.1357), B-1666 (FQ1 2020 call, p.869); executives BX-0220
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's own history shows that ceding a segment lets a rival fill it cheaply: Airbus acquired an A220 franchise of about 950 aircraft (482 delivered plus 467 backlog, A-0240) for nothing. In the model, an exit should raise the rival's share and margin in adjacent segments.
findings.quote: Embraer's not going away. They're going to fight tooth and nail to win at that low end of the marketplace, and they'll battle Airbus, the former Bombardier... I don't think that's going to move the market in any significant way (B-1666)

findings.topic: Boeing's own segment gap: the 757 / A321 segment
findings.claim: Without a dedicated 757 successor, Boeing's derivative MAX 9/10 won only 29% of high-end narrowbody orders against 71% for the A321neo, out of 2,065 orders by August 2017 (Avolon). In 2016 the A321neo was outselling the MAX 9 by about five to one. Boeing itself conceded the A321's seat advantage. The end of 757 production in 2004 is widely reported but was not verified in this pass.
findings.source: AIN, 31 Aug 2017, 'Avolon sees clear winners, losers in 737 MAX lineup' (https://backend.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2017-08-31/avolon-sees-clear-winners-losers-737-max-lineup); Forecast International, 13 Sep 2016 (https://flightplan.forecastinternational.com/2016/09/13/airbus-takes-lead-in-orders-race-a321neo-outselling-737-max-9-five-to-one/); repo B-1153 / BX-0521 (Investor Day 2016-05-11, p.1629), B-2508 (FQ4 2020 call, p.774)
findings.use_in_model: Calibrates the share Boeing keeps when it competes with an ageing derivative against a newer rival product: about 25-30%. Use it as the floor of Do Nothing MAX share against an Airbus NGSA before the phase-out, rather than a constant share.
findings.quote: Airbus has been very successful with the 321XLR, which can do a lot of the 757 missions and can't really see how the MAX can compete up on those missions. (B-2508, analyst)

findings.topic: Lockheed L-1011: exit and no return
findings.claim: Lockheed needed about 500 sales to break even but sold 250 TriStars. In December 1981 it announced the end of production, with the last delivery in 1984, and it left commercial airliners for good. In 1971 it had needed a $250m federal loan guarantee. Secondary sources put the 1981 write-off at about $26 a share and the total programme loss at about $2.5bn; the $2.5bn is single-sourced.
findings.source: Aussie Airliners (https://aussieairliners.org/l-1011/tristar.html); GAO PSAD-78-66 on the Emergency Loan Guarantee (https://www.gao.gov/assets/./psad-78-66.pdf); Peter Lynch, One Up on Wall Street, notes (https://www.goodreads.com/notes/18832742-one-up-on-wall-street/52261425-eetu-m-ki/1bcb94e2-cb6a-4d06-9b71-cf00015bf89b); PlaneFYI (https://planefyi.com/aircraft/lockheed-l-1011-tristar/)
findings.use_in_model: Evidence that a full airframer exit is permanent: no re-entry in 45 years. Supports setting the value of an option to re-enter after a full exit to about zero. Lockheed survived only because it was diversified into defence.

findings.topic: Convair 880/990: exit and no return
findings.claim: General Dynamics lost about $185m on the Convair 880/990 (some sources say $425m), built only 65 and 37 aircraft, and left airliner design for good.
findings.source: HistoryNet (https://historynet.com/why-convairs-speedy-990-lost-out-to-the-boeing-707/); Convair (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convair); Yesterday's Airlines blog, $425m figure (https://www.yesterdaysairlines.com/airline-history-blog/blue-streak-the-convair-990-american-airlines)
findings.use_in_model: Another permanent exit with no re-entry, adding to the base rate behind a re-entry option value of about zero.

findings.topic: Fokker 1996: bankruptcy, but the aftermarket survived
findings.claim: Daimler-Benz ended its support on 22 Jan 1996 and Fokker went bankrupt on 15 Mar 1996, with 5,664 jobs lost. DASA booked a DM2.3bn charge for its Fokker investment. Stork bought the healthy parts, including Fokker Services, which went on supporting the F70/F100 fleet. Rekkof's attempts to relaunch the F70/F100 never reached production; whether they definitively failed is not confirmed.
findings.source: FlightGlobal 'A brief history of Fokker' (https://flightglobal.com/a-brief-history-of-fokker/9972.article); Deseret News, 15 Mar 1996 (https://www.deseret.com/1996/3/15/19230772/filing-of-bankruptcy-grounds-dutch-airplane-manufacturer/); Stork B.V. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stork_B.V.); FlightGlobal on Rekkof (https://www.flightglobal.com/rekkof-ready-to-resurrect-fokker-jet-line/23271.article)
findings.use_in_model: Two lessons. First, support and aftermarket units keep their value after the OEM exits, so tail value is separable and saleable. Second, a pure-play airframer's exit ends in bankruptcy and revival attempts fail. Include an installed-base tail value in Do Nothing beyond 2060, separate from new-aircraft profit.

findings.topic: Saab 1997: regional exit and its tail liabilities
findings.claim: On 15 Dec 1997 Saab's board ended 340/2000 production. The programmes had lost about SKr3bn over three years. Saab set an SKr4bn after-tax provision for restructuring, servicing the existing fleet and honouring lease commitments, with liabilities on 296 aircraft rising to 326, and still owed about SKr1.5bn to the state.
findings.source: FlightGlobal 'Saab decides to terminate turboprop products' (https://www.flightglobal.com/saab-decides-to-terminate-turboprop-products/18893.article); Aviation Week (https://aviationweek.com/saab-considers-ending-production-saab-340-2000-turboprops)
findings.use_in_model: Leaving carries a tail liability for fleet support, residual values and leases. Here it was about 1.3x the segment's three-year operating losses. Add a one-off exit liability to Do Nothing at the phase-out.
findings.unit: SKr bn after-tax provision (vs SKr3bn 3-yr losses)
findings.quote: A provision of SKr4 billion after tax ... to cover restructuring costs, servicing the existing fleet, and honouring leasing commitments

findings.topic: BAE 2001: regional jet exit
findings.claim: BAE Systems cancelled the Avro RJX on 27 Nov 2001 and ended RJ production (173 RJs delivered 1993-2003). It took a £250m exceptional charge, with £210m of cash closure costs (£145m after tax), plus a further £150m restructuring and support charge for other commercial aerospace activities.
findings.source: BAE Systems trading update, Nov 2001 (https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/bae-systems--ba./trading-update-/335893); Asia Travel Tips, 27 Nov 2001 (https://www.asiatraveltips.com/travelnews2001/27November2001BAE.htm); BAE Systems Regional Aircraft (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAE_Systems_Regional_Aircraft)
findings.use_in_model: Exit-charge calibration for a small airframer: about £400m in total, mostly cash. BAE kept a regional aircraft support business, again showing the tail value can be separated.
findings.quote: Regrettably it has been concluded that our regional jet business is no longer viable in this environment.

findings.topic: Fairchild Dornier 2002: insolvency and failed revival
findings.claim: Fairchild Dornier filed for insolvency in April 2002, days after the first 728 rollout, with about $670m of debt. It had underestimated 728 development, earlier put at about $500m, and held 125 firm orders. Lufthansa and GECAS cancelled. The 328JET went to AvCraft, and the successor that tried to revive the 728 became insolvent in 2004.
findings.source: Aviation Strategy, Apr 2002 (https://aviationstrategy.aero/newsletter/Apr-2002/3/Fairchild-Dornier's-insolvency:an-RJ-duopoly-now); FlightGlobal 'Insolvency hits 728 once more' (https://flightglobal.com/insolvency-hits-728-once-more/55103.article); Fairchild Dornier 728 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Dornier_728_family)
findings.use_in_model: Order books disappear on exit: firm orders are cancelled once the OEM's future is in doubt. Revivals by successor companies failed. Supports a near-zero option to re-enter and a backlog-erosion term in Do Nothing.

findings.topic: Bombardier CSeries: sunk about $6bn, sold control for C$1
findings.claim: CSeries development cost grew from $3.4bn (2008) to $5.4bn (2015), about $6bn in total. Bombardier took a $3.2bn charge in Q3 2015, inside a $4.9bn quarterly loss, and Quebec put in US$1bn for 49.5%. In Oct 2017 Airbus took 50.01% for 'no cash consideration' (a symbolic C$1). In Feb 2020 Bombardier sold its remaining stake for $591m ($531m plus about $60m), avoiding about $700m of future investment, after a $1.6bn impairment on the partnership in 2019.
findings.source: Leeham, 29 Oct 2015 (https://leehamnews.com/2015/10/29/bombardier-3-2bn-charge-1bn-from-quebec/); CTV (https://www.ctvnews.ca/business/bombardier-says-cseries-delays-pushing-program-cost-up-to-us-4-4b-1.1684187); Globe and Mail (https://beta.theglobeandmail.com/report-on-business/bombardier-sells-majority-stake-in-c-series-to-airbus/article36610340/); CNBC, 16 Oct 2017 (https://www.cnbc.com/2017/10/16/airbus-teams-up-with-bombardier-on-c-series-program.html); Bombardier FY2019 release, 13 Feb 2020 (https://bombardier.com/node/2010393); CBC (https://www.cbc.ca/1.5462182)
findings.use_in_model: A franchise that never reached scale was worth about nothing even after $6bn of spending. Value went to the incumbent that had the distribution (Airbus). This puts a floor of about $6bn plus a high failure risk on the cost of any later Boeing re-entry. It also shows that sunk development is not recovered on exit.
findings.quote: Exit of commercial aerospace completed with sale of remaining interest in A220 partnership for ~$600M cash proceeds and the elimination of future investments of ~ $700M (Bombardier, 13 Feb 2020)

findings.topic: Bombardier CRJ sale: market price of an out-of-production aftermarket franchise
findings.claim: MHI paid about $550m in cash and took on about $200m of liabilities for the CRJ programme: maintenance, support, refurbishment, marketing, sales and the type certificates, but no production rights. Bombardier kept credit and residual-value guarantees of $288m at closing (1 Jun 2020). Cirium counted about 820 CRJs in operation in 2020.
findings.source: CBC (https://www.cbc.ca/1.5188779); Bombardier closing release (https://www.aviationpros.com/aircraft-maintenance-technology/aircraft-technology/business-general-aviation/press-release/21140385/bombardier-aerospace-bombardier-concludes-sale-of-the-crj-series-regional-jet-program-to-mitsubishi-heavy-industries); AIN (https://ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2020-05-07/mitsubishi-close-crj-acquisition-june-1)
findings.use_in_model: Inference: about $750m of enterprise value over about 820 active aircraft is roughly $0.9M per aircraft in service for a support franchise with no new production. Use it to size the installed-base tail value, or the sale value of a support business at exit, scaled up for 737 size and utilisation.

findings.topic: Mitsubishi SpaceJet: the cost of building capability from scratch
findings.claim: MHI ended SpaceJet on 7 Feb 2023 after about ¥1tn (about $7.6bn) of development, without a single delivery. It blamed an 'insufficient initial understanding of the complex type certification process' and a lack of money for long-term development. Losses included ¥263.3bn in FY2019 (with ¥122.4bn of impairment of capitalised assets) and an ¥80.6bn impairment in FY2021. The unit (MSJ) had ¥641.3bn of debt in March 2024. MHI kept the CRJ support business.
findings.source: MHI notice, 7 Feb 2023 (https://mhi.com/notice/notice_230207.html); AirInsight (https://airinsight.com/mitsubishi-discloses-full-impairment-on-spacejet/); ch-aviation (https://www.ch-aviation.com/news/124254-mitsubishi-confirms-spacejet-program-termination); Aviation Week (https://aviationweek.com/mro/services-support/spacejet-axe-leaves-mitsubishi-crj-support); AirDataNews (https://airdatanews.com/mitsubishi-continues-to-make-losses-even-with-spacejet-program-frozen)
findings.use_in_model: An entrant without an engineering and certification base spent about $7.6bn and failed. Losing Boeing's narrowbody engineering and certification base after an exit would make any re-entry face similar costs and a low chance of success. Use it in the re-entry option, with a success probability well below 1.

findings.topic: Airbus A380: exiting a sub-segment while staying in the market
findings.claim: In Feb 2019 Airbus ended the A380 after Emirates cut its order from 162 to 123, saying it had no substantial backlog and hence no basis to keep producing. It booked a net -€463m EBIT impact in FY2018. Investment was about €25bn by analyst estimates (Airbus published €15bn in 2015), against 400-600 sales needed to break even; 251 were delivered. Governments had lent more than €3.3bn. Airbus expects the fleet to stay in service well into the next decade.
findings.source: Airbus FY2018 results release (https://www.airbus.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2019-02-airbus-reports-strong-full-year-2018-results-delivers-on-guidance); AFP via TechXplore (https://techxplore.com/news/2019-02-airbus-costly-a380-superjumbo.html); Bloomberg, 8 Mar 2019 (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-03-08/european-taxpayers-face-hard-landing-from-airbus-a380-s-demise); repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/airbus/evidence.jsonl A-0257 (Airbus Board Report FY2025, p.17)
findings.use_in_model: The exit write-off was small compared with the sunk cost (€463m against about €25bn) because Airbus stayed in widebodies through the A350/A330, keeping its engineering base and customer access. The contrast with full exits: leaving a niche costs little, while leaving the core market costs the franchise. Do not treat the A380 as an analogue for Boeing leaving narrowbodies.
findings.quote: While the final five deliveries of the A380 took place during 2021, some customer airlines are investing in updating their cabins, and the aircraft is likely to remain in service well into the next decade. (A-0257)

findings.topic: Rolls-Royce IAE exit: sale terms
findings.claim: RR sold its 32.5% IAE equity and programme share to P&W for $1.5bn plus a payment for each hour flown by the V2500 fleet in service at completion, for 15 years (to June 2027). It stayed on as a manufacturing supplier (high-pressure compressors, fan blades and discs, final assembly of 50% of engines). P&W then launched the A320neo GTF in IAE LLC without RR.
findings.source: RR press release, 29 Jun 2012 (https://www.rolls-royce.com/media/press-releases-archive/yr-2012/120629-restructuring-iae.aspx); SEC exhibit, Oct 2011 (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/101829/000119312511273891/d244967dex991.htm); repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/rolls_royce/evidence.jsonl R-1891 (RTX 10-K FY2023 p.128), R-1826, R-1892
findings.use_in_model: A template for exit by sale: the exiting partner capitalises its share of the installed base (upfront payment plus usage-linked earn-out) but gives up the next-generation position for nothing. In the model, an exit can recover the present value of the aftermarket tail but not the franchise.
findings.quote: Rolls-Royce shall receive an agreed payment for each hour flown by the current installed fleet of V2500-powered aircraft for 15 years from completion of the transaction.

findings.topic: Rolls-Royce IAE exit: realised value and annual tail
findings.claim: The deal brought about $1.5bn (about £940m) of proceeds and about £700m of one-off profit. RR guided about £140m a year from the revised trading arrangements and booked £92m in the second half of 2012. Morgan Stanley models the V2500 royalty at $388m (2015), $300m (2019), $100m (2020), $325m (2024) and $250m (2027e), falling to zero from 1H28e, at an 80% margin.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf p.1134 (RR Fixed Income Call, 14 Feb 2013) and p.1144; repo R-1709 (Morgan Stanley RR model, 28 Jan 2026, analyst estimate)
findings.use_in_model: Inference: about $300m a year for the hours of about 5,000 engines is roughly $60-65k per engine per year paid to a non-producing ex-partner. Together with the $1.5bn upfront, about $5-6bn nominal over 2012-27. Calibrates the size and decay of an installed-base tail term (roughly flat for about 15 years, then zero as the contract ends or the fleet retires).
findings.unit: $B proceeds / £bn proceeds / £bn one-off profit; $B per year royalty
findings.quote: we concluded the IAE transaction at the half-year, resulted in about a $1.5 billion of proceeds or GBP 940 million or so ... and profits -- the one-off profits at the time of about GBP 700 million.

findings.topic: Rolls-Royce: the installed base is where the value lies
findings.claim: RR's executives said the IAE sale showed that the installed base holds most of a business's value, and that the market had undervalued it.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf p.899 (RR FY2014 Earnings Call, 13 Feb 2015) and p.1050 (RR Investor Day, 19 Jun 2014)
findings.use_in_model: Supports adding an explicit installed-base (aftermarket) value term, which the game lacks. The fps creates a new installed base after 2035; Do Nothing lets the MAX base decay from the 2040s. The gap in installed-base value is a franchise term.
findings.quote: our installed base grows year-by-year, and this is where the majority of the value of the business lies. This is demonstrated, I think, quite clearly when we sold our stake in IAE, when, I know, many of you were surprised by the value we've realized for what was just one small component of the Civil aerospace business. (p.899) / the value ... generally was assumed by the market for our IAE business was a little lower than we actually realized. And that, again, is the installed value (p.1050)

findings.topic: Rolls-Royce: why it exited and what it lost
findings.claim: RR left because it had resources for only three of four new engines (Trent 900, 1000 and XWB, not the neo) and because the partners were no longer aligned. Its executives later valued narrowbody at about 71% of volume and 50% of value, and said being in both segments gives deeper 'customer intimacy'. In 2015 the new CEO said 'we don't have to be in narrow-body'.
findings.source: repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/pratt_whitney/evidence.jsonl P-2000 (RR Investor Day, 19 Jun 2014, p.1030); repo rolls_royce/evidence.jsonl R-0318, R-1350 (Investor Day 2014, p.1030), R-0952 (Nov 2015, p.768), R-0310 (FH1 2011, p.1228)
findings.use_in_model: Being in both segments has customer and engineering value. Model it as a small capture or margin uplift on the remaining widebody products when Boeing stays in narrowbody (the cross-sell term the game lacks), and as a loss under Do Nothing. Size is not quantified (inference).
findings.quote: It's about 71% of the volume and about 50% of the value. ... Customer intimacy: If we're only talking about wide body, it's just part of it. If you're talking about the whole wide and narrow, it's -- you're much more into it with your customer. (R-1350) / we've only got the resources to do 3 of the 4 ... So getting out of IAE was a consequence of the earlier decision. (P-2000)

findings.topic: Rolls-Royce: single-segment exposure in a shock
findings.claim: With no narrowbody engine, RR's aftermarket was mostly widebody and long-haul. In 2020 it raised about £2bn through a rights issue plus new loans as large-engine flying hours collapsed. Its remaining narrowbody income, the IAE royalty, fell only 'very roughly 50%', and RR noted that short-haul recovers before long-haul.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf p.311 (RR FY2020 Earnings Call, 11 Mar 2021); repo R-1253 (Trading Statement Dec 2021, p.245); Business Standard, 27 Oct 2020 (https://www.business-standard.com/amp/article/international/rolls-royce-rescue-plan-flies-as-shareholders-back-2-bn-pound-rights-issue-120102701126_1.html)
findings.use_in_model: Staying in both segments diversifies risk: narrowbody cash recovers first in a downturn. In the game, a lower debt penalty or discount-rate premium for the two-segment Boeing (fps), against a widebody-only Boeing after 2060 under Do Nothing (inference).
findings.quote: IAE royalties simply pretty good reflection of the flying hours for that V2500 engine. And so in 2020, very roughly, 50% down. ... Don't forget that this is effectively a single-aisle. It's a short-haul aircraft. Short-haul recovers before long-haul.

findings.topic: Rolls-Royce re-entry: cost and timing
findings.claim: Fourteen years after exiting, RR said it was 'well positioned to reenter the narrow-body market' through a partnership (Nov 2023). By Feb 2026 it had spent more than £1bn on UltraFan and was seeking partners for the £3bn UltraFan 30 development. Ground tests of the demonstrator are planned for 2028, with no entry into service before about 2035, about 23 years after the exit. RR's game calibration puts narrowbody re-entry at $7.5B, including $4-5B of industrialisation from zero.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf p.91 (RR Capital Markets Day, 28 Nov 2023); Leeham, 26 Feb 2026 (https://leehamnews.com/2026/02/26/rolls-royce-boosts-mid-term-targets-ceo-dismisses-ultrafan-loan-speculation/); RR press release, 17 Mar 2026 (https://www.rolls-royce.com/media/press-releases/2026/17-03-2026-rr-secures-euro-64m-to-advance-ultrafan-30-demonstrator-through-unified-partnership.aspx); repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/rolls_royce/calibration.md row programs.uf_nb.capex_b; repo R-1011
findings.use_in_model: Re-entry costs: (a) more than 20 years of absence; (b) development plus industrialisation from zero, about 2-3x the development bill alone (calibration inference); (c) a partner needed, which halves the value. For Boeing after a 2060 exit, discount any re-entry option heavily: about zero within the game horizon.
findings.quote: In Civil Aerospace, we believe we are well positioned to reenter the narrow-body market. By choosing a partnership approach for the next program, our UltraFan technology is a vital step towards this. At the right time, with the right partner, we will decide the next steps. (p.91)

findings.topic: Pratt & Whitney: exiting widebody by harvesting it
findings.claim: P&W lost the 787 contest in 2004 and has no engine on any new-generation widebody (787, A350, A330neo, 777X). Its CEO later admitted it 'passed on' the 787, under-invested and 'over-earned' on aftermarket. In 2020 the legacy PW4000/PW2000 still provided 20-25% of P&W's aftermarket and was 'highly profitable'. P&W expected most of that fleet to retire within a couple of years. A GTF-derived widebody engine planned in 2019 for the mid-2020s was never built.
findings.source: repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/pratt_whitney/evidence.jsonl P-1125 (Barclays, Feb 2016, p.1778), P-0403 (BofA, May 2020, p.856), P-0409 (UBS, Jun 2020, p.843), P-0945 (Laguna, Sep 2020, p.810), P-1842 / P-1839 (Noealt 2019 brief); pratt_whitney/calibration.md programs.pw_wb.dev_years; InsideFlyer (https://www.insideflyer.com/posts/pratt-and-whitney-exits-widebody-engine-market/)
findings.use_in_model: The harvest profile of an exit: Do Nothing shows higher near-term earnings (no development spending) and an aftermarket tail lasting about 30 years after the last new programme (PW4000 entered service in 1987), then a permanent loss of the next-generation position. Re-entry plans tend not to be carried out (P&W). Model Do Nothing cash as front-loaded with a decaying tail after 2060, not cut off at 2060.
findings.unit: % of P&W aftermarket from legacy widebody/757 engines (2020)
findings.quote: back in the 2000s, Pratt was over-earning because it was all aftermarket and there was no new product being developed, right? We did not build an engine for the 787, right? We passed on that... we under-invested at Pratt for a long time. (P-1125)

findings.topic: Pratt & Whitney: the buyer of an exiting share pays away the margin
findings.claim: After buying RR's IAE share, P&W's V2500 aftermarket margins ran below those of its older engines (JT8D, JT9D, PW4000) because of the flight-hour payments to RR and the related intangible amortisation. P&W capitalises those payments as collaboration assets.
findings.source: repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/pratt_whitney/evidence.jsonl P-0296 (UTC Q4 2017 call, p.1352), P-1723 (RTX 10-K FY2021, p.348)
findings.use_in_model: An exit sale transfers roughly the present value of the aftermarket tail to the buyer. For Boeing, selling the 737 support business at exit would realise that tail value once, not keep a franchise. Model 'exit by sale' as present value of the tail minus a buyer's margin.
findings.quote: the traditional old margin rates on aftermarket that we used to get on JT8Ds, JT9Ds or PW4000s was much higher than what we expect to get on V2500, first of all, because there is the payment to Rolls-Royce that we have for buying over their portion of the business

findings.topic: Embraer: a transaction price for a commercial franchise
findings.claim: In 2019 Boeing agreed to pay $4.2bn for 80% of Embraer's commercial aviation business, implying about $5.25bn for 100%. It terminated the deal in April 2020 and settled the arbitration in Sept 2024 for $150m. BofA called this about half of the termination costs Embraer's management had estimated.
findings.source: ch-aviation (https://www.ch-aviation.com/news/144833-boeing-settles-failed-commercial-aviation-jv-with-embraer); AirDataNews (https://airdatanews.com/boeing-to-pay-usdollar150-million-to-embraer-after-failed-joint-venture); TipRanks/BofA (https://www.tipranks.com/news/the-fly/embraer-award-from-boeing-disappointing-but-reaction-overdone-says-bofa)
findings.use_in_model: A market price for a third-ranked commercial OEM with a full product line, installed base and engineering team: about $5bn. As a floor (inference), the narrowbody capability Boeing would give up under Do Nothing is worth far more than a regional franchise.

findings.topic: COMAC C919: the cost of entering narrowbodies from scratch
findings.claim: CSIS counted RMB328.5bn ($49bn) of identified state support to COMAC and up to $72.1bn of potential support through 2020. The C919's announced ¥58bn development budget was estimated to have ended up above ¥125bn (about $20bn).
findings.source: CSIS, 'China's COMAC: An Aerospace Minor Leaguer', Dec 2020 (https://www.csis.org/blogs/trustee-china-hand/chinas-comac-aerospace-minor-leaguer); Comac C919 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comac_C919)
findings.use_in_model: An upper bound for rebuilding narrowbody capability after it is lost: $20-72bn and more than 15 years, even with a captive home market. Implies Boeing's option to re-enter after 2060 is worth near zero, while keeping the capability (fps) avoids that cost. The estimates are think-tank figures, not audited.

findings.topic: Boeing's revealed preference: stay in, and value franchises beyond the first programme
findings.claim: Boeing has repeatedly taken large losses rather than leave a segment. The 747-8 drew reach-forward losses of $685m (4Q08), $1.35bn (2009) and $885m (4Q15), and Boeing said 'We don't intend to kill the program', though it later admitted keeping the 747 alive 'maybe too long'. Its executives justify upfront losses by franchise life: KC-46 as a '50-, 60-year widebody franchise'; T-X/MQ-25 bids counting 'the considerable market potential ... not just the initial' contract; and the 737 and 777 called 'franchise programs'.
findings.source: repo /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-0168 (10-K FY2008 p.851), B-0563 (10-K FY2011 p.1215), B-1108 (10-K FY2015 p.662), B-0192 (FQ1 2009 call p.2834), B-2522 (Bernstein, Jun 2022, p.550), B-2397 (Investor Conference 2011-05-24 p.2605); boeing/executives/evidence.jsonl BX-1033 (Investor Day 2016-05-11 p.1629), BX-1545 (FQ3 2018 call p.1150)
