findings.use_in_model: Boeing's own valuation practice includes franchise and follow-on value beyond a single programme's 20-year window. Adding terminal and franchise terms to the fps valuation is consistent with how Boeing values bids and programmes; the game's 20-year cut-off is not.
findings.quote: So this is a 50-, 60-year widebody franchise. And that's the way we think about it in terms of our company strategy. (BX-1033) / we are taking into account the considerable market potential in our business cases and not just the ini[tial] (BX-1545)

findings.topic: Synthesis: base rates for exits (inference)
findings.claim: No airframer that fully left large commercial aircraft ever returned: Convair/GD (1962), Lockheed (1981), Fokker (1996), Douglas (1997), Saab (1997), BAE (2001), Fairchild Dornier (2002), Bombardier (2020). Diversified exiters survived by retreating to defence or business jets, pure plays went bankrupt, and Douglas was absorbed. Only Rolls-Royce, an engine maker, is attempting a return, more than 14 years later and with a partner. Exit charges were roughly 1-3 years of the segment's losses. Installed-base support kept its value and was sold or kept (Fokker Services, CRJ to MHI, IAE royalty, BAE regional support).
findings.source: Inference from the findings above (EC M.877; FTC; Boeing 1998 release; FlightGlobal Saab/Fokker; BAE trading update 2001; Bombardier 13 Feb 2020 release; MHI notice 7 Feb 2023; RR digest p.91/p.1134; repo R-1709, P-1125)
findings.use_in_model: Parameter suggestions for the franchise terms: (1) re-entry option after a full exit about 0; (2) a Do Nothing share-decay hazard (MDC: about 12% to 3-4% of orders within about 5 years once no product is credible; 757 segment: 29% share against a newer rival); (3) an exit charge of about $1.5-3bn in 2026 dollars at the phase-out (scaled from the Douglas, Saab and BAE cases); (4) an installed-base tail that keeps decaying after the last delivery over about 20-25 years, credited to both branches (Do Nothing's MAX tail after 2060 and the fps's new base); (5) a diversification or risk benefit for staying in both segments.

findings.topic: Terminal value conventions: Airbus DCF (repo)
findings.claim: The Goldman Sachs Airbus DCF does not stop at a fixed programme horizon. It forecasts explicitly to 2031E, extends group EBIT by formula to 2036E (7% growth tapering to 3%), then adds a perpetuity, all at a 9% nominal discount rate. The result is 240 EUR a share.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/airbus/analyst_models_2026.md line 111 and line 127 [GS DCF Valuation r7, r14, r21, r38, r39, r51]
findings.quote: its DCF gives 240 EUR per share and runs group adjusted EBIT out to 18,820m in 2036E by formula (7% growth tapering to 3%, 9% discount rate)
findings.use_in_model: Analyst convention is an explicit period, then a fade, then a Gordon perpetuity. Replace the game's hard cutoff at fps EIS+20 with TV = CF(EIS+21)/(r-g). In constant 2026 dollars, use g of 0-1% real (3% nominal less 2.2% CPI).

findings.topic: Terminal value share of EV in aerospace DCFs (repo)
findings.claim: In the GS Rolls-Royce DCF, about 64% of enterprise value is terminal value beyond 2036, at an 8.46% discount rate and 3% long-term growth. In sell-side aerospace valuations most of the value sits after the explicit horizon.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/rolls_royce/analyst_models_2026.md line 90 [GS DCF Valuation D18-D48]
findings.quote: using an 8.46% discount rate (its cost of equity, with a 100% equity weight) and 3% long-term growth. About 64% of enterprise value (GBP 85.9bn) is terminal value beyond 2036
findings.use_in_model: Sanity check: a valuation that drops everything after year 20 (as the game does for fps) would leave out roughly two-thirds of what analysts count for an aerospace franchise. Report the fps decision with and without a terminal term.

findings.topic: Morningstar moat-based horizon convention
findings.claim: Morningstar values companies with a three-stage DCF: an explicit forecast, a fade, then a perpetuity. A wide-moat firm (Morningstar rates Boeing wide moat, on duopoly, intangibles and switching costs) is assumed to earn excess returns for at least 20 years. In the perpetuity stage, return on new invested capital equals WACC, so new investment creates no value but existing cash flows go on forever. One Boeing note uses an 8.6% WACC.
findings.source: Morningstar Equity Research Methodology (https://s21.q4cdn.com/198919461/files/doc_downloads/press_kits/2014/MorningstarEquityResearch_Methodology.pdf; https://advisor.morningstar.com/Enterprise/VTC/MasterEquityResearchMethodology_Oct2020.pdf); Boeing notes at https://www.morningstar.com/stocks/after-earnings-is-boeing-stock-buy-sell-or-fairly-valued-8 and https://global.morningstar.com/en-gb/stocks/after-earnings-is-boeing-stock-buy-sell-or-fairly-valued (seen via WebSearch extracts only)
findings.quote: In general, we assume narrow-moat companies can earn excess returns on capital for at least 15 years, while wide-moat companies can earn excess returns on capital for at least 20 years.
findings.number: 20 years excess returns; WACC 8.6%; fair value $238-249/share
findings.use_in_model: Franchise term for 'Continue': after the fade, count a perpetuity of steady-state narrowbody NOPAT with zero excess return on new capital. For 'Exit' (Do Nothing to 2060), the perpetuity is zero. The 8.6% WACC was seen in a search extract only, not in the full note.

findings.topic: Share of Boeing value in the 737 franchise
findings.claim: Morningstar estimates, in several notes from 2025-2026, that half of Boeing's enterprise value comes from the 737 product line. This is an analyst estimate, not a company figure.
findings.source: Morningstar Boeing stock notes, e.g. https://www.morningstar.com/stocks/after-earnings-is-boeing-stock-buy-sell-or-fairly-valued-9 and https://www.morningstar.com/stocks/boeing-earnings-turnaround-is-nearly-there (via WebSearch extracts)
findings.quote: We estimate that half of Boeing's enterprise value is derived from its 737 product line.
findings.use_in_model: Anchor for the size of the franchise term (inference): 50% of the board's Boeing EV of $130B (combined_dash.py line 878) is about $65B. That is the same size as the $60-65B fps bill. Losing the narrowbody line by 2060 should therefore cost on the order of the whole bill, which the current 20-year window does not register.

findings.topic: PV of the whole narrowbody industry and value per share point
findings.claim: Barclays (October 2019) put the present value of the total narrowbody industry at $238B, so that a 50/50 split was worth 140 EUR a share to Airbus, 20% above the share price then. Barclays also expected the A321 family alone to contribute about 3.4B EUR of free cash flow over five years.
findings.source: CNBC, 15 Oct 2019, https://www.cnbc.com/2019/10/15/barclays-time-to-buy-airbus-as-it-will-be-more-cash-rich-than-boeing.html (also RT and eTurboNews reprints); sell-side analyst estimate reported in press
findings.quote: We estimate the present value of the total narrowbody industry at $238 billion, which implies that a 50/50 split is worth 140 euros per share to Airbus
findings.use_in_model: Value of one point of narrowbody share is about $2.4B (2019 $), or about $3.1B in 2026 $ at roughly 29% CPI uplift (inference). A 50% share is worth about $119B (2019 $). Use this to check a share-point value: one point of share times $2.4-3.1B, scaled to the game's margins.

findings.topic: Discount rate gap between the game and analysts (inference)
findings.claim: The game discounts constant-2026-dollar (real) flows at 10.5% (WACC_B = 0.105). At 2.2% CPI that is about 12.9% nominal. Analysts use about 8-10% nominal: Morningstar Boeing 8.6%, GS Airbus 9%, GS Rolls-Royce 8.46%, independent Boeing DCFs 8-10% with 2.5-3% terminal growth. That is about 6.3-6.7% real. The gap almost erases any distant franchise value. $1 a year in perpetuity from 2062 is worth $0.29 in 2026 at 10.5% real, against $1.58-1.91 at 6.3-6.7% real. For fps-level profit of about $7.05B a year (500 aircraft x $55M x 25.64%), the perpetuity after 2061 is worth about $2.0B at 10.5% against about $13.4B at 6.3%.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/dashgame/board/combined_dash.py lines 711, 884-909 (WACC_B, prices, margins); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/analyst_models_2026.md line 96 (2.2% CPI); vcpscanner.com/valuation/ba/dcf (8.9% WACC, 3% terminal growth); discountingcashflows.com BA model (about 7.95% WACC)
findings.use_in_model: Run the franchise terms at two rates: the game's 10.5% and an analyst-consistent real rate of about 6.5% (9% nominal less 2.2%). Report how much of the fps-versus-Do-Nothing gap comes from the discount rate alone. The arithmetic is computed and is inference.

findings.topic: Market-implied perpetuity in Boeing price targets
findings.claim: Sell-side Boeing targets are mostly set on a multiple of normalised free cash flow, not a finite programme life. One analyst's $275 target applies 22.5x to about $10B of 2028E FCF (the firm is not named in the extract). BofA's $190 rests on about $10 a share of 2026 FCF. The average 12-month target was about $267 in October 2026, against a share price of about $188.
findings.source: Finviz summary https://finviz.com/news/290503/why-boeing-is-emerging-as-the-ultimate-recovery-play ; TipRanks/TheFly BofA note https://www.tipranks.com/news/the-fly/boeing-price-target-lowered-to-190-from-210-at-bofa ; beinsure https://beinsure.com/news/boeing-stock-forecast/ (WebSearch extracts)
findings.use_in_model: At 8.6-9% WACC, a 22.5x FCF multiple implies perpetual nominal FCF growth of about 4.2-4.6% (inference: g = WACC - 1/22.5). The market prices Boeing as a going concern with a permanent narrowbody franchise. A 'Do Nothing = exit by 2060' path contradicts the market's base case and would carry a re-rating loss not captured in the game.

findings.topic: Programme accounting horizons: blocks of about 10 years, extended in steps
findings.claim: Boeing sizes a programme's accounting block to firm orders plus market potential, typically about 10 years of output. Initial blocks are about 400 for new models and 1,000-1,100 for the 787 (787: 1,100 units against a 5,000-unit addressable market). Blocks are then extended as orders arrive: the 737 got +600 in 2011, +200 in 2012 and 2014, and +800 in 2023, reaching 11,600 at end-2023 with 4,332 still on firm order. Extensions depend on how much of the next block is sold.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-0087, B-0476, B-0571, B-0334, B-0671, B-0945, B-0617, B-2117, B-2118
findings.quote: we estimate the addressable market for the 787 class of airplanes at 5,000 units. At current plan production rates, the initial quantity of 1,100 units represents approximately 10 years of production. (B-0476, CFO Bell, FQ3 2011)
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's own valuation horizon is a sequence of roughly 10-year blocks, each extension conditional on orders. That is a rolling option to continue, not a 20-year hard stop. Model 'Continue' as block extensions after fps EIS+20 with a probability tied to share. Model Do Nothing as letting the 737 block run out with no successor block.

findings.topic: Boeing treats a derivative as continuation of one franchise
findings.claim: Boeing put the 737 MAX into the same accounting quantity as the NG, so the franchise is valued as one continuing programme. UBS (2012) estimated NG margins of about 20% before R&D across the block and an MAX break-even of about 200 units, with MAX folded into the NG block.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-0708 (10-K FY2012 p.31), B-0671 (FQ3 2012 call); Leeham News 14 Jun 2012 'UBS estimates MAX break-even at 200' https://leehamnews.com/2012/06/14/6191/ (analyst estimate via WebSearch extract)
findings.quote: The accounting quantity for the 737 program includes NG and MAX units. (B-0708)
findings.number: about 20% NG pre-R&D margin; MAX break-even about 200 units
findings.use_in_model: Attach the franchise term to the 737 lineage, not to fps alone. If fps launches, the franchise continues (block-extension value after the horizon). If not, the lineage ends with the MAX phase-out in 2045-2060. The game's 8% 737 margin (combined_dash.py line 908) is well below historical block margins of about 20%, an input to flag.

findings.topic: Exit under programme accounting: wind-down charges and fixed-cost loading
findings.claim: Boeing told investors that ending a line at the end of its block is financially immaterial: the 747 ended in 2022-23 and the 767F was set to end in 2027. But each step down cost a reach-forward charge: the 747 took $885M (2015), $70M and $1,188M (2016), and the 767F $398M + $182M (2024). Cutting the 737 rate to 42 a month added about $1B because fixed costs for the 3,100-aircraft block were spread over a longer period.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-1499, B-1639, B-2121, B-1235, B-2246, B-1543
findings.quote: The additional costs are due to the lower production rate causing fixed costs for the 3,100 aircraft in the block to be amortized over a longer period of time. (B-1543, CFO Smith, FQ1 2019)
findings.use_in_model: The MAX phase-out 2045-2060 under Do Nothing should carry wind-down charges as the rate falls (inference: about $1B per large rate step at 737 scale), plus the overhead term below. Book them in the Do Nothing column.

findings.topic: Overhead absorption: what idle narrowbody capacity costs
findings.claim: Boeing's 10-K says a large part of commercial aircraft production cost is infrastructure that does not vary with rate. When the MAX line was suspended and slowed, Boeing expected about $4.0B, later about $5.0B, of abnormal production costs for 2020-21, expensed as incurred, on top of $6.3B added to programme cost. GS counts unabsorbed overhead of $1.1-3.7B a year in 2019-2023.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-0164 (10-K FY2008 p.850), B-1650 (10-K FY2019 p.517), B-1675 (FQ1 2020); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/analyst_models_2026.md line 70 [GS BA BCA margin r88]
findings.quote: Commercial aircraft production costs include a significant amount of infrastructure costs, a portion of which do not vary with production rates. (B-0164)
findings.number: $4-5B abnormal costs over about 2 years; $1.1-3.7B a year unabsorbed overhead
findings.use_in_model: Add an overhead-absorption penalty to Do Nothing. As narrowbody volume runs off in 2045-2060, the share of BCA fixed infrastructure that the 737 carried falls on the widebody and BGS lines until it is cut. Suggested size (inference): $1-3B a year (2026 $), phasing in with the MAX phase-out and declining as capacity is cut over about 5 years.

findings.topic: Boeing's revealed practice: value franchises on full multi-decade potential
findings.claim: Boeing has repeatedly priced bids and programmes on the whole franchise, not the first contract. KC-46 was framed as a '50-, 60-year widebody franchise' with a market of about 400 aircraft against 179 on contract. The T-X and MQ-25 bids took a $541M after-tax charge, justified by 'considerable market potential... not just the initial order quantity'. In 2011 Boeing counted the 737 and 777 as its two 'franchise programs' that fund the company.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/executives/evidence.jsonl BX-1033 (Investor Day 2016-05-11 p.1629), BX-1545 (FQ3 2018 call p.1150); evidence.jsonl B-1458, B-2397 (Albaugh, 2011-05-24 p.2605)
findings.quote: we're going to build at least 179. We think the market's more like 400. ... So this is a 50-, 60-year widebody franchise. And that's the way we think about it in terms of our company strategy. (BX-1033, Muilenburg)
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's own business cases run on horizons of 50 years or more for franchise programmes. That supports replacing the 20-year fps window with a franchise term: an explicit 20 years plus a terminal value, or a 40-50-year horizon.

findings.topic: Boeing's narrowbody choices: share at risk is the trigger
findings.claim: In 2011 Boeing said it would re-engine rather than wait for a clean sheet if waiting put meaningful share at risk. It later said it chose the MAX because a clean sheet's EIS 'will have placed years of near-term market share strength at risk'. In 2016 Muilenburg said a new airplane 'will not be based on market share'. The profile treats share as a franchise floor of about 40%, not a trophy.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-0422 (FQ2 2011 p.2551), B-1038 (Investor Day 2015 p.1765), B-1131 (Barclays conf. 2016 p.1689); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/profile.md line 73
findings.quote: It has always been our view that if it looked like we are putting meaningful market share at risk by waiting to do a new airplane, we would re-engine instead. (B-0422, McNerney)
findings.use_in_model: Make the franchise term conditional on a share floor: switch on the loss of franchise value when Boeing's narrowbody share is projected below about 30-35%, or at exit. This matches Boeing's own trigger: it reacts when share is at risk, not to chase share.

findings.topic: Current leadership on the next airplane and keeping engineering capability
findings.claim: In Q3 2026 Ortberg said nothing had changed on the new airplane and that a product-development team is defining it. He said engineering resources will shift to new programmes as the 737-7/-10 and 777X finish. In Q2 2026 he called the next airplane the chance to change Boeing's share of aerospace profitability.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest (4).pdf p.16 (FQ3 2026 call, 27 Oct 2026) and p.46 (FQ2 2026 call, 28 Jul 2026)
findings.quote: When we finish the 777 program, you will see a shift of resources and spending from those development programs to new programs. (p.16) / So it points to the next airplane as the opportunity to change that. (p.46)
findings.use_in_model: Supports a capability-continuity term. The engineering workforce rolls from the 737-7/-10 and 777X into the next programme. If no fps follows, that capability decays (see the forgetting and RAND findings), and the option to re-enter or to win a larger value-chain share is lost.

findings.topic: Development bill benchmarks for a 737 successor
findings.claim: Calhoun (CNBC, April 2024) said the next new airplane would be a '$50 billion investment'. Aboulafia said then-CFO Bell had put a new single-aisle family at $10-12B in 2011, about $15B after inflation. Analysts put the NMA at $10-15B (BofA's Epstein; Aboulafia). The CSeries cost about $6B.
findings.source: airguide.info 'Boeing's Next New Airplane Could Cost $50 Billion, Says CEO David Calhoun' https://airguide.info/?p=375146 ; Leeham 15 Apr 2024 https://leehamnews.com/2024/04/15/dissecting-boeing-ceos-statement-next-new-airplane-will-cost-50bn/ ; Aboulafia April 2024 letter https://richardaboulafia.com/?p=2347 ; NMA: https://www.traveller.com.au/boeing-797-allnew-plane-design-generates-interest-from-united-continental-guulcn (WebSearch extracts)
findings.quote: Our next leader is going to develop and call out the next airplane for the Boeing Co. ... It will be a $50 billion investment.
findings.use_in_model: The game's $60-65B fps bill sits at or above the top of the published range. The franchise term should be compared with a bill of $15-50B as a sensitivity, along with the game's own value.

findings.topic: Airbus A320neo (2010): cheap franchise defence
findings.claim: Airbus launched the A320neo on 1 Dec 2010 for just over 1B EUR of investment, expecting 4,000 aircraft over 15 years, without the usual launch commitments. The main motive was the Bombardier CSeries threat to the A320. Leahy said the NEO left 'virtually no business case left' for the CSeries. Airbus cited a 60% share in 2014, and the family had 11,529 firm orders by end-2025. Boeing answered with the MAX within about 8 months.
findings.source: FlightGlobal 'A320neo kills business case for CSeries: Leahy' https://www.flightglobal.com/a320neo-kills-business-case-for-cseries-leahy/97184.article ; CAPA https://centreforaviation.com/news/airbus-formally-offers-a320neo-76980 ; Aviation Week https://aviationweek.com/special-topics/crossover-narrowbody-jets/airbus-prepares-much-higher-a220-rates-new-versions ; /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/airbus/evidence.jsonl A-0246 (Airbus Board Report FY2025 p.15); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/profile.md line 197
findings.quote: Since its launch in December 2010, the A320neo Family has received 11,529 firm orders from more than 150 customers (A-0246)
findings.number: about 1B EUR investment; 4,000 aircraft/15 years planned; 11,529 orders
findings.use_in_model: Precedent that defending an incumbent franchise against an entrant is worth many times its cost. In the model, the franchise term is what a defence move protects. A derivative or re-engine that keeps share inside the window has positive franchise value even when its standalone NPV is modest.

findings.topic: Airbus A350 XWB (2006): paying to stay in a segment from behind
findings.claim: Airbus's first A350 (2004-05, an A330 derivative, about $5.3B / 5.5B EUR) was rejected by customers. GECAS's Udvar-Hazy called it 'a Band-aid reaction to the 787' and warned of lost share. EADS approved the clean-sheet XWB on 1 Dec 2006 at about 10B EUR of R&D plus 1.6B EUR of capex. It was funded from cash flow, Power8 savings and risk-sharing partners, with about 1.8B EUR asked of suppliers. By then Boeing had a three-year lead and about 450 787 orders.
findings.source: EADS ad-hoc release 1 Dec 2006 https://www.airbus.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2006-11-ad-hoc-release-1-december-2006-eads-a350-xwb-launch-eads-gives-go ; China Daily/AP 5 Dec 2006 https://covid-19.chinadaily.com.cn/world/2006-12/05/content_750660.htm ; Flight International https://www.flightglobal.com/john-leahy-airbus-caught-napping-by-787/74988.article ; Gulf News https://gulfnews.com/amp/story/business%2Faviation%2Fflying-back-on-course-the-inside-story-of-the-new-airbus-a350-jet-1.1432312 (WebSearch extracts)
findings.quote: a Band-aid reaction to the 787 (Udvar-Hazy, as reported)
findings.use_in_model: Airbus chose to stay in the 250-350-seat segment, late and at roughly double the derivative cost, rather than cede it. That is evidence that incumbents value continued presence above standalone programme NPV. It is the analogue for fps launched behind the Airbus NGSA.

findings.topic: Franchise programmes often fail standalone payback
findings.claim: Several flagship programmes did not pay back on their own. The A380 cost about $25B to develop, 251 were built against a stated break-even of about 250 (later analyst estimates were 400 or more), and termination cost a 463M EUR charge. On the 787 (about $20B of development, about $29-32B of deferred cost), Leeham said in 2015 that the programme would not show an overall profit. BofA said Boeing needed about $30M of profit on each of the remaining 900. Credit Suisse thought only about $22B of $29B of deferred cost was recoverable. The L-1011 needed about 500 to break even, built 250, lost about $2.5B, and Lockheed left airliners in 1981.
findings.source: Motley Fool 16 Feb 2019 https://www.fool.com/investing/2019/02/16/airbus-wont-miss-the-a380-jumbo-jet.aspx ; IndustryWeek https://www.industryweek.com/operations/article/21212156/grand-finale-airbus-delivers-last-a380-superjumbo ; Leeham 19 Oct 2015 https://leehamnews.com/2015/10/19/do-the-boeing-787-sums-add-up/ and 11 Apr 2016 https://leehamnews.com/2016/04/11/boeing-wont-take-charge-787s/ ; aussieairliners L-1011 https://aussieairliners.org/l-1011/tristar.html (WebSearch extracts; analyst estimates)
findings.quote: We believe it is pretty clear that the program will not record an overall profit with the cost of development as well as production costs included. (Leeham on 787, 2015)
findings.number: A380 about $25B dev / 251 built; 787 $30M per unit needed on 900; L-1011 $2.5B loss
findings.use_in_model: A negative standalone NPV for fps is the norm for franchise programmes, not a disqualifier. The launch case rests on the franchise term. The A380 and L-1011 show the downside when the franchise premise (market size) is wrong, so add a probability that the franchise term fails to materialise.

findings.topic: Exit precedent: McDonnell Douglas (1996)
findings.claim: MD's board cancelled the MD-XX on 25 Oct 1996. Stonecipher said the decision turned not on the MD-XX's own cost (about $2B) but on the roughly $15B over ten years needed to stay a full player. Boeing agreed to merge with MD on 15 Dec 1996 for about $13.3B in stock, by which time MD's commercial share was about 7%. MD had not designed a clean-sheet airliner since the 1970s.
findings.source: FlightGlobal 'Where next for MDC' https://www.flightglobal.com/where-next-for-mdc/4457.article ; CNN Money 28 Oct 1996 https://money.cnn.com/1996/10/28/companies/mcdonnell/ ; KUOW https://www.kuow.org/stories/inside-the-90s-merger-that-started-boeing-s-long-decline ; Airways https://airwaysmag.com/boeing-mcdonnell-douglas-merger (WebSearch extracts)
findings.quote: The investment required to make us into a full-fledged major player is probably in the order of $15 billion over the next ten years (Stonecipher, as reported)
findings.use_in_model: Direct analogue of Do Nothing as exit. Once an airframer declines the 'stay a full player' investment, its commercial franchise ends within about a year as an independent business. $15B (1996) is about $31B in 2026 $ (inference, CPI about 2.1x). Use it as the order of magnitude for the cost of staying versus the franchise lost.

findings.topic: Exit value captured is a fraction of franchise value
findings.claim: BAE Systems exercised its put and sold its 20% of Airbus to EADS in 2006 for 2.75B EUR (about GBP 1.87B), at an independent Rothschild valuation well below both parties' expectations, during the A380 crisis. Bombardier sold 50.01% of the CSeries to Airbus for a nominal C$1 plus liabilities (agreed 2017, closed July 2018). It sold its remaining stake for $591M in Feb 2020 and left commercial aviation, after estimated programme losses of $8-9B.
findings.source: Defense Industry Daily https://www.defenseindustrydaily.com/bae-exercising-its-put-option-re-airbus-02214/ ; CAPA https://centreforaviation.com/analysis/bae-advises-shareholders-to-sell-stake-in-airbus-to-eads-1285 ; CBC https://www.cbc.ca/1.5462182 ; American Machinist https://www.americanmachinist.com/news/article/21122909/bombardier-sells-a220-share-for-591m-airbus ; AirInsight https://airinsight.com/insight-friday-14-february-2020-bombardiers-sale-of-the-a220-stake-what-it-means/ (WebSearch extracts)
findings.number: 2.75B EUR for 20% of Airbus (2006); C$1 for 50.01% CSeries; $591M remaining stake (2020)
findings.use_in_model: Option value of staying in: exits are priced at the trough. Inference: 20% of Airbus at a 212.9 EUR share price (repo analyst_models, Aug 2026) and about 0.79B shares is about 34B EUR, more than 12x BAE's price. Do Nothing should not be credited with any sale or exit proceeds near franchise value.

findings.topic: Cost and odds of entry or re-entry: COMAC, Mitsubishi
findings.claim: CSIS tallied COMAC state-related financing of $49B through late 2016 and about $72B if continued to 2020, excluding R&D grants, land and tax support. Jamestown notes reported losses of only about $3B. Cirium forecasts COMAC at about 5% of global fleet allocation by 2045 (Airbus 47%, Boeing 39%). Mitsubishi spent about 1 trillion yen (about $7.5B) on the SpaceJet before cancelling it in Feb 2023 and leaving regional jets.
findings.source: CSIS 'China's COMAC: An Aerospace Minor Leaguer' https://www.csis.org/blogs/trustee-china-hand/chinas-comac-aerospace-minor-leaguer ; Jamestown https://jamestown.org/program/comacs-homegrown-aircraft-goes-global/ ; aviationa2z 19 Oct 2026 https://aviationa2z.com/index.php/2026/10/19/comac-eyes-5-of-the-aircraft-market-share-by-2045/ ; MHI notice 7 Feb 2023 https://mhi.com/notice/notice_230207.html ; ch-aviation https://www.ch-aviation.com/news/124254-mitsubishi-confirms-spacejet-program-termination (WebSearch extracts)
findings.quote: These figures, which total to RMB 328.5 billion (or $49 billion), certainly are far from complete. (CSIS)
findings.number: $49-72B (COMAC state support); about $7.5B (SpaceJet); 5% fleet share by 2045
findings.use_in_model: Re-entry option after a Boeing exit (inference): its strike price is a new-entrant cost ($7.5B for a regional jet up to $49-72B of state-backed money for a narrowbody), and the record of success is poor. No airframer that left large jets (Lockheed, MD, Fokker, Bombardier) has returned. Set the value of the re-entry option under Do Nothing near zero, and its loss counts against Do Nothing.

findings.topic: Embraer: how a smaller player values entry
findings.claim: Embraer chose the E2 re-wing and re-engine (announced Nov 2011) as lower risk and lower cost than a clean sheet. Boeing's 2018-19 deal valued Embraer's commercial aircraft and services business at $5.26B for 100% ($4.2B for 80%), framed as a counter to Airbus-Bombardier. Leeham (Sept 2026) calls a large Embraer narrowbody a 'bet-the-company' decision. Embraer has sounded out Saudi PIF and partners in Turkey, India and South Korea (WSJ 2024).
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-1492 (10-K FY2018 p.2557), B-1792; UPI https://www.upi.com/Embraer-shareholders-approve-sale-to-Boeing/4721551205060/ ; Leeham 4 Sep 2026 https://leehamnews.com/2026/09/04/will-embraer-go-big-by-developing-a-large-narrowbody-jet/ ; WSJ via https://www.tovima.com/wsj/brazils-embraer-plots-a-new-737-sized-jet-to-rival-boeing/amp/
findings.quote: in which Boeing will acquire an 80 percent ownership stake for $4.2 billion (B-1492)
findings.use_in_model: Competitive externality of exit (inference): a Boeing narrowbody exit opens the market that Embraer or COMAC need. Their entry would then also press Boeing's widebody and services pricing. Use this to justify a widebody cross-sell and pricing penalty under Do Nothing, sized as a sensitivity because there is no direct estimate.

findings.topic: Learning and forgetting: how fast capability decays
findings.claim: Benkard's study of L-1011 production (AER 2000) found organisational forgetting. Monthly retention of experience was about 0.96, so only about 61% of experience survives a year, about 39% annual depreciation. His dynamic model of widebody aircraft (RES 2004) explains high concentration and pricing below static marginal cost, up to about 50% below cost at introduction (secondary survey). Learning-by-doing works as an entry barrier on top of development cost.

findings.number: 0.96 monthly retention, about 39% a year lost; about 9% left after 5 years, under 1% after 10 (computed)
findings.use_in_model: Capability term: after the last narrowbody design or production work, the experience stock decays at about 39% a year. Re-entry 5-10 years after the MAX line ends is effectively a new entry. Firms' willingness to price below static cost also implies each sale is worth more than price x margin (a learning premium), which argues for a per-unit share premium.

findings.topic: Cost of a capability gap: RAND and the F-22 restart
findings.claim: RAND (MG-608, 2007) found the cheapest way through a submarine design gap was to sustain about 800 Electric Boat and about 1,050 Newport News designers, or to start the next design early, rather than let skills lapse. RAND's Australian work found about a 20% cost increase if skills were not augmented, and that a workforce at 40% of the current pool needs about 3 more years and 15% more man-hours. For the F-22, RAND-reported figures put 75 more jets at about $173M each after a restart against about $139M on a hot line, about 24% more, roughly $17-20B in total.

findings.number: +15-20% cost and +3 years after a skills gap; +24% unit cost on restart
findings.use_in_model: Parameterise a capability-loss penalty: if Boeing ever re-enters after Do Nothing, add 15-25% to the development bill and 3 years to EIS. Or price the alternative of keeping the team: a 'keep capability' carrying cost of about 1,000 engineers at about $0.2-0.3B a year (inference).

findings.topic: Real-options framing of platform continuation
findings.claim: The aircraft-programme real-options literature models a programme as a chain of choices: keep producing the baseline, launch a derivative, sell, or abandon (Miller and Clarke, Real Options Conference 2005). Markish and Willcox (AIAA J. 2003; MIT thesis) value programmes by dynamic programming, which prices demand uncertainty and management flexibility explicitly. A follow-on MIT thesis (Peoples) found value-based design 2.3% higher in programme value than minimum-weight design. Esty and Ghemawat (HBS WP 02-061, 2002) argue that deterring entry through new products (or holding back a launch) can be incredible even with large cost advantages.

findings.quote: entry-deterrence through new product introductions may be incredible even if the incumbent enjoys large cost advantages (Esty and Ghemawat abstract, as reported)
findings.use_in_model: Treat fps as buying a compound option: future derivatives and stretches, block extensions, and a later re-engine. Treat Do Nothing as giving it up. Esty-Ghemawat implies Do Nothing will not deter the Airbus NGSA, so do not credit Do Nothing with a 'rival restraint' benefit. Numeric option values were not accessible.

findings.claim: American's July 2011 order of 460 narrowbodies split 260 Airbus (half A320neo) and 200 Boeing. It was American's first Airbus order since the 1980s and ended Boeing's exclusivity, and it pushed Boeing to re-engine the 737 rather than wait for a clean sheet. Boeing's direct 737 MAX grounding costs were about $20B ($8.6B compensation, $5B abnormal production, $6.3B programme cost). findings.topic: Aftermarket and installed-base annuity
findings.claim: Boeing's 2025 outlook forecasts 33,285 single-aisle deliveries out of 43,600 in 2025-2044. Single-aisle aircraft rise from 66% to 72% of the world fleet. Boeing sizes the commercial services market at $4.7 trillion over the same 20 years. BGS revenue was $19.95B in 2024 at an 18.1% margin; Q3 2026 margin was 18.3% with a $33B backlog. research.summary:
I have 28 findings on how analysts and companies value staying in versus leaving a core aerospace market. Each carries a source, a quote where I had one, a confidence level, and a note on how it could enter the game.

**Access limits**
- WebFetch and curl were blocked for every host I tried (nber.org, stanford.edu, wikipedia, sec.gov, rand.org, airbus.com, morningstar.com and others). So every web figure comes from WebSearch result extracts, not the full documents. Those findings are marked medium or low confidence, and any analyst estimate is labelled as such.
- The repo items are first-hand. "Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf" holds Rolls-Royce transcripts, not Boeing ones. "Transcript Digest (4).pdf" holds Boeing's Q2 and Q3 2026 calls.

**What the evidence says**
1. **Analysts never stop at a fixed horizon.** Their DCFs run an explicit forecast, then a fade, then a perpetuity:
   - GS Airbus: 9% discount, 3% long-term growth, formula to 2036E.
   - GS Rolls-Royce: 8.46%, 3%, with 64% of EV after 2036.
   - Morningstar: a wide moat (Boeing's rating) means at least 20 years of excess returns, then a perpetuity; one Boeing note uses an 8.6% WACC.
   - Market price targets of about 22.5x FCF imply roughly 4-5% perpetual nominal growth.
2. **Published sizes of the franchise:**
   - Morningstar: half of Boeing's EV comes from the 737 line. That is about $65B on the board's $130B EV, the same size as the $60-65B fps bill.
   - Barclays (2019): the whole narrowbody industry has a PV of $238B, or about $2.4B per share point ($3.1B in 2026 dollars).
3. **Boeing's own practice is long-horizon.** Programme accounting runs in blocks of about 10 years, extended in steps; it treats the NG and MAX as one 737 programme; and management called KC-46 a "50-, 60-year franchise". In 2011 Boeing re-engined because share was at risk.
4. **What exit costs:**
   - Overhead: $1.1-3.7B a year of unabsorbed overhead, and $4-5B of abnormal costs during the MAX suspension.
   - Capability: experience decays about 39% a year (Benkard's L-1011 study); restarts or design gaps add 15-25% to cost and about 3 years (RAND).
   - Re-entry is priced like new entry: Mitsubishi spent about $7.5B, COMAC has $49-72B of state support, and the McDonnell Douglas precedent is $15B over 10 years (1996 dollars) to stay a full player.
   - Exits are sold at the trough: BAE's 20% of Airbus went for 2.75B EUR; Bombardier sold the CSeries for C$1.
   - No airframer that left large jets has come back.
5. **Defending a franchise is cheap next to what it protects.** The A320neo cost about 1B EUR against the CSeries threat and now has 11,529 orders. Airbus paid about 11.6B EUR to relaunch the A350 rather than cede the segment. Many flagship programmes (A380, 787, L-1011) never paid back on their own, so launch cases rest on franchise value.

**Suggested terms for the game**
- A terminal value after fps entry into service plus 20 years.
- An aftermarket annuity tied to Boeing's own fleet.
- An overhead-absorption penalty and wind-down charges on the Do Nothing path.
- Capability decay, and a re-entry option valued near zero, under Do Nothing.
- Share erosion of 10-15 points after the Airbus NGSA enters service (about 2037), at a set value per share point.
- Discount-rate sensitivity. The game's 10.5% on constant-dollar flows is about 12.9% nominal. At that rate a perpetuity starting in 2062 is worth $0.29 per dollar a year, against $1.6-1.9 at an analyst-like 6.3-6.7% real. The rate alone can decide whether these terms matter.

Nothing in the repo was modified. A small scratch folder was created at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aero-engine-gameboard/95fa875c-ca9d-5564-a6e5-4c9b461d7e56/scratchpad/franchise/ for the text extracted from the transcript PDFs.

How much aftermarket profit Boeing would give up by exiting narrowbodies. Main result: the airframe maker's services profit on one narrowbody in service is about $0.05-0.15M a year in 2026 dollars, central $0.09M (inference). That is about $0.3-0.45M of revenue per narrowbody-year at a 20-30% margin. Each delivered aircraft gives about 25 aircraft-years of this stream. At the game's 10.5% rate, the present value at delivery is $0.36M / $0.64M / $1.07M (low / central / high). That is roughly 5-15% on top of the profit the game books on each delivery. Pricing is airplane-first: Boeing and Airbus book their margin at delivery and services add a modest amount. Engine makers are the reverse. GE's commercial engines unit earns about 74% of its revenue from services, and engine maintenance on a narrowbody runs about $1.8M per aircraft-year (inferred from a LEAP-1B contract), against $0.3-0.45M for the airframe maker.

Evidence:
- **Boeing Global Services (10-K):** commercial revenue went from $7.6B (2017) to $10.2B (2019), fell to $6.9B (2020) and reached $11.7B (2024). Segment margin rose from about 14-15% to 18.1% (2024), about 18.5% in 2025 excluding the $9.6B gain on the Digital Aviation Solutions (Jeppesen) sale, and 18.1-18.3% in 2026. I estimate the commercial margin at 21-24% (inference).
- **Mix (Goldman Sachs model, an analyst estimate):** about 40% of commercial is parts distribution (Aviall and KLX), which sells parts for any maker's aircraft, about 28% is Boeing spares and about 33% is support services. Only about 55-70% is tied to Boeing's own fleet (inference). Weighted toward the 737/757 fleet of about 8,400 aircraft (inference), this gives the per-narrowbody figure.
- **Airbus cross-check:** commercial services were about 11% of €52.6bn in 2025, or about €5.8bn, across 14,256 aircraft in operation. Weighted by aircraft size, that is about $0.38M per narrowbody-year.
- **Bombardier cross-check:** Mitsubishi paid $550M plus about $200M of liabilities for the out-of-production CRJ support franchise. That implies about $60-90k of profit per aircraft-year (inference).

What happens when an airframe maker stops building a type. It does not lose the support stream on the fleet already flying:
- Boeing promised MD-80/90 and MD-11 operators the same long-term support out of production, and still supports types back to the 707 and DC-8.
- FAA rule 14 CFR 21.50 requires the type-certificate holder to keep maintenance instructions current.
- Survival after production ends (multiple sources):
  - 737 Classic: 83% still in service 10 years after the last delivery.
  - 757: about 42% after 21 years.
  - MD-80: about 8% after about 25 years.
  - Boeing forecasts less than 10% of previous-generation aircraft still flying by 2045.
- Narrowbodies now retire at about 24-25.5 years (Cirium, IBA).
- Used serviceable parts take a growing share of spending as retirements rise: 9% (2019) to 11% (2020).

In my age-profile model, a type's services stream keeps rising for 5-10 years after the last delivery. It then falls to about 30% of the end-of-production level at 20 years, about 7% at 25 years and nearly zero by 30 years.

What this means for the game:
- In the MAX phase-out world, Do Nothing still earns MAX aftermarket after 2060, running off to about 2085. What exit really loses is the services on the replacement fleet, which goes to Airbus.
- The fps services term should be built from deliveries times the age-profile stream, not limited to the 20-year operating-profit window.
- It is worth about $66 / $119 / $198M of 2026 present value per 1,000 fps deliveries over 2035-54 (low / central / high).
- On its own this term is unlikely to flip the fps decision. It is a small add-on next to the narrowbody operating profit and the $60-65B development bill.
- Boeing's attitude to services has swung. In 2018 Muilenburg wanted lifecycle and services value in the airplane business case. In 2022-23 Calhoun and West dropped the $50B services revenue target. In 2026 the CFO (Malave) said BGS will not be a huge incremental contributor.

Limits:
- The fetch tool could not reach sec.gov, boeing.mediaroom.com or other sites, which are outside this session's allowed network domains. Web figures therefore come from search-result excerpts; the repo's 10-K PDF, Capital IQ and Goldman Sachs files, and transcripts were read directly.
- No source gives an airframe maker's narrowbody aftermarket per aircraft directly. Those figures, the Boeing fleet split and the decay curve are my inferences, marked as such.
- Scratch files (not in the repo): the model script at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aero-engine-gameboard/95fa875c-ca9d-5564-a6e5-4c9b461d7e56/scratchpad/franchise/pv_services.py, and text extracts in the 10k/, td/ and airbus/ subfolders of /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aero-engine-gameboard/95fa875c-ca9d-5564-a6e5-4c9b461d7e56/scratchpad/franchise/. The Airbus board-report PDF's text could not be extracted (garbled fonts); its data comes from the repo's Airbus evidence.jsonl.

Survival of out-of-production Boeing/Douglas narrowbodies:
- 737 Classic: 1,988 built, last delivered 2000; 1,651 in service in July 2010, 83% ten years on.
- MD-80: 1,194 built, last delivered about 1999-2000; 1,042 active in 2005 (87%); about 100 active in August 2025 (about 8% after about 25 years).

findings.topic: Support continues after the maker stops building a type
findings.claim: When Boeing ended the Douglas lines it promised continued support. MD-80/90 operators were told to expect the same long-term support whether a type was in or out of production. Selling them shrinks Boeing's commercial services base, and Boeing did it to repair its balance sheet.

It explicitly asked how investments in services and in-house supply ('verticals') add value beyond the airplane's own NPV, set a $50B services revenue target, and cut parts prices to capture share. Calhoun and West (2022-23) dropped the target as having driven 'undisciplined capital allocation'. CFO Malave (2026) said BGS will not be a huge incremental contributor to cash flow.

research.summary:
STRANDED OVERHEAD AND CROSS-SELLING if Boeing leaves the narrowbody market: what the evidence supports for the war-game valuation.

1. Boeing has a shared "hard to vary" cost pool, and its own statements show how it behaves. When one programme's in-house work disappears, Boeing re-allocates these fixed costs to the programmes that remain. It happened with the 787 slip in 2008, the 747 rate cuts in 2009-16, the KC-46A charge in 2020 and the 737/787 rate cuts in 2019-20. CFO Bell said in 2008: "The infrastructure cost remained constant... that differential went to the production programs and flowed through the earnings."
   - Accounting rule: Boeing's policy is to expense, as a period cost, any fixed cost that is "not appropriately attributable to our programs". If the narrowbody goes, its share of shared overhead would therefore fall straight on widebody and segment margins.

2. How big the hit is (calibration, inference from the GS analyst models plus 10-K figures):
   - Unabsorbed fixed cost in the first year of a volume loss is about 9-15% of the revenue lost.
   - Boeing 2020: GS "unabsorbed overhead" of $3.7B on $41.3B of lost BCA revenue gives 9%. Adding the $2.57B of 737 MAX abnormal costs gives 15%.
   - Airbus 2020: GS "fixed cost absorption" of €3.1B on €20.5B of lost sales gives 15%.
   - How fast it can be cut: Rolls-Royce removed about a third of its Civil Aerospace headcount and went from 11 sites to 5 in about two years. Boeing booked severance for about 26,000 employees in 2020.

3. The 737's share of BCA (GS analyst estimates):
   - 53-55% of BCA revenue (2018A, 2028E).
   - 69-74% of BCA programme profit before R&D.
   - 72-74% of units and backlog.
   - These are the allocation keys for how much shared overhead would be stranded.
   - Inferred size of the shared pool: BCA R&D of $2.0-2.4B, plus D&A of about $0.74B, plus a share of $5.0B consolidated G&A. That is roughly $4.6-5.5B a year, of which the narrowbody carries about $2.5-4B.

4. Cross-selling: the evidence is qualitative.
   - Bundling is strongest within a family. Examples are NG+MAX combination deals and 777 with 777X. Muilenburg said widebody buying "tend[s] to be a little bit different".
   - Narrowbody-plus-widebody packages do exist. Air India's 2023 commitment was 190 737 MAX, 20 787s and 10 777Xs. Boeing says it prices "holistically across airplanes and services".
   - Airbus calls cross-crew qualification across its families "an important competitive advantage".
   - Customers often split orders between Boeing and Airbus (United, Continental, Air France-KLM, American). United's 2021 order of 270 jets went 200 to Boeing and 70 to Airbus.
   - The extreme precedent is McDonnell Douglas. Once Douglas lost commercial relevance, the FTC (1997) judged it "no longer... a meaningful competitive force", and the MD-11 widebody ended in 2000.
   - No source in this pass puts a number on how much widebody share an OEM loses when it leaves the narrowbody market. The 0 / 5 / 15 point scenarios proposed for the model are judgement.

5. A long tail after exit. In 2012, 79% of Boeing's customer-financing carrying value by model was in out-of-production types (717, 757, MD-80, MD-11). Orphaned fleets need OEM balance-sheet support for years.

Caveats on sources:
- The shared web-search budget ran out partway through. WebFetch could not reach ftc.gov or australiancompetitionlaw.org, and the proxy log shows sec.gov refused to other agents in this session. The McDonnell Douglas FTC findings, Lockheed TriStar, Reinhardt (1973) and Benkard (2000) items rest on search-result snippets and are marked medium or low confidence.
- Not verified, so left out: the EU decision text (IV/M.877), Airbus's A380 press release, the Qatar A321neo/737-10 swap, A220 sales after Airbus took it over, and Boeing's Embraer synergy figure.
- "Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf" is mostly Rolls-Royce transcripts. Boeing quotes come from "Transcripts from 2006-2025_Compressed.pdf" and "Transcript Digest (4).pdf".

Scratch extracts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aero-engine-gameboard/95fa875c-ca9d-5564-a6e5-4c9b461d7e56/scratchpad/franchise/ (tenk/boeing_10k.txt, tr/all.txt, tr/fixed_hits.txt, tr/bundle_hits.txt, emb/emb.txt, digests/). Nothing in the repo was modified.

findings.topic: BCA cost structure
findings.claim: Boeing reports BCA costs only as R&D plus a single 'other segment items' line (cost of products and services plus G&A). It does not disclose a fixed vs variable split. BCA R&D, a period cost, was $1.5-2.4B a year in 2022-2024.
