findings.quote: Other segment items (1) ... (1) Primarily includes costs of products and services and general and administrative expenses.

findings.topic: BCA cost structure
findings.claim: Centrally managed assets are a shared overhead that Boeing allocates to segments by usage. BCA bore $400M of its own D&A plus $339M of the $705M of central-asset D&A allocated to segments in 2024. Most capex ($1,214M of $2,230M) sits in 'unallocated' centrally managed assets.
findings.source: Boeing FY2024 10-K, Note 23, printed p.119 (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF p.2290)
findings.use_in_model: Add about $0.74B a year of BCA D&A to F_shared. Allocation is by 'usage and occupancy', so if the 737 vacates Renton floor space, widebody programmes would carry more of the central-asset charge until the space is shed.
findings.quote: Depreciation and amortization for centrally managed assets are allocated to business segments based on usage and occupancy. In 2024, $ 705 was allocated to the primary business segments, of which $ 339 , $ 289 and $ 77 was allocated to BCA, BDS and BGS, respectively.

findings.topic: BCA cost structure
findings.claim: Boeing's consolidated G&A was $4.2-5.2B a year in 2022-24 ($4.6B in 2018). The BCA share is not disclosed. Inference: if BCA carries 40-50%, about $2.0-2.5B of G&A is a BCA period cost.
findings.source: Boeing FY2024 10-K consolidated statement of operations (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF p.2219); FY2018 10-K (PDF p.2529)
findings.use_in_model: The third component of F_shared. With R&D and D&A this gives an inferred shared BCA pool of about $4.6-5.5B a year. Treat the BCA share of G&A as a tunable parameter.
findings.quote: General and administrative expense ( 5,021 ) ( 5,168 ) ( 4,187 )

findings.topic: Accounting rule for stranded fixed costs
findings.claim: Boeing inventories programme overhead (fringe benefits, production-related indirects, plant management and plant services). Fixed costs that are not appropriately attributable to a programme, or that relate to an abnormal event, are expensed in the period. So overhead stranded by a programme exit would hit earnings directly rather than being spread over a block.
findings.source: Boeing FY2024 10-K, Note 1 Inventories (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF p.2233; same wording in every 10-K, e.g. FY2012 p.66)
findings.use_in_model: Model stranded overhead as an annual period charge in the Do Nothing world, not as a change to programme margin. Apply it to the widebody business from the start of the 737 phase-out (2045).
findings.quote: To the extent a material amount of such costs are related to an abnormal event or are fixed costs not appropriately attributable to our programs or contracts, they are expensed in the current period rather than inventoried.

findings.topic: Cross-programme overhead absorption (Boeing's own words)
findings.claim: When the 787's in-house work slipped in 2008, constant 'hard to vary' infrastructure costs were re-allocated to Boeing's other production programmes and cut BCA earnings. The CFO described the mechanism directly: infrastructure cost is constant and is allocated on in-house work. He said about half of the Q2 2008 margin pressure was overhead absorption and half period expenses.
findings.source: Transcripts from 2006-2025_Compressed.pdf (repo root), FQ2 2008 call 23 Jul 2008, CFO James Bell, PDF pp.2904, 2913, 2916-2917; repo evidence B-0098 (boeing/evidence.jsonl)
findings.use_in_model: Core mechanism for a stranded-overhead term. Narrowbody work leaves, the shared infrastructure cost does not, so the remaining (widebody) programmes absorb it. Set SO(t) = F_shared x s_NB x (lost narrowbody share of in-house work) x (1 - c(t)).
findings.quote: The infrastructure cost remained constant. What we assumed is we'd have more 787 work in-house than we did after the schedule slide, so less of that constant cost was allocated to 787 ... The remaining, since the 787 work did not show up, that differential went to the production programs and flowed through the earnings.

findings.topic: Cross-programme overhead absorption (defense derivatives)
findings.claim: Lower commercial volume in 2020 pushed fixed costs onto a defense derivative built on a commercial line. Boeing booked a $151M KC-46A tanker charge 'primarily driven by additional fixed cost allocation'. BDS also builds 'commercial derivative aircraft, including anti-submarine and tanker aircraft'.
findings.source: Transcripts from 2006-2025_Compressed.pdf, FQ2 2020 call 29 Jul 2020, PDF p.841; Boeing FY2024 10-K Item 1 (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF p.2165)
findings.use_in_model: Exiting the narrowbody also strands overhead now absorbed by the anti-submarine derivative (the 10-K wording; it is the 737-based P-8, which is inference). Extend SO(t) to include a BDS spillover, or at minimum flag it as an unmodelled cost of Do Nothing.
findings.quote: $151 million KC-46A tanker charge primarily driven by additional fixed cost allocation resulting from lower commercial airplane production volume due to COVID-19.

findings.topic: Rate effects on unit cost (747)
findings.claim:
Lower 747 volume repeatedly raised unit cost by spreading fixed costs over fewer aircraft:
- 2009: deferring a 747-8 rate increase cost $362M ('higher allocations of fixed costs' plus supplier volume penalties). In Q1 2009 'redistribution of hard to vary costs over fewer units' cut earnings by about $200M.
- 2015: a rate cut drove an $885M reach-forward loss.
- 2016: a further $1,258M loss from 'higher costs to produce fewer airplanes'.
findings.source: Boeing 10-K FY2009 p.1729 (repo evidence B-0247); Transcripts 2006-2025 PDF p.2825 (FQ1 2009, 22 Apr 2009); 10-K FY2015 p.662 (B-1108); FY2018 10-K (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF p.2507)
findings.use_in_model: Calibrates the cost penalty when a low-rate widebody line has to carry more fixed cost. Treat a narrowbody exit as a permanent version of these rate cuts for the shared overhead.
findings.quote: Rate change disruption costs and redistribution of hard to vary costs over fewer units in the accounting quantity are the principle drivers. The impact recorded in the first quarter reduced earnings by approximately $200 million

findings.topic: Rate effects on unit cost (737)
findings.claim: Cutting the 737 rate from 52 to 42 a month added about $1.0B (Q1 2019) plus $1.7B (Q2 2019) to the cost of the ~3,100-aircraft block. That is about $0.87M per aircraft, or about 1.6% of the GS 2018 unit price of $53M (computed). The CFO agreed with an analyst that 'fixed cost' means the total internal cost of keeping the 737 programme's resources, and said it includes facilities, tooling and support.
findings.source: Transcripts 2006-2025 PDF pp.1042, 1049, 1051 (FQ1 2019, 24 Apr 2019, CFO Greg Smith) and p.981 (FQ2 2019); repo evidence B-1543
findings.use_in_model: Gives the size of 737-line-specific fixed cost (avoidable in an exit), as distinct from shared BCA overhead (stranded). Use it to separate the two pools in the model.
findings.quote: The additional costs are due to the lower production rate causing fixed costs for the 3,100 aircraft in the block to be amortized over a longer period of time.

findings.topic: Rate effects on unit cost (737 abnormal costs)
findings.claim: With 737 output suspended or abnormally low, Boeing expensed $2,567M of 737 MAX abnormal production costs in 2020 (797 / 712 / 590 / 468 by quarter) and about $5.0B over 2020-21. It deliberately kept the labour and infrastructure. Inference: about $2.5B a year is about 11% of the 737's normal annual programme cost (about $23.8B at the GS 2018 margin of 22.5% on $30.7B revenue).
findings.source: Boeing FY2020 10-K, quarterly note (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF p.1476) and p.1393 (repo evidence B-1789); FQ4 2019 call (B-1618)
findings.use_in_model: Upper bound on the line-specific capacity cost of a narrowbody line with no output, about $2.5B a year. This cost goes away in an exit but would be incurred if Boeing kept the 737 capability alive at low rate as a re-entry option.
findings.quote: As we are producing at abnormally low production rates in 2020 and 2021, we expect to incur approximately $5.0 billion of abnormal production costs that are being expensed as incurred.

findings.topic: Minimum efficient rate (widebody)
findings.claim: Boeing treats a 787 rate below 5 a month as abnormally low. The resulting abnormal costs were $1,240M in 2022 and $1,014M in 2023 (total estimate raised to $2.8B). The 777X added $325M (2022) and $513M (2023). Widebody lines already struggle to absorb their own fixed costs at low rates.
findings.source: Boeing FY2022 10-K p.1540 (repo evidence B-2014, B-2015); FY2024 10-K MD&A (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF p.2198)
findings.use_in_model: Stranded narrowbody overhead piles onto widebody lines that already run near their minimum efficient rate. Do not assume they have spare absorptive margin. Treat SO(t) as a straight reduction in widebody operating margin.
findings.quote: In the third quarter of 2021, we determined that production rates below 5 per month represented abnormally low production rates and result in abnormal production costs.

findings.topic: 737 share of BCA (allocation key)
findings.claim:
Goldman Sachs analyst estimates of the 737's share of BCA:
- 2018A: 580 units at $53.0M = $30.7B, or 53% of BCA revenue ($57.5B), and $6.9B of $10.1B pre-R&D programme EBIT (69%).
- 2028E: 656 units at $59.7M = 55% of BCA revenue ($70.7B) and $7.4B of $10.1B pre-R&D EBIT (74%), with 656 of 887 deliveries.
- The 737 is 4,404 of the 6,130 backlog aircraft (72%) at end-2025.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/GoldmanSachs_BA12826_Jan_28_2026.xlsx, sheet 'BCA margin' rows 6-10, 77-79 (analyst estimate); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/analyst_models_2026.md (GS BA Data r219-226); financials.md §8c
findings.use_in_model: Set s_NB (the narrowbody's share of the shared overhead) at about 0.55 on revenue, or 0.72-0.74 on units, backlog or profit. Run both as a sensitivity.
findings.number: Revenue share 53-55%; pre-R&D EBIT share 69-74%; backlog share 72%

findings.topic: Calibration of unabsorbed overhead (Boeing)
findings.claim:
Goldman Sachs records BCA 'unabsorbed overhead' separately from one-time and abnormal items:
- 2019: -$1,775M; 2020: -$3,711M; 2021: -$1,530M; 2022: -$1,720M; 2023: -$1,071M.
- Inference: BCA revenue fell from $57.5B (2018) to $16.2B (2020). Unabsorbed overhead was therefore about 9% of the lost revenue, or about 15% including the $2.57B of 737 abnormal costs.
- That is about $5.7-9.7M per lost delivery (806 deliveries in 2018 vs 157 in 2020).
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/GoldmanSachs_BA12826_Jan_28_2026.xlsx 'BCA margin' rows 77, 87, 88, 90 (analyst estimate); deliveries from repo evidence B-1775 (10-K FY2020 p.1371); 2018 deliveries from GS model
findings.use_in_model: Gives the coefficient phi for first-year under-absorption of about 0.09-0.15 of the narrowbody revenue lost. SO(t) = phi x (R_NB,base - R_NB(t)) x (1 - c(t)).

findings.topic: Calibration of unabsorbed overhead (Airbus)
findings.claim: Goldman Sachs's Airbus Commercial earnings bridge has a 'Fixed Cost Absorption' item of -€3,108M in 2020. That year sales fell from €54,775M to €34,250M (-37.5%) and deliveries from 863 to 566. Inference: the implied fixed-cost base is about €8.3B, about 15% of 2019 sales. GS also books negative A330 'operating leverage' of -€400M (2016) and -€200M in each of 2017 and 2018 when the A330 rate was cut.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/GoldmanSachs_AIRPACompanyModel_Aug_27_2026.xlsx, sheet 'Airbus Commercial' rows 2, 69, 121, 133 (analyst estimate)
findings.use_in_model: An independent check that an airframer's fixed cost is about 15% of revenue, consistent with the Boeing figure of 9-15%. Use 15% as the high case for phi. The A330 numbers give the cost of running a widebody line slower.

findings.topic: Programme exit cost: Airbus A380
findings.claim: In Goldman Sachs's compilation of Airbus one-offs, A380 provisions were €463M (2018, the year the end was decided), €202M (2019) and €385M (2020), followed by releases of -€274M (2021) and -€28M (2022). Sustaining A380 R&D was €450M (2014) and €175-250M a year in 2015-18, then zero from 2019. The last five A380s were delivered in 2021.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/GoldmanSachs_AIRPACompanyModel_Aug_27_2026.xlsx 'Income Statement' row 79 and 'Airbus Commercial' row 174 (analyst compilation); Airbus Board Report FY2025 p.17 (repo evidence A-0257)
findings.use_in_model: Analogue for one-off exit costs (about €0.75B net over 2018-22) against avoided sustaining R&D (about €0.2B a year). The narrowbody is about 50x the A380's volume, so scale exit provisions by revenue, not by programme count.

findings.topic: Speed of resizing fixed cost (supplier analogue)
findings.claim: Rolls-Royce put its fixed costs at £3.1B across four areas: commercial and admin, R&D, certification and participation fees, and capex. After the 2020 volume collapse it cited 'under-recovery of fixed costs, particularly on civil OE'. Its response was to remove more than 9,000 roles, cut Civil Aerospace headcount by about a third, consolidate 11 sites to 5 and target £1.3B of annual savings by end-2022.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf (mostly Rolls-Royce): Investor Day 15 Jun 2018 PDF p.540; FY2020 call 11 Mar 2021 PDF pp.296, 300
findings.use_in_model: Sets the resizing path c(t): about a third of fixed cost removable in about 2 years under duress. In the gradual 2045-2060 MAX phase-out, assume c rises to about 0.5 after about 5 years and 0.7-0.8 in the long run. The floor is inference.
findings.quote: The majority of our cost savings are targeting fixed costs in our Civil Aerospace business. We're reducing headcount by approximately 1/3

findings.topic: Speed of resizing fixed cost (Boeing)
findings.claim:
Boeing's infrastructure does not scale with volume, but it can be cut in steps:
- 2014: floor space down 25% since 2004 while revenue rose 60%.
- 2020: severance for about 26,000 employees, a planned ~30% cut in office space, and 787 production consolidated in South Carolina, which 'did not have a significant financial impact on the program'.
- 2021: Calhoun tied BCA margin recovery to 'that underlying infrastructure cost' and to consolidating a couple of plants.
findings.source: Transcripts 2006-2025 PDF p.1968 (Investor Conference 21 May 2014); Boeing FY2020 10-K MD&A (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF pp.1361, 1375); Transcripts PDF pp.686-687 (FQ2 2021, 28 Jul 2021)
findings.use_in_model: Supports a decaying stranded-overhead charge rather than a permanent one. Site consolidation (moving widebody work into freed Renton or Everett space) is the mitigation lever. Model c(t) as stepwise.
findings.number: -25% floor space vs +60% revenue; ~26,000 severance; ~30% office space
findings.quote: 25% reduction in floor space since 2004, although revenues going up by 60%.

findings.topic: Overhead absorption as a reason to keep programmes
findings.claim: BCA's CEO in 2012 valued even low-rate programmes for the indirect cost they absorb: the 767 at a couple a month and the 747-8 at 1.5-2 a month. He flagged the question of 'what's going to happen when these programs go away'.
findings.source: Transcripts 2006-2025 PDF p.2370 (Shareholder/Analyst Call 15 May 2012, James F. Albaugh)
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's own management treats absorption as real value. The 737 at 40-60 a month is by far the biggest absorber, so the Do Nothing exit should carry the overhead charge, and fps gets credit for avoiding it.
findings.quote: We don't talk much about 767, a couple of airplanes a month ... And that's going to absorb an awful lot of indirect. The 747-8, a big airplane, even at the rate of 1.5 to 2 a month, it absorbs a lot of overhead. People ask about, well, what's going to happen when these programs go away?

findings.topic: Procurement scale across programmes
findings.claim: Boeing uses volume on one programme to win supplier price cuts on others. Extra 777X volume bought price reductions on the F-18, F-15 and rotorcraft. The 737 is Boeing's largest purchasing volume (inference).
findings.source: Repo evidence B-0905 (boeing/evidence.jsonl): Investor Conference 21 May 2014, Transcripts PDF p.1961, Dennis Muilenburg
findings.use_in_model: Add a supplier-price penalty on remaining widebody material cost in Do Nothing, e.g. 0-2% of widebody cost of sales. This is a judgement range; no source quantifies it.
findings.quote: additional volume with some suppliers on 777X allowed us to get some price reductions on F-18, F-15 and rotorcraft.

findings.topic: Value of sitting inside a full-line OEM (Embraer-Boeing)
findings.claim: Embraer pitched the 2018 Boeing joint venture partly on access to 'Boeing's marketing and procurement resources' to speed the E2 ramp, plus at least $50M a year of cost synergy for Embraer's remaining businesses. Separating the commercial unit cost $120M in 2019 and, on an analyst's reading not disputed by the CFO, about $300M of carve-out and carve-in in total. After the deal failed, Embraer had to remove the duplicated structures.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Embraer Transcripts 2010-2020 (1).pdf: special call 17 Dec 2018 PDF pp.561-562; FQ4 2019 call 26 Mar 2020 p.498; FQ2 2020 call 5 Aug 2020 p.452; FQ4 2023 call 18 Mar 2024 p.247
findings.use_in_model: Evidence that commercial-aircraft overhead is entangled with the rest of the firm: separating it costs real money and duplicates functions. Supports a one-off exit or restructuring cost in Do Nothing of a few hundred million dollars, scaled up for Boeing.
findings.number: EV 5,260 (100% of JV); separation 120 (2019), ~300 (total); synergy >=50 per year
findings.quote: Improved competitive position and Boeing's marketing and procurement resources to accelerate E2 ramp up.

findings.topic: Cross-sell mechanism: crew commonality
findings.claim: Airbus says cross-crew qualification across its aircraft families is unique to Airbus and, in management's opinion, an important competitive advantage. Boeing's quoted commonality claim is within its widebody family: the same flight crews can fly the different airplanes. Inference: the narrowbody-to-widebody pull through crew commonality is mainly an Airbus asset. Boeing's cross-sell runs more through relationships, packages and services.
findings.source: Airbus Board Report FY2025 p.14 (repo evidence A-0238, airbus/evidence.jsonl; OCR spacing restored); Transcripts 2006-2025 PDF p.1919 (conference 16 Sep 2014, Raymond Conner)
findings.use_in_model: In Do Nothing, Airbus gains a structural widebody advantage at former 737 operators that move to the A320 family. Put it into a widebody win-rate penalty (see the McDonnell Douglas finding for ranges).
findings.quote: Cross-crew qualification across families of aircraft ... is a unique feature of Airbus that, in management's opinion, constitutes an important competitive advantage.

findings.topic: Bundling within families vs across segments
findings.claim: Boeing filled the 737 NG-to-MAX bridge with 'combination deals' (NG plus MAX), and the 777 bridge by pairing 777 with 777X. Its CEO said widebody buying behaviour 'tend[s] to be a little bit different', and the early 777X backlog was mostly large one-off orders.
findings.source: Transcripts 2006-2025 PDF p.2016 (conference 10 Mar 2014, Dennis Muilenburg); repo evidence B-0554 (FQ4 2011 p.2443), B-0979 (FQ4 2014 p.1869)
findings.use_in_model: The bundling effect is strongest within a family and over transitions. Use a modest cross-segment coefficient. Do not assume each lost narrowbody sale loses a widebody sale.
findings.quote: in many cases, those were combination deals where we'd have customers taking both MAXs and NGs. ... That said, the buying behavior and fleets tend to be a little bit different on the widebody side.

findings.topic: Narrowbody plus widebody package campaigns
findings.claim: Mixed packages do happen. Air India's 2023 commitment to Boeing was 190 737 MAX, 20 787s and 10 777Xs. In 2018 Boeing's CEO said it prices 'holistically across airplanes and services' across its narrowbody and widebody lines. In 2025 a BofA analyst cited Airbus's success bundling the A220 with the A320 (analyst view).
findings.source: Transcripts 2006-2025 PDF p.348 (FQ1 2023, 26 Apr 2023); PDF p.1209 (FQ2 2018, 25 Jul 2018, Muilenburg); Embraer Transcripts PDF p.104 (FQ1 2025, 6 May 2025, Kristine Liwag, BofA)
findings.use_in_model: A Boeing without narrowbodies cannot bid full-fleet packages. Model this as a lower widebody win probability in campaigns tagged 'package', or as a lower widebody price premium.
findings.quote: as you look across our narrowbody and widebody product lines ... we think about pricing, and we're looking at it holistically across airplanes and services, which, I think, is a unique part of the Boeing value proposition.

findings.topic: Limits of loyalty: split orders
findings.claim:
Large carriers often split between Boeing and Airbus:
- United, Continental and Air France-KLM split orders (2011).
- American split its 2011 narrowbody order despite Boeing's claim of 'very high' switching costs.
- United's 2021 order of 270 jets went 200 to Boeing and 70 to Airbus.
All-Boeing accounts are valued by both sides: Southwest (2021), and Air Canada becoming all-Boeing (2014).
findings.source: Repo evidence B-2410 (FQ3 2011 p.2506), BX-0020 / B-2395 (2011-05-24 p.2602); Transcripts PDF p.687 (FQ2 2021, 28 Jul 2021, Calhoun); PDF p.1975 (21 May 2014, Conner)
findings.use_in_model: Cap the cross-sell penalty. Single-supplier accounts (Southwest-type) are where a narrowbody exit costs the widebody relationship most. Multi-supplier majors already split by segment.
findings.quote: Southwest, we benefit from it being an all-Boeing fleet and they benefit from it being all Boeing.

findings.topic: Installed-base lock-in
findings.claim: Boeing describes its customers as tending to 'stay with you once your technology has made it into their operations'. In 2016 it had more than 250 737 customers, about 200 of them not yet committed for follow-on. By 2018 the 787 had 485 repeat orders from 33 customers.
findings.source: Repo evidence B-2439 (Sep 2013 p.2091, McNerney), B-1166 (11 May 2016 p.1615, Conner), B-2489 / A-0135 (May 2018 p.1221)
findings.use_in_model: The Do Nothing world gives up Boeing's 250+ customer narrowbody relationships to Airbus and COMAC by 2060. Treat this as the base on which any widebody cross-sell penalty and any re-entry option value are computed.
findings.quote: customers are hard-fought partners that tend to stay with you once your technology has made it into their operations and so everything is a death-dealing event

findings.topic: Backlog fungibility across a family
findings.claim: Boeing's contracts let delayed customers terminate, claim compensation or 'substitute orders for other Boeing aircraft'. A full family lets Boeing keep customers within the family when one programme slips.
findings.source: Boeing FY2024 10-K risk factors (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF p.2171; repo evidence A-0751)
findings.use_in_model: A widebody-only Boeing loses this hedge: a widebody slip would push customers to Airbus rather than to another Boeing model. Add a small extra cancellation probability on widebody backlog in Do Nothing (judgement).
findings.quote: Delays on the 737, 777X and 787 programs have resulted in, and may continue to result in, customers having the right to terminate orders, be compensated for late deliveries and/or substitute orders for other Boeing aircraft.

findings.topic: Exit precedent: McDonnell Douglas
findings.claim: With its commercial share down to single digits and no new products, Douglas was judged by the FTC in 1997 to be no longer a meaningful competitive force. The judgement drew on interviews with more than 40 airlines. Commissioner Azcuenaga's dissent records that her colleagues concluded most airlines would not buy planes from Douglas. Boeing wound the Douglas lines down: MD deliveries were 54 (1997), 54 (1998), 47 (1999), 7 (2000) and 2 (2001). The MD-11 widebody ended in 2000 after about 200 built. One secondary source puts Douglas at about 6% market share (unverified).
findings.source: FTC Statement of Chairman Pitofsky and Commissioners, 1 Jul 1997, https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/cases-proceedings/public-statements/statement-chairman-robert-pitofsky-commissioners-janet-d-steiger-roscoe-b-starek-iii-christine, and Statement of Commissioner Azcuenaga (ftc.gov), both via search snippets because ftc.gov could not be fetched; GoldmanSachs_BA12826_Jan_28_2026.xlsx 'BCA margin' rows 48-58; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonnell_Douglas_MD-11
findings.use_in_model: The extreme case: losing narrowbody relevance and stopping investment took the widebody franchise down too. Use it to bound a widebody share-penalty scenario of 0 / 5 / 15 points in Do Nothing after 2045. These numbers are judgement; no source quantifies the penalty.
findings.quote: McDonnell Douglas, looking to the future, no longer constitutes a meaningful competitive force in the commercial aircraft market (FTC statement, as returned by search)

findings.topic: Post-exit tail: orphaned-fleet financing
findings.claim: In 2012 Boeing said its customer financing portfolio 'consists primarily of financing receivables for out-of-production aircraft'. By model: 717 $1,781M, 757 $561M, MD-80 $446M and MD-11 $269M, which is $3,057M of the $3,882M listed by model (79%, computed). Boeing named 717 concentration as a risk factor.
findings.source: Boeing FY2012 10-K, customer financing note, printed p.75 (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF p.82) and risk factors PDF p.15
findings.use_in_model: Add a negative tail term to Do Nothing after 2060: residual-value and financing support for an orphaned 737 MAX fleet, sized as a share of fleet value. This is the opposite of the missing aftermarket and terminal value.
findings.quote: Our customer financing portfolio consists primarily of financing receivables for out-of-production aircraft.

findings.topic: Exit precedent: Lockheed L-1011 (single-product airframer)
findings.claim: Lockheed built about 250 TriStars against 446 DC-10s, lost about $2.5B on the programme and left commercial airliners (exit announced 1981, production ended 1984). Reinhardt (1973) showed that counting the opportunity cost of capital raised the programme's break-even to almost twice Lockheed's testimony of 195-205 aircraft.
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_L-1011_TriStar (via search snippet); U. E. Reinhardt, 'Break-Even Analysis for Lockheed's Tri Star: An Application of Financial Theory', Journal of Finance 28(4), Sep 1973 (bibliographic details and argument via search results, https://store.hbr.org/product/investment-analysis-and-lockheed-tri-star/291031); full text not read
findings.use_in_model: A widebody-only airframer with no narrowbody to share overhead has a poor exit record. Also supports keeping cost of capital in break-even tests, as the game does at 10.5%.

findings.topic: Low-rate penalty: organisational forgetting
findings.claim: Benkard's study of L-1011 production data finds that production experience depreciates. Secondary summaries put the rate at about 4% a month, about 39% a year (about 61% retained after one year). Only part of the experience carries over to a new model. Low or variable rates therefore raise unit labour cost.
findings.source: C. L. Benkard, 'Learning and Forgetting: The Dynamics of Aircraft Production', American Economic Review 90(4):1034-1054 (2000), https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/aecrev/v90y2000i4p1034-1054.html; rate per Besanko et al. appendix https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/satterthwaite/research/Appendix-Learning%20by%20doing.pdf and ESB summary (search snippets; paper not read)
findings.use_in_model: Supports (a) a unit-cost penalty on low-rate widebody lines carrying extra overhead, and (b) a fast decay of any re-entry option value. Boeing's narrowbody know-how would depreciate about 39% a year after the MAX line closes.

findings.topic: Illustrative sizing (inference)
findings.claim:
Combining the findings above gives a first-pass stranded-overhead size (inference, not a sourced figure):
- Shared BCA pool F_shared of about $4.6-5.5B a year: R&D $2.0-2.4B, D&A $0.74B and 40-50% of $5.0B G&A. A cross-check is GS's $3.7B unabsorbed in 2020 at about 80% volume loss.
- Times the narrowbody share s_NB of 0.55-0.74, that is about $2.5-4.1B a year with no narrowbody to carry it.
- After resizing of 0.5-0.8, about $0.5-2.0B a year stays on the widebody business.
- On first loss, phi of 9-15% of lost narrowbody revenue gives the same order of magnitude.
findings.source: Derived from: Boeing FY2024 10-K Note 23 and G&A (Boeing 10ks.pdf PDF pp.2219, 2285, 2290); GoldmanSachs_BA12826_Jan_28_2026.xlsx 'BCA margin' r6-10, r77-88; GoldmanSachs_AIRPACompanyModel_Aug_27_2026.xlsx 'Airbus Commercial' r133; Rolls-Royce FY2020 call (Transcript Digest 2010-26 PDF p.300)
findings.use_in_model: Add to Do Nothing a charge that ramps from 2045 with the MAX phase-out to about $1.3-3B a year by 2060. Let it decay with c(t), and keep the residual beyond 2060 through a terminal term; truncating at 2060 hides most of it. The fps world avoids the charge. Run phi, s_NB and the c(t) floor as tornado factors.
findings.unit: US$ billion per year (constant dollars, approximate)

research.summary:
Other industries give three ways to value staying in a core franchise rather than leaving it. All three can be moved to an airframer.
(1) A declining baseline. Christensen et al. (2008) and BCG's Rudden say the do-nothing case is a "nonlinear decline", not a steady state. Kodak/Fujifilm shows how fast that can happen: film demand fell more than 90% in 10 years. BlackBerry lost more than 80% of its value in 3 years.
(2) Continuing value. McKinsey's value-driver formula is CV = NOPAT(1-g/RONIC)/(WACC-g). Mauboussin's competitive-advantage period works the same way: excess returns fade, but the cash flows do not stop.
(3) Option and hysteresis value. In Dixit (1989), exit is rational only well below breakeven because the cost of re-entering is sunk. Kester's growth options and the learning/forgetting work point the same way.
Exit cases show leaving costs money and keeps little: GM paid a $6.2B net charge to sell Opel for about €2.2B; IBM left PCs only after $965M of losses; Microsoft wrote off almost the whole price it paid for Nokia within about 15 months. Successful exits (Intel DRAM 1985, GE under Welch) shared two conditions: the position was already lost, or the business was not #1 or #2, and the capital had a better use. Boeing's narrowbody line meets neither (inference).
Calibration against the game's data (inference, script at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aero-engine-gameboard/95fa875c-ca9d-5564-a6e5-4c9b461d7e56/scratchpad/franchise/tv_illustration.py): at 10.5%, a continuing value after 2059 adds only about $1.2-2.2B to the 10-year fps. A faster, nonlinear Do Nothing decline adds at most about $1.9B. A GM-sized exit charge in 2060 adds about $0.2B. Together that is about $4B, short of the -$6.37B gap (-$8.71B for the 7-year). So franchise terms can only flip the decision if they hit cash flows in the 2040s: services, widebody overhead absorption and cross-sell, which are other topics.
Limits on the evidence:
- This session's network policy blocked fetching full pages (hbr.org, hbs.edu, sec.gov, wikipedia, ssrn and others returned 403 or did not resolve). Quotes come from web-search excerpts and were not checked against the full text.
- The shared web-search budget (200 per turn) ran out partway through. The Burgelman, Argote and Benkard figures therefore come from memory and are marked low confidence. Ghemawat-Nalebuff, Harrigan-Porter, Intel's later move into foundry versus AMD going fabless, and McKinsey's figures for continuing value as a share of total value were not covered. The user can send a follow-up to continue the search.

findings.topic: Do-nothing baseline (Christensen critique of DCF)
findings.claim: Christensen, Kaufman and Shih argue that standard DCF/NPV understates the return on investing. The reason is that the do-nothing comparison wrongly assumes the company's present health continues if it does not invest.
findings.source: Christensen, Kaufman & Shih, 'Innovation Killers', Harvard Business Review, Jan 2008; abstract at https://www.hbs.edu/faculty/Pages/item.aspx?num=31559 (wording as shown in a web-search excerpt; the page itself is blocked in this session)
findings.quote: most executives compare the cash flows from innovation against the default scenario of doing nothing, assuming - incorrectly - that the present health of the company will persist indefinitely if the investment is not made.
findings.use_in_model: The game already meets the core of this critique for the narrowbody line: Do Nothing has the MAX phasing out 2045-2060, so the fps is measured against decline, not stasis. What is missing is that the decline touches only narrowbody operating profit. Generalise the baseline to Baseline_DN(t) = status-quo narrowbody profit + sum over businesses k of d_k(t) x profit_k(t), where d_k captures knock-on effects of exiting (services, widebody overhead, cross-sell). Today every d_k is effectively 1, meaning no effect. Christensen gives the method, not a coefficient.

findings.topic: Do-nothing baseline is a nonlinear decline (BCG)
findings.claim: BCG's Eileen Rudden, quoted in the Innovation Killers discussion, says the most likely cash stream under 'do nothing' is a nonlinear decline in performance, not a continuation of the status quo.
findings.source: Emerald, Strategy & Leadership (2008), 'Strategy in the media', https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/sl.2008.26136caf.002/full/html (citing the HBR article); also ft.lk column https://www.ft.lk/Columnists/killing-innovation-and-being-rewarded/4-375998
findings.quote: the most likely stream of cash for the company in the do-nothing scenario is not a continuation [of] the status quo. It is a nonlinear decline in performance.
findings.use_in_model: Replace the linear 2045-2060 MAX phase-out in Do Nothing with a logistic (S-curve) substitution that starts at the rival's NGSA entry into service: s_MAX(t) = s0 / (1 + exp(k(t - t_mid))). Upper bound (calculation from repo data, inference): the present value of status-quo MAX profit is $1.87B for 2045-2060 and $4.56B for 2040-2060 (wargame/reports/dash-2050-phaseout/data/fps_cash_flows_2030.csv). A faster collapse can therefore add at most about $1.9B to the fps versus Do Nothing, because the fps plan has no MAX deliveries from 2046 anyway.

findings.topic: Real-options exit and re-entry (hysteresis)
findings.claim: Dixit (1989) treats an idle firm and an active firm as call options on each other. A firm enters only when price exceeds variable cost plus interest on the entry cost, and exits only when price falls below variable cost minus interest on the exit cost. The gap between the two (hysteresis) is significant even when sunk costs are small.
findings.source: Dixit, A. (1989), 'Entry and Exit Decisions under Uncertainty', Journal of Political Economy 97(3):620-638; abstract via RePEc/IDEAS https://ideas.repec.org/a/ucp/jpolec/v97y1989i3p620-38.html (as summarised in a web-search result)
findings.quote: hysteresis is significant even when sunk costs are small (per RePEc abstract as rendered in search excerpt)
findings.use_in_model: Two terms. (a) Exit is close to irreversible. After exiting in 2060, Boeing could only re-enter by paying K_reentry (at least the fps bill of $60-65B, plus learning-curve and share-rebuild costs) and starting at a new entrant's share. The re-entry option in Do Nothing is therefore worth about zero; book it explicitly as 0 rather than leave it implicit. (b) A negative stand-alone NPV for the narrowbody alone (-$6.37B) is not by itself an exit signal under Dixit. The comparison should include exit costs and the avoided re-entry cost: V_stay - V_exit = NPV_fps + C_exit + PV(re-entry option lost).

findings.topic: Intel exits DRAM (1985)
findings.claim: Intel left DRAM in 1985. By then it had become a minor player in a crowded, loss-making market, and its fabs had a better use in microprocessors. Grove's test was to ask what a new CEO brought in by the board would do. Moore's answer was that a new CEO would take Intel out of memories.
findings.source: Intel 1986 shareholder letter (Grove & Moore) quoted at https://aletteraday.substack.com/p/rp-letter-15-andy-grove-and-gordon ; NPR 2016 https://www.npr.org/2016/03/22/471389537/digital-pioneer-andrew-grove-led-intels-shift-from-chips-to-microprocessors ; Stanford GSB case 'Intel Corporation (A) The DRAM Decision' https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/case-studies/intel-corporation-dram-decision
findings.quote: phased out of the dynamic random access memory (DRAM) business in 1985 ... a minor participant in the crowded, loss-plagued DRAM market (1986 letter, as quoted)
findings.use_in_model: Turn Intel's two conditions into tests for the Do Nothing branch: exit creates value only if (i) the market position is already lost and (ii) the released capital and capacity earn more elsewhere. Model it as Redeploy_DN = sum over t of (ROIC_alt - WACC) x capital released(t). For Boeing the default should be about 0 (inference): its narrowbody share is a franchise floor of about 40% (wargame/profiles/boeing/profile.md citing B-0638), and no alternative product has comparable volume.

findings.topic: Intel exit method: margin per unit of constrained capacity
findings.claim: Burgelman's account of Intel's DRAM exit shows that Intel's internal rule, allocating wafer starts by margin per wafer, moved capacity out of DRAM before top management formally decided to exit. In this account Intel's DRAM share fell from about 83% (1974) to about 1% (1984). These figures are from memory and were not verified in this session.
findings.source: Burgelman, R. A. (1994), 'Fading Memories: A Process Theory of Strategic Business Exit in Dynamic Environments', Administrative Science Quarterly 39(1):24-56 (from memory; not retrieved in this session because the search budget ran out)
findings.use_in_model: Compare narrowbody and widebody on operating profit per scarce resource: engineering hours, final-assembly slots, balance-sheet capacity. That is Intel's margin-per-wafer-start rule applied to an airframer. Treat the share figures only as an illustration of how far a position has to erode before exit is the obvious move.

findings.topic: IBM leaves PCs: exit only after sustained losses
findings.claim: IBM's PC unit lost $965M from 1 Jan 2001 to 30 Jun 2004: $397M in 2001, $171M in 2002, $258M in 2003 and $139M in the first half of 2004. IBM sold it only after this run of negative operating profit.
findings.source: IBM Form 8-K (Dec 2004), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000051143/000110465904041643/a04-14476_28k.htm ; InfoWorld https://www.infoworld.com/article/2212068/ibm-s-pc-unit-lost-money-from-2001-onwards.html
findings.quote: IBM's personal computer business racked up $965 million in losses between Jan. 1, 2001, and June 30, 2004, according to a filing with the SEC.
findings.use_in_model: Add an exit-trigger rule to the Do Nothing branch: exit becomes value-maximising only when the incumbent product's operating profit turns persistently negative. IBM's unit averaged about -$275M a year (calculation). In the game the MAX earns a positive 8% margin ($3.84M per aircraft) up to its phase-out, so the IBM rule would not trigger exit before then. Pair it with a margin fade for the MAX (see Kodak).

findings.topic: IBM leaves PCs: an exit structured to keep part of the franchise
findings.claim: Lenovo paid $650M in cash and $600M in its own stock and took on $500M of liabilities, about $1.75B in total. IBM came away with an 18.9% stake in the merged company. eWeek reported that the unit's profits had been 'nearly negligible' (under $100M in the latest year), which conflicts with the 8-K's loss figures.
findings.source: Silicon Republic https://www.siliconrepublic.com/careers/ibm-sells-pc-division-for-us1-75bn ; eWeek https://www.eweek.com/pc-hardware/ibm-spins-off-pc-division-with-chinese-partner/
findings.quote: IBM receives 18.9pc of the new merged company.
findings.use_in_model: A partial-stay variant of exit: V_exit = P_sale + s x PV(successor's profit) + retained services - C_exit, with s = retained stake (IBM: 0.189). In game terms the closest move is 'Launch fps via Embraer'. A Do Nothing in which Boeing licenses or partners its narrowbody line would get s > 0 instead of a flat zero after 2060.

findings.topic: Nokia: an under-reinvested franchise, and what the seller kept
findings.claim: Microsoft paid €3.79B for Nokia's Devices & Services business and €1.65B to license Nokia's patents, €5.44B in total. The IP Nokia kept and licensed was about 30% of the deal value (calculation).
findings.source: Nokia/Microsoft announcement, Sept 2013, as quoted by PhoneArena https://www.phonearena.com/news/Microsoft-to-acquire-Nokias-Devices---Services-for-7.17-billion_id46994 and Computerworld https://www.computerworld.com/article/2945371/microsoft-writes-off-76b-admits-failure-of-nokia-acquisition.html
findings.quote: Microsoft will pay EUR 3.79 billion to purchase substantially all of Nokia's Devices & Services business, and EUR 1.65 billion to license Nokia's patents, for a total transaction price of EUR 5.44 billion in cash.
findings.use_in_model: In Do Nothing, split what Boeing keeps after exit into IP and installed-base support versus production franchise. Nokia kept about 30% of its exit value as IP. For Boeing the analogue is the MAX type certificate, data rights and fleet support. These feed the services/aftermarket term, which another topic covers, rather than the production term.

findings.topic: Nokia: franchise value of a non-renewed platform falls to about zero
findings.claim: In July 2015 Microsoft took a write-down of about $7.6B on Phone Hardware assets and goodwill. That was close to the whole purchase price, about 15 months after the April 2014 close. It also announced up to 7,800 job cuts.
findings.source: Computerworld, July 2015, https://www.computerworld.com/article/2945371/microsoft-writes-off-76b-admits-failure-of-nokia-acquisition.html ; GSMArena https://m.gsmarena.com/microsoft_lays_off_7800_people_writes_off_nokia_acquisition-news-12959.php
findings.quote: the company concluded that an impairment adjustment of its Phone Hardware segment assets and goodwill of approximately $7.6 billion is required.
findings.use_in_model: Give a product line that is no longer competitive and not renewed no residual or salvage franchise value. Set the Do Nothing terminal value of the narrowbody production franchise to 0, which is consistent with the game's zero deliveries after 2060, and do not add back a 'brand' value for the exited line.

findings.topic: BlackBerry: speed of franchise decay, then hardware exit
findings.claim: RIM was once valued at about $83B (June 2008 peak). It had lost more than 80% of that (about $70B) by 2011 and 93% by 2012, after iPhone and Android arrived. In Sept 2016 it ended all in-house hardware development.
findings.source: AP via Coeur d'Alene Press 2012 https://cdapress.com/news/2012/may/31/blackberry-maker-at-a-crossroads-5/ ; Bloomberg-syndicated 2011 report via TI Inside https://tiinside.com.br/en/22/06/2011/rumores-sobre-a-venda-da-rim-ganham-forca-no-mercado/ ; AFP via Gulf Times 2016 https://www.gulf-times.com/story/515433/blackberry-to-outsource-handsets-will-halt-production/amp ; Canadian Encyclopedia https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/blackberry-limited
findings.quote: The company plans to end all internal hardware development and will outsource that function to partners. (CEO John Chen, Sept 2016)
findings.use_in_model: Calibrates an upper bound on the decay rate in a fast-cycle industry. Losing 80% in about 3 years implies lambda of about ln(5)/3, or 0.54 a year, in V(t) = V0 x exp(-lambda t). That is market value, not unit share. To transfer it to an airframer, scale lambda by the ratio of product cycles, roughly 2-3 years in phones to 25-30 years in airframes (inference). Use it only as a stress case for how fast the MAX could decline once NGSA is in service.

findings.topic: Kodak versus Fujifilm: the same decline, different reinvestment
findings.claim: In 2000, film made up about 60% of Fujifilm's sales and up to 70% of its profit; another source says almost 60% of operating profit. By 2010 world film demand was below 10% of its 2000 level. Fujifilm reinvested in adjacent businesses (VISION 75 plan, 2004) and survived. Kodak filed for Chapter 11 in January 2012.
findings.source: PetaPixel 2018 https://petapixel.com/2018/10/19/why-kodak-died-and-fujifilm-thrived-a-tale-of-two-film-companies/ ; HBS Digital Initiative https://d3.harvard.edu/platform-rctom/?p=19824 ; Marketplace 2012 https://www.marketplace.org/story/2012/01/19/kodak-files-bankruptcy
findings.quote: by 2010, global demand for photographic film had fallen to less than one-tenth of what it was in 2000
findings.use_in_model: (a) Calibration for the nonlinear decline curve: the core product lost 90% of demand within about 10 years once a substitute matured. (b) Kodak went bankrupt because fixed costs and legacy obligations did not shrink with revenue. That is the overhead-absorption mechanism the game omits. Use it as the precedent for a Do Nothing term in which the BCA fixed-cost base is spread over the widebody line alone after the narrowbody exits (inference).

findings.topic: Kodak: margin erodes before volume collapses
findings.claim: Kodak's company-wide gross margin fell from 50% (1992) to 36% (2002) and 32% (2003). Kodak's 1981 internal market-intelligence study (Vince Barabba) had warned that digital could replace film but that adoption would stay small for a while, giving roughly a ten-year window.
findings.source: Rochester Business Journal, 26 Mar 2004 https://rbj.net/2004/03/26/shrinking-profit-margin-forces-kodak-to-adapt ; Chunka Mui https://chunkamui.medium.com/how-kodak-failed-e1f929e12aa7
findings.quote: digital photography had the potential capability to replace Kodak's established film based business (Mui, describing the 1981 study)
findings.use_in_model: Add a margin fade to the declining incumbent product. In Do Nothing the MAX margin is a flat 8% to 2060; let it fade toward 0 after NGSA's entry into service, m(t) = 8% x exp(-phi(t - t_NGSA)). Kodak's 18-point fall over 11 years is a rough guide for phi. This makes Do Nothing worse and so raises the fps's relative value (inference). Size it with the bound above: about $1.9B PV at most for 2045-2060.

findings.topic: GE portfolio rule: No.1 or No.2, else fix, sell or close
findings.claim: Welch ruled that each GE business had to be No.1 or No.2 in its market or be fixed, sold or closed. Between 1981 and 1990 GE sold more than 200 businesses, which had made up 25% of 1980 sales, freeing over $11B of capital.
findings.source: Bartlett & Wozny, 'GE's Two-Decade Transformation: Jack Welch's Leadership' (HBS case), https://eclass.aueb.gr/modules/document/file.php/ODE462/3.-GE_s-Two-Decade-Transformation-Jack-Welch_s-Leadership.pdf ; CEIBS https://www.ceibs.edu/new-papers-columns/22566 ; Selling Power https://www.sellingpower.com/2010/02/02/4905/the-best-manager-in-america
findings.quote: Between 1981 and 1990, GE freed up over $11 billion of capital by selling off more than 200 businesses, which had accounted for 25% of 1980 sales.
findings.use_in_model: Add a market-position gate on the franchise term. If Boeing's projected narrowbody rank is #1 or #2, keep the franchise value; at #3 or below (for example behind Airbus and COMAC), set it to 0 and value exit. Boeing today is #2 of 2, so it passes. GE's exits made money because buyers existed. In the game's Do Nothing, the 2060 exit is a wind-down with no buyer, so the sale value is about 0 (inference).

findings.topic: GM sells Opel: what exiting costs
findings.claim: GM sold Opel/Vauxhall to PSA in 2017 for about €2.2B (€1.32B for Opel plus €0.9B for GM Financial's European unit). It first estimated a $4-4.5B charge; the final charge in the 10-K was $6.2B net of tax. GM Europe had lost money for 16 years in a row.
findings.source: GM Form 10-K FY2017 https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001467858/000146785818000022/gm201710k.htm ; GM 10-Q Q3 2017 https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001467858/000146785817000133/gm2017q3.htm ; Yahoo/Reuters https://news.yahoo.com/gm-sells-opel-vauxhall-psa-183016554.html
findings.quote: total charge from the sale of the European Business of $6.2 billion, net of tax
findings.use_in_model: Add an exit-cost term to Do Nothing: C_exit = severance + pensions + supplier termination + impairment, booked in the exit year. GM's charge was about 2.8 times its sale proceeds (calculation). Timing matters: Boeing's Do Nothing exit falls around 2060, with a game discount factor of 0.0335, so even a GM-sized $6.2B charge is only about $0.2B in 2026 present value (calculation). Exit costs that land in the 2040s, as volume falls, are worth much more.

findings.topic: Ford leaves sedans but keeps the Mustang
findings.claim: In April 2018 Ford said it would not invest in further generations of traditional sedans for North America. It kept only the Mustang and a Focus Active crossover, raised its cost-cut target to $25.5B by 2022, and aimed for an 8% margin by 2020.
findings.source: Fortune, 25 Apr 2018 https://fortune.com/2018/04/25/ford-stop-making-cars-sedans ; Marketing Dive https://marketingdive.com/news/ford-eyes-big-marketing-cuts-as-it-drops-most-sedans-from-lineup/522295
findings.quote: will not invest in next generations of traditional Ford sedans for North America
findings.use_in_model: A partial-exit template: leave the commodity part of a segment, keep the one nameplate that carries franchise value, and move capital to higher-return segments (trucks and SUVs). Transfer: add a 'stay small' alternative to the binary fps/Do Nothing choice, such as a niche narrowbody (MAX 10 continuation or derivative) at reduced share and reduced bill. Value it as share s_small x market x margin, minus a smaller bill.

findings.topic: Nameplate equity lasts after a product lapses (Ford Taurus)
findings.claim: Ford dropped the Taurus in 2006, and Mulally brought the name back in Feb 2007. Ford's surveys showed 80% of consumers still recognised Taurus, while only 40% knew the Five Hundred existed. Mulally cited a name bought by 7 million buyers and backed by hundreds of millions of dollars of advertising over 20 years.
findings.source: NBC News 2007 https://www.nbcnews.com/id/17033668 ; Consumer Reports 2007 https://www.consumerreports.org/cro/news/2007/08/bully-about-the-return-of-taurus/index.htm ; Honolulu Advertiser 11 Feb 2007 https://the.honoluluadvertiser.com/article/2007/Feb/11/bz/FP702110302.html
findings.quote: Taurus name was still recognized by 80% of consumers, while only 40% of buyers knew the Five Hundred existed (as reported)
findings.use_in_model: Add a franchise-retention parameter rho: the share of the incumbent's customer base (737 operators, fleet commonality, crews, spares) that a successor inherits without paying full campaign cost. In the fps branch rho > 0 applies to the fps share ramp. In Do Nothing that customer equity decays to 0 by the 2060 exit. Ford's evidence: awareness of the old name was 2 times that of the new one even after the product lapsed.

findings.topic: Automotive platform renewal economics
findings.claim: Automakers fund segments as a chain of renewals. A new volume platform costs about $1-2B. The typical cadence is a facelift around year 2, major body changes around year 4 and an all-new platform around year 8. GM planned to double platform lifespans (2016). Ford expected $7B of savings from consolidating platforms. Audi and Porsche estimated about 30% more cost each to develop EV platforms separately.
findings.source: Gardner Web https://www.gardnerweb.com/news/gm-targets-fewer-platforms-longer-product-cycles ; GM Authority 2016 https://gmauthority.com/blog/2016/10/general-motors-will-double-lifespan-of-new-vehicle-platforms-architectures/ ; WhichCar https://whichcar.com.au/news/ford-to-cull-vehicle-platforms-to-just-five ; Engadget 2018 https://www.engadget.com/2018-02-10-porsche-and-audi-will-share-electric-car-platform.html
findings.use_in_model: Value staying as a series of generations rather than one 20-year window: V_franchise = v_gen / (1 - (1+r)^-T), with T the generation cycle. For an airframer (707 -> 737 Classic -> NG -> MAX, roughly 25-30 years) at r = 10.5% and T = 25, the multiplier is 1/(1 - 0.0824) = 1.09 (calculation). Later generations add only about 9% to the first generation's value at the game's discount rate (inference). The figures are dated (1998-2018) secondary sources.

findings.topic: Continuing value (McKinsey value-driver formula)
findings.claim: McKinsey's Valuation (Koller, Goedhart, Wessels) recommends the value-driver formula for post-horizon value, CV = NOPAT_{t+1} x (1 - g/RONIC) / (WACC - g), over the plain Gordon formula. When RONIC = WACC, growth adds nothing and CV = NOPAT/WACC. The firm loses excess returns but keeps its cash flows.
findings.source: Jennergren (Stockholm School of Economics), 'Value Driver Formulas for Continuing Value' https://research.hhs.se/esploro/outputs/workingPaper/Value-Driver-Formulas-for-Continuing-Value/991001535499306056 ; Financial Edge https://felix.fe.training/video-lesson/lesson/advanced-valuation-techniques/?video=8709 ; Ed Bodmer https://edbodmer.com/mckinsey-value-driver-formula-distortions/
findings.quote: The influential valuation book by an author team from McKinsey recommends the so-called value driver formula rather than the Gordon formula for the continuing value in the post-horizon period
findings.use_in_model: Add a CV at the end of the fps window. Calculation from repo data (wargame/reports/dash-2050-phaseout/data/fps_cash_flows_2030.csv): the 10-year fps delivers 402 aircraft in 2060 (not counted) x $14.10M = $5.67B profit. With RONIC = WACC = 10.5%, CV(2059) = $54.0B and PV(2026) = $2.00B (discount factor 0.03707). With g = -6.5%, matching the 402 -> 376 decline, PV = $1.24B; with g = +1%, $2.21B. Against the -$6.37B gap a continuing value alone does not flip the decision (inference). Do Nothing's CV is 0 because it has no deliveries after 2060.

findings.topic: Competitive advantage period and fade (Mauboussin)
findings.claim: Mauboussin defines the competitive advantage period (CAP, also called fade rate, value growth duration or T) as the time during which returns on incremental investment exceed the cost of capital. Competition then drives returns down to the cost of capital, not to zero cash flow. Later work notes that the average CAP is shrinking, and suggests basing the terminal-value fade on empirical sector data.
findings.source: Mauboussin & Johnson, 'Measuring the Moat' (CSFB 2002) https://www.safalniveshak.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/07/Measuring-The-Moat-CSFB.pdf ; Mauboussin & Callahan, 'Measuring the Moat' (Consilient Observer) https://eatonvance.com/content/dam/im/assets/publication/thought-leadership/consilient-observer/article_measuringthemoat.pdf ; Damodaran CAP notes https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/pdfiles/eqnotes/cap.pdf ; Hedge Fund Alpha summary https://hedgefundalpha.com/education/michael-mauboussin-assessing-the-magnitude-and-sustainability-of-value-creation/
findings.quote: Companies earning high returns attract competitors willing to take a lesser, albeit still attractive, return which will drive down aggregate industry returns to the opportunity cost of capital.
findings.use_in_model: The game's 20-year cutoff acts as CAP = 20 followed by zero cash flow, which is stricter than practice. Practice keeps zero-economic-profit cash flows (CV = NOPAT/WACC) or fades the margin: m(t) = m* + (m0 - m*) x exp(-phi(t - EIS)), with m* the margin that earns exactly WACC. Expose phi and m* as sliders. The 2059 value is so heavily discounted that the result moves by at most about $2B (see the continuing-value finding).

findings.topic: Terminal value for declining firms (Damodaran)
findings.claim: Damodaran: the stable growth rate in a terminal value can be negative, which implicitly assumes the firm disappears over time, yet analysts almost never assume this. A declining firm ends in distress, as a smaller but healthier firm, or in liquidation, whichever pays more. For distress he weights survival against failure; one example uses a 20% chance of failure with liquidation recovering 50% of book.

findings.quote: pushing the company either into distress (where equity will be worth nothing) or into a terminal value, as a smaller, but healthier, company or into a liquidation value, if that yields a higher payoff.
findings.use_in_model: In Do Nothing, value Boeing Commercial after the exit as V = p_survive x V(smaller widebody-only going concern) + (1 - p_survive) x liquidation value. The negative-growth Gordon formula is already implied by the MAX phase-out (g = -100% at 2060, so TV = 0). The new piece is an enterprise-level probability weight for the sub-scale remaining business. That is a parameter (default 1, meaning no distress) to be calibrated by the overhead-absorption topic.

findings.topic: Growth options and present value of growth opportunities (Kester)
findings.claim: Kester (HBR 1984) attributes the part of a firm's market value not explained by assets in place to the present value of its growth options. Later studies find growth opportunities account for a larger share of market value than assets in place under standard assumptions, though the estimates depend on the model used.
findings.source: Kester, W. C. (1984), 'Today's Options for Tomorrow's Growth', Harvard Business Review, Mar-Apr, 153-160 (cited via https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/3690 and https://emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1016/S0742-3322(07)24017-3)
findings.quote: the value of growth opportunities is found to account for a larger proportion of market values than assets-in-place under standard assumptions (later study, not Kester's own figure)
findings.use_in_model: Add an option-value term only to the stay branch: Option_fps2 = BlackScholesCall(S = PV of next-generation profits, K = next bill, T = years to that decision, sigma = demand/margin volatility). Do Nothing extinguishes it. Because any successor decision falls around 2060 or later, discount factors are about 0.03, so the term is likely under $1B at 10.5% (inference). Its main use is to show that this channel cannot close the gap.

findings.topic: Capability decay: learning and forgetting
findings.claim: Organisational knowledge from production depreciates quickly. Argote, Beckman and Epple (1990) found rapid knowledge depreciation in Liberty-ship yards; from memory, only a few percent of the knowledge stock remained after a year. Benkard (2000) found that experience depreciated in Lockheed L-1011 production, which explains cost increases after output cuts. Neither figure was verified in this session.
findings.source: Argote, Beckman & Epple (1990), 'The Persistence and Transfer of Learning in Industrial Settings', Management Science 36(2):140-154; Benkard (2000), 'Learning and Forgetting: The Dynamics of Aircraft Production', American Economic Review 90(4):1034-1054 (both from memory; search budget ran out before verification)
findings.use_in_model: Add a capability-decay parameter delta to the re-entry cost: K_reentry(tau) = K_new x [1 - (1 - delta)^tau x learning credit], where tau is years since the last clean-sheet narrowbody programme. With delta in the tens of percent a year, a Do Nothing Boeing re-entering after 2060 faces new-entrant costs. That supports setting the re-entry option to about 0 and treating exit as irreversible.

findings.topic: Boeing's own franchise valuation practice (bridge to the airframer)
findings.claim: Boeing's business cases already value franchises on market potential and multi-decade lives, not on an initial window. Smith (CFO, 2018) said they count market potential, not just the initial order quantity. Muilenburg called the 777X a 50- to 60-year widebody franchise. Albaugh (2011) named the 777 and the 737 as Boeing's two franchise programmes. Boeing bid the tanker's development phase at 0% margin for a 400-plus aircraft market.
findings.source: Repo: wargame/profiles/boeing/executives/evidence.jsonl BX-1545 (FQ3 2018 call, p.1150), BX-1033 (2016 investor day, p.1629), BX-1411 (FQ2 2014 call, p.1932); wargame/profiles/boeing/evidence.jsonl B-2397 (2011-05-24 investor conference, p.2605), B-0918
findings.quote: we are taking into account the considerable market potential in our business cases and not just the initial order quantity (Greg Smith, BX-1545); So this is a 50-, 60-year widebody franchise (Muilenburg, BX-1033)
findings.use_in_model: Justifies replacing the 20-year window with a franchise horizon of 50-60 years, or a CV, in Boeing's own valuation language. It also means a strict 20-year cutoff is less generous than Boeing's stated practice. Flag this in the brief as 'Boeing values franchises this way; the game does not'.

findings.topic: Calibration: how big the franchise terms must be to flip the fps decision
findings.claim: Inference from repo data: the 10-year fps is -$6.37B against Do Nothing (7-year: -$8.71B). The transferable cross-industry terms add roughly: continuing value after 2059 about +$1.2-2.2B; a nonlinear (Kodak/BlackBerry-style) Do Nothing decline of the MAX at most about +$1.9B; a GM-sized exit charge in 2060 about +$0.2B; options on later generations under about $1B. That totals about $4B, short of the gap. The rest (about $2.4B or more for the 10-year) would have to come from cross-business effects that hit in the 2040s: services, widebody overhead absorption and cross-sell.

design.how_boeing_frames_it:
Boeing has never treated leaving the narrowbody market as an option. It frames the trade-off in two layers.

(1) For niches it uses a plain forward-looking business case and leaves.
- 717 ended in 2005 with about $380M of charges, because 'the overall market for the airplane does not support continuing 717 production'.
- 757 ended in 2004, with the 737NG said to cover the space.
- 747X dropped in 2001, leaving the very-large segment to the A380.
- 747-8 was kept going through about $4.2B of reach-forward losses (B-0143, B-0235, B-1108, B-1243). The stop test is remaining revenue against remaining cost (B-0153).
- NMA (a 4,000-5,000-aircraft segment) was shelved in 2020 when its own case did not close (B-1436, B-1613).
The 757 exit is the clearest cost of leaving: the A321neo later won 71% of the upper narrowbody against 29% for the MAX 9/10 (Avolon via AIN, 2017-08-31), and the attempt to get back in never launched.

(2) For the core narrowbody, share at risk is decisive.
- In 2011 McNerney: 'if it looked like we are putting meaningful market share at risk by waiting to do a new airplane, we would re-engine instead' (B-0422). The 2015 justification was 'years of near-term market share strength' (B-1038). Boeing chose the cheapest adequate defence, a re-engine at about 10-15% of a clean sheet's R&D (B-0432).
- That followed a defection. McNerney said in April 2011 that a 3-4-year gap would not lose customers (B-0338). In July 2011 American put 260 of 460 aircraft with Airbus, and Boeing 'got half of it' (B-0803).
- The red line is about 40% share. Albaugh in 2012: 'We do not want them to get to 60% and us, 40%', because the leader gets learning-curve and pricing advantages (B-0638). Calhoun in 2022 accepted a stable 40% (B-1936). Boeing now holds about 34% of the single-aisle backlog (AIN, 2026-01-07).

Since 2016 the public doctrine has been 'It will not be based on market share' (B-1131, Muilenburg). Yet Boeing's own practice already includes the franchise terms the game omits:
- KC-46 was valued as 'a 50-, 60-year widebody franchise' (BX-1033), and the T-X/MQ-25 bids counted 'considerable market potential ... not just the initial order quantity' (BX-1545).
- The NMA case added lifecycle services value to the airplane's own NPV (B-1457).
- Programme accounting runs in roughly 10-year blocks extended in steps, with NG and MAX in one 737 accounting quantity (B-0476, B-0708).
- Albaugh valued low-rate programmes for the overhead they absorb (2012 transcript p.2370).
- Boeing spent about $5B to keep the 737 workforce and supply chain through the grounding (B-1618, B-1794).

Today's leadership treats a successor as inevitable but gated by three conditions: market, technology and Boeing's own financial and capacity readiness (Ortberg, BX-1296), with debt paid down first.
- CFO Malave, March 2026: 'there will be a day where we have to enter into a new program. That day is not today' (Transcript Digest (4).pdf p.100).
- Ortberg, July 2026, called the next airplane 'the opportunity to change' Boeing's share of industry profit (p.46). He expects to be able to fund it by about 2030, with entry into service by the end of the 2030s (FT via Irish Times, 2026-07-20, search excerpt).
- The CFO calls a new airplane a 50-year product (B-2278).

So Boeing frames the decision as business-case first, with franchise effects as explicit, sized cash terms and share mattering when its loss is large and near. That is the structure of C1-C6.
design.how_others_value_it:
Sell-side and rating analysts never stop at a programme horizon.
- They run an explicit forecast, then a fade, then a perpetuity. Goldman Sachs's Airbus DCF uses 9% and 3% long-term growth (repo airbus/analyst_models_2026.md l.111). Its Rolls-Royce DCF puts about 64% of EV after 2036 (rolls_royce/analyst_models_2026.md l.90).
- Morningstar gives wide-moat firms such as Boeing at least 20 years of excess returns, then a perpetuity in which new capital earns WACC. It estimates 'half of Boeing's enterprise value is derived from its 737 product line', about $65B on the board's $130B EV (analyst estimate, search excerpt).
- Barclays (2019) put the whole narrowbody industry at $238B PV, about $2.4B per share point (analyst estimate, CNBC 2019-10-15).
- Price targets of about 22.5x FCF imply a permanent franchise (inference).
- McKinsey's value-driver formula, CV = NOPAT(1-g/RONIC)/(WACC-g), and Mauboussin's competitive-advantage period are the standard tools. Damodaran allows a negative-growth terminal value and adds a distress weight for a shrinking firm.

Airbus pays to stay in.
- The A320neo cost about EUR 1bn and left the CSeries 'virtually no business case' (Leahy, FlightGlobal). It has 11,529 orders (A-0246).
- It relaunched the A350 as the XWB for about EUR 11.6bn rather than cede the segment (EADS, 2006-12-01).
- Faury on the next single-aisle: 'If we move first, the supply chain will come to us' (Aviation Week).

Exits show the franchise is lost at the decision and almost never rebuilt.
- MDC took about 3-4% of 1996 orders against a 12% ten-year average once it stopped launching products (EC M.877; Boeing, 1997-05-21). The FTC judged it 'no longer ... a meaningful competitive force'.
- None of eight airframer exits since 1962 has come back.
- Exits are priced at the trough: BAE sold 20% of Airbus for EUR 2.75bn; Bombardier sold 50.01% of the CSeries for C$1.
- Exit charges run to about 1-3 years of the segment's losses (Douglas $1.4B, Saab SKr4bn, BAE GBP 400M, GM-Opel $6.2B).
- The installed-base aftermarket outlives the exit and can be sold: Rolls-Royce's IAE stake brought $1.5bn plus flight-hour payments to 2027 (RR release 2012-06-29), and Mitsubishi paid $550M plus $200M of liabilities for CRJ support. Rolls-Royce's CEO: 'our installed base ... is where the majority of the value of the business lies' (RR digest p.899).
- Rolls-Royce has been trying to re-enter narrowbodies since its 2012 exit, only through a partner, and expects no entry into service before about 2035.
- Pratt & Whitney harvested widebody and 'over-earn[ed]' on aftermarket before losing the next generation (P-1125).

Other industries say the same.
- Christensen et al. (HBR 2008): the do-nothing case wrongly assumes 'the present health of the company will persist'.
- Dixit (1989): exit and re-entry are hysteretic, so an exit is close to irreversible.
- Intel left DRAM (1985) and GE applied its No.1-or-No.2 rule only when the position was already lost and the capital had a better use.
- Kodak's fixed costs outlived its revenue.

Boeing's narrowbody meets neither of the Intel/GE exit conditions (inference).
design.recommended_base_case:
Add the six terms to the fps-vs-Do-Nothing bridge as separate visible lines, at the game's 10.5% on constant 2026 dollars, computed per round from the game's own delivery rows. Base settings:
- **C1 continuing value:** the game's uncounted rows to 2060, then share x the 2060 market held at 1,166 a year, with RONIC = WACC. Deduct a sustaining derivative of 12.5% of the bill at EIS+27. Services on post-window deliveries go in C1b.
- **C2 services:** $0.09M profit per narrowbody-year, or $0.642M PV per delivery, on every counted MAX and fps delivery in both branches. Cohort tails are not cut at 2060.
- **C3 stranded overhead:** F_shared $5.0B x s_NB 0.64 = $3.2B a year, residual rho 35% (a permanent $1.1B a year after exit), cut speed alpha 15% a year, from 2040.
- **C4 widebody erosion:** 5 pp in Do Nothing, phased with the run-off. Label it judgement and show it as a slider.
- **C5 Do Nothing price fade:** 1.5% of MAX price from NGSA entry in 2037, ramped over 5 years; full in Do Nothing, half on fps-plan MAX deliveries.
- **C6 exit charge:** $3.0B in 2060, with the re-entry option booked at 0.

**Result at 10.5% (franchise_model.py):**

| Plan | Game gap vs Do Nothing | Base terms | New gap | Low terms | High terms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10-year | -$6.37B | +$3.93B | -$2.44B | +$1.50B (gap -$4.86B) | +$8.16B (gap +$1.80B) |
| 7-year | -$8.71B | +$5.38B | -$3.32B | +$2.68B (gap -$6.03B) | +$10.08B (gap +$1.37B) |

The 10-year base terms break down as C1+C1b +1.97, C2 +0.24, C3 +0.61, C4 +0.27, C5 +0.75 and C6 +0.10. A strict-evidence variant, without the weak C4 and C5, adds +$2.92B and +$4.26B, leaving gaps of -$3.45B and -$4.45B.

**Verdict at 10.5%:** the franchise terms close about 60% of the gap, but Do Nothing still ranks first. The 10-year stays the better fps plan. The fps flips only in the high case, or if the real discount rate is about 9.3-9.4% or lower. Most franchise value lands after 2055, where discount factors are 0.05 or below. The rate is therefore the decisive input. Report the bridge at both:
- **10.5%** (the game's rate).
- **About 8.1% real** (10.5% treated as nominal, less 2.2% CPI): base gaps +$4.45B (10-year) and +$6.70B (7-year).
- **About 6.5% real** (analyst-consistent: 9% nominal less 2.2% CPI): even the game's own gaps shrink to -$1.73B and -$0.59B. Low terms give +$4.58B and +$9.51B; base terms give +$15.6B and +$21.4B.

**Rules for implementation:**
- Apply any perpetuity symmetrically: if C1 runs forever, so do C3 and C4.
- Never extend the window and add a CV in the same run.
- Keep the game's debt penalty and Ortberg's balance-sheet gate. Franchise terms raise the value of being ready to launch; they do not relax the cash constraint.
- Treat Do Nothing in 2030 as a deferral. The game's 2035, 2045 and 2050 rounds can still launch the fps, so C3-C6 bite only on the path that ends in exit. Recompute them each round.
caveats: The discount rate decides the result. The game discounts constant-2026-dollar flows at 10.5%, about 12.9% nominal at 2.2% CPI. Analysts use about 8-10% nominal: Morningstar Boeing 8.6% (search extract only), GS Airbus 9%, GS Rolls-Royce 8.46%. The base franchise terms flip the decision at a real rate of about 9.3-9.4% or lower. If 10.5% was meant as a nominal WACC, the consistent real rate is about 8.1% and the fps wins in the base case. Re-discounting the game's flows at other rates uses the CSV's net_vs_status_quo column (it reproduces the game's PV exactly at 10.5%). The game's debt-penalty logic is not re-run, so treat those results as approximate.

The post-2060 demand tail drives C1. The run's demand curve falls after 2060 because it holds only replacement of today's fleet plus growth (1,166 a year in 2060, 320 in 2072, 78 in 2080; tail.py docstring). The base uses tail.py's 'held' variant. Under the as-run curve C1 is about $1.1B (10-year) instead of $1.9B. The conservative game curve gives $3.6B.

Do Nothing in round 1 (2030) is a deferral, not an exit. The game lets Boeing launch the fps in the 2035, 2045 and 2050 rounds. C3-C6 value only the path that ends in exit by 2060 and must be recomputed per round. C6's re-entry option is zero only after 2060.

Several key inputs are inferences, not sourced figures: services profit per narrowbody-year ($0.05-0.15M), the overhead residual rho and cut speed alpha, the widebody share loss (0/5/15 pp), and the MAX price concession (0/1.5/3%). No source gives any of them directly. C4 and C5 are rated weak and should be shown as sliders, with a strict-evidence view that leaves them out (base +$2.92B / +$4.26B instead of +$3.93B / +$5.38B).

The game's margins have no documented derivation in the repo; fps 25.64% and MAX 8% appear only as defaults in harness.py line 102 and combined_dash.py lines 908-909. If the fps margin already includes lifecycle or services value, cut C2. The 8% MAX margin is far below GS's 2018 737 programme margin of about 22.5% (analyst estimate), which makes Do Nothing's MAX stream, and so C5, small.

Calibration gap against analysts (inference). The game values Do Nothing's whole 2026-2060 MAX profit at $20.1B PV, against Morningstar's implied ~$65B for the 737 line (half of the board's $130B EV; analyst estimate). One fps share point (20 aircraft a year x $14.1M over 2040-59) is worth about $0.63B PV in the game, against Barclays' ~$2.4B (2019 $) per narrowbody share point (analyst estimate). The game's combination of a 10.5% real rate, an 8% MAX margin and a 20-year window values the narrowbody franchise at roughly one-third of what the market prices.

Execution haircut not in the base case. Franchise defence has carried very large costs: MAX grounding about $18.6B (Boeing, January 2020) and $45.6B of one-time and abnormal BCA costs over 2019-25 (GS, analyst estimate). Flagship programmes have also failed to pay back (A380, L-1011). A probability that the franchise premise fails, for example 20%, would cut C1 and C2 for the fps by that share. The researchers' tail-risk findings support adding it as a sensitivity.

Limits on source access: WebFetch could not reach sec.gov, boeing.mediaroom.com, ftc.gov, nber.org, rand.org, morningstar.com and others. Quotes from those hosts come from search-result excerpts, not full documents. 'Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf' holds Rolls-Royce transcripts; Boeing's 2026 calls are in 'Transcript Digest (4).pdf'. The Benkard (39% a year forgetting), Argote and Burgelman figures come from secondary sources or memory and are low confidence. CSIS's COMAC figures are think-tank estimates.

Analyst estimates used and labelled: Goldman Sachs (BCA split, unabsorbed overhead, Airbus fixed-cost absorption, BGS mix), Morningstar (737 = 50% of EV), Barclays ($238B industry PV), BofA's Epstein (share below 40% without a new plane by 2035), and Aboulafia and Reuters development-cost ranges.

problems.problem: About $2.0-2.4B of the pool is BCA R&D. That is development spend on specific programmes, not shared overhead that a narrowbody exit would strand. Only the D&A and G&A parts are shared costs, and these are verified: p.2290 'In 2024, $705 was allocated ... $339 ... to BCA' plus BCA own D&A $400; p.2219 G&A (5,021). The 'conservative' label rests only on Boeing's aspirational 40% and 50% figures, and the 50% one is mis-sourced (see the B-0222 finding).

problems.fix: Use the game's trend for the base, for example declining 0.8 pp a year to a floor tied to the game's long-run split. Keep the flat 2060 share as the high case, and drop the word 'conservative'.

problems.parameter: C1 fps operating profit per aircraft after the window (14.1/14.1/14.1)

The source cited for this parameter, Mauboussin's 'Measuring the Moat', prescribes the opposite: excess returns fade toward the cost of capital. The fade appears only as a side sensitivity. As a result the low case of the largest term has no downside on margin, and the low/high band of the whole bridge is too narrow.
problems.evidence: Design: 'fading to the game's A320neo margin of 13.14% ($7.23M) roughly halves C1, to 10-year +0.90 and 7-year +1.39 $B at base' (reproduced: (1.877+0.126)x0.5125-0.126 = 0.90; 7-year 1.39). problems.fix: Put the Mauboussin fade (to 13.14%, or to a zero-excess-return margin) into the low case. Optionally use a fade over 10-20 years in the base. Keep the 25.64% hold for the high case only.

problems.parameter: Do Nothing baseline in round 1: C1 = 0 for Do Nothing, and the C3-C6 charges on Do Nothing
problems.problem: The headline bridge treats Do Nothing in 2030 as a certain exit, but the design's own rule calls it a deferral, and the game offers fps launches in 2035, 2045 and 2050. C3-C6 measure the value of not exiting. A 2035 launch captures most of that value too. So these terms barely separate launching in 2030 from launching later, and adding them to 'fps in 2030 vs never' biases the round-1 result toward launching now.
problems.evidence: At base, C3+C4+C5+C6 = +1.73 of the +3.93 total (10-year) and +1.98 of +5.38 (7-year). The Do-Nothing-only pieces are C3 -0.97, C4 -0.27, C5 -0.99 and C6 -0.10 (franchise_model.py at 0.105, reproduced). The game's item values (plan minus Do Nothing, held tail, data/tail.json), 10-year at Renton: -6.37 (2030, S2) and -6.51 (2030, NGSA on Alt) vs -5.09 / -5.13 (2035), -2.85 (2045), -1.83 (2050). 7-year at Renton: -8.71 / -9.28 (2030) vs -7.38 / -7.50 (2035). A 2035 launch avoids the Do Nothing exit charges and keeps w_fps = 0.5 in C5, since c5() uses 0.5 for any launched plan from 2037. It loses part of C1 (inference: about $1.1B from 2065, against $1.97B for C1+C1b in 2030), but it gains $1.3-1.9B in the game's own gap. Design text: 'Treat Do Nothing in 2030 as a deferral ... C3-C6 bite only on the path that ends in exit', yet the results table charges them in full.
problems.fix: Value every round's fps plans with the same C1-C6 terms. Compare fps-2030 with the best deferral path (Do Nothing in 2030, then the best launch in 2035, 2045 or 2050, each valued with the terms), or weight C1 = 0 and the Do Nothing C3-C6 charges by the probability that the deferral path ends in exit. Report 'launch eventually vs never' separately from 'launch in 2030 vs later'.
