In 2037-38 Do Nothing delivers at or above the status quo (618 vs 621, 543 vs 495; preference 0.40-0.44). Only 2046-49 are demand-limited (508, 482, 472, 469 against capacity 598, 556, 513, 470). The game already books that loss: cashflows.json Do Nothing nb_vs_sq -0.347, -0.284, -0.156, -0.006 $B, PV -0.10. Of C5's Do Nothing charge of -0.99, -0.75 falls in sold-out years, -0.08 in 2037-38 and -0.16 in 2046-49, which are already charged as lost volume. The design's own text says the low case of 0 'covers the case where the game's supply cap means Boeing sells out without discounting'. That is the game's state.
problems.fix: Set c = 0 in the base case and keep C5 only as a sensitivity outside the game's model. Alternatively, charge price only in demand-limited years, netted against the game's volume loss there. Base terms fall by 0.75 (10-year) and 0.86 (7-year); high by 1.50 and 1.72.

problems.parameter: C3 stranded overhead: sign, and the basis of the game's margins
problems.problem: C3's sign cannot be set from the game, because the game's per-unit margins have no documented basis. C3 is positive only if the 8% and 25.64% margins are fully loaded at D_ref. If they are programme margins before shared overhead, the game never charged that overhead: the fps branch carries it and Do Nothing sheds (1-rho) of it after exit, so C3 turns negative. The design also takes the favourable reading for each term separately: C3 uses 'fully loaded', while C2 assumes no services sit inside the margin.
problems.evidence: Margins: combined_dash.py l.908-909 and harness.py l.102, with no derivation (the design says so itself). Recomputed C3 from 2026, low/base/high (scratch logic_check/c3sign.py). Fully-loaded reading (the design's): 10-year +0.23/+0.61/+1.37, 7-year +0.26/+0.69/+1.48. Programme-margin reading (correction = -K): 10-year -0.91/-1.14/-1.37, 7-year -1.03/-1.27/-1.48. Under the fully-loaded reading the V<=1 cap ignores over-absorption in fps years above 684 a year (745-884 a year in 2045-56). Removing the cap gives base +1.25 (10-year) and +2.49 (7-year), at which point C3 is re-pricing the game's in-window margins. Under the Airbus-Commercial-style reading that the design raises in C2 risk (a), where services are inside the margin, C2 turns negative (10-year -0.06/-0.11/-0.19, 7-year -0.09/-0.16/-0.26) and C1b halves (scratch c2half.py).
problems.fix: First document the margin basis: BCA segment operating margin, programme margin, or Airbus-Commercial style including services. Then apply that one reading to C2 and C3 together. Until then, show C3 as a two-sided slider (base about -1.1 to +0.6) and keep it out of the headline. If the margins are fully loaded, either credit over-absorption symmetrically or restrict C3 to years outside the game's counted window.

problems.parameter: C1 high case: tail = demand_conservative.json after 2060
problems.problem: The high case breaks its own 'RONIC = WACC, so growth adds nothing' rule and joins two different market curves end to end. The 2060 share is computed on the page curve and then applied to the conservative curve. fps deliveries jump 47% in 2061 and then more than double by 2070, all at the full margin with no growth investment. The only route to a 10.5% flip, the high case, also stacks C3-high with C4-high, which C4's own risk (d) says not to do without saying so, and relies on C5-high (see the C5 finding).
problems.evidence: nb_path: s60 = 402.2 / 1,166 (page curve), then s60 x the conservative curve from 2061 (1,710.7, rising to 2,531 in 2070). The 10-year fps goes from 402 (2060) to 590 (2061) to about 873 a year; the 7-year from 428 to 628. Holding the conservative level at its 2060 value of 1,632 gives C1-high 2.63 (10-year) and 3.70 (7-year), against 3.62 and 4.75. Holding 2060 deliveries flat gives 1.90 and 2.93 (scratch checks.py). High gaps of +1.80 / +1.37 become +0.27 / -0.34 with C1-high level-held, C4 at base and the C3 start fix. Without C5-high as well they become -1.23 / -2.06.
problems.fix: In the high case, hold the post-2060 level (no value from growth), or state RONIC > WACC and justify it, for example by the spare fps capacity of 1,200 a year (supply_demand.fps_full). Remove the splice: rescale the conservative curve to the page's 2060 level, or use it inside the window too. Report the high case without stacking C3-high and C4-high, and state that the fps flips at 10.5% only under those stacked assumptions.

problems.parameter: C3 F_shared (base $5.0B) includes BCA R&D
problems.problem: BCA R&D is programme development (mostly 777X, plus 737-7/-10), not shared narrowbody overhead. Applying s_NB = 0.64 assigns 64% of mostly-777X R&D to the narrowbody, and rho = 0.35 then keeps it stranded forever. The 777X part is widebody and is not stranded by a narrowbody exit. The narrowbody part can be avoided on exit, and in the fps branch it is the game's fps bill.
problems.evidence: FY2024 10-K R&D table: Commercial Airplanes $2,386M (2024), $2,036M (2023), $1,510M (2022). 'Research and development expense increased by $435 million in 2024 compared with 2023 primarily due to the 777X program at BCA' (scratch franchise/tenk/boeing_10k.txt l.99053-99065; repo Boeing 10ks.zip > Boeing 10ks.pdf). About 2.2 of the 5.0 F_shared is R&D, which implies about $0.49B a year of permanent 'stranded R&D' in Do Nothing (inference). Removing it gives base C3 +0.34 (10-year) and +0.38 (7-year), against +0.61 and +0.75.
problems.fix: Remove programme R&D from F_shared. Keep G&A, central D&A, and any shared-technology R&D that can be identified separately.

problems.parameter: C3 start year (2040 for both plans)
problems.problem: The code starts C3 in 2040, 'the first year the plans differ', but the 7-year plan differs from 2037. Its transition dip in 2038-39, below Do Nothing, is therefore never charged.
problems.evidence: fps_cash_flows_2030.csv, Boeing deliveries in 2037-39: 7-year 636 / 512 / 552, Do Nothing 618 / 543 / 684. Starting from 2026 (the plans are identical before 2037) gives 7-year C3 of +0.26/+0.69/+1.48, against the design's +0.29/+0.75/+1.60. The 10-year is unchanged.
problems.fix: Start the ratchet in 2026, or at the first year any plan differs, with K set from the shared path.

problems.parameter: C1 netting against the status quo in years Do Nothing is counted but the plan is not (7-year, 2057-2059)
problems.problem: Do Nothing's window runs to 2060 because the unlaunched fps defaults to an EIS of 2041 (+19). In 2057-59 the game counts Do Nothing minus status quo, which is 0, and C1 adds the gross fps profit. The true delta is fps minus Do Nothing gross, i.e. fps minus status quo, so C1 leaves out the status quo's MAX profit.
problems.evidence: combined_dash.py l.1077 (_b_nb_end_t = fps EIS - 2026 + 19) and model.py DEFAULT_EIS (fps 2041). cashflows.json status quo MAX units in 2057-59 are 128.2, 85.5 and 42.8, at $3.84M each. C1 (7-year) is overstated by $0.042B. The 10-year is unaffected (status quo = 0 in 2060).
problems.fix: For years counted for Do Nothing but not for the plan, add fps profit + the plan's MAX profit - status quo profit, which is the game's own in-window convention.

problems.parameter: C6 exit charge booked only in Do Nothing (E_fps = 0)
problems.problem: Part of C_exit comes with the end of MAX production, not with leaving the market, and MAX production ends in the fps plans too, 14-15 years earlier. Booking all of it in Do Nothing gives C6 the wrong sign.
problems.evidence: CSV: the 10-year plan's MAX is 180 in 2045 and 0 from 2046; the 7-year's is 23 in 2044 and 0 from 2045; Do Nothing's ends in 2060. Residual-value and financing support for an orphaned MAX fleet (FY2012 10-K: 'financing receivables for out-of-production aircraft') and closing the Everett North Line (supply_demand.json: 'about $1B') follow the end of MAX production in every plan. If one-third to one-half of the $3.0B is booked at 2045/46 in the fps plans (DF 0.136-0.150 vs 0.0335), the C6 bridge moves from +0.10 to between -0.03 and -0.10 (10-year) and between -0.05 and -0.12 (7-year).
problems.fix: Split C_exit into exit-only items (severance, site and IT impairment, restructuring) booked in Do Nothing, and MAX-end items (supplier termination, line closure, fleet residual-value support) booked in every plan at its last MAX year.

problems.parameter: C1 horizon and reinvestment (perpetuity with one 12.5% derivative)
problems.problem: C1 counts fps profit forever with a single derivative. That keeps the profits of the fps's successor without charging its bill, which contradicts the design's own rule (d) that a successor has zero NPV under RONIC = WACC. It also runs past Boeing's own 50-year product framing. The derivative is booked without the game's debt penalty.
problems.evidence: B-2278 (CFO, 2025): 'a product that's going to be out there for 50 years'. The 737 needed derivatives every 14-19 years (1968, 1984, 1998, 2017; inference). The game adds a 32-34% debt penalty to fps bills (CSV: 19.12 on 60.32, 22.01 on 65.0). At 10.5%, capping at EIS+50 and adding the penalty to the derivative costs -0.14 (10-year) and -0.20 (7-year). At 6.5%, the life cap alone cuts base C1 from 10.35 to 8.70 (10-year) and from 13.93 to 11.81 (7-year) (scratch checks.py).
problems.fix: End the fps stream at EIS+50, or charge a clean-sheet bill then. Charge recurring derivatives, and apply the game's true_cost debt penalty to each one.

problems.parameter: C5 applied to the MAX only
problems.problem: C5's mechanism (below about 40% share, the leader gets pricing power) applies equally to the fps share that C1 holds after the window, yet C1 keeps the full 25.64% margin.
problems.evidence: B-0638 (Albaugh 2012: 'they have pricing power in the marketplace'). C1 holds the fps at 34.5% (10-year) and 36.7% (7-year) of the market from 2060. The same 1.5% of $55M on fps deliveries after the window costs -0.12 (10-year) and -0.18 (7-year) (scratch misc.py).
problems.fix: Apply the concession to both products or to neither. Given the C5 finding, prefer neither.

problems.parameter: Discount-rate verdict (9.3-9.4% flip; 8.1% and 6.5% real cases)
problems.problem: The quoted flip rate and the low-rate verdicts are computed before the logic fixes. The '6.5% analyst-consistent' rate also borrows an Airbus WACC for Boeing and removes the game's deliberate Boeing premium.
problems.evidence: Verified flip as designed: 10-year between 9.3% and 9.4%, 7-year between 9.4% and 9.5%. With the fixes for C5 (c = 0), the C3 R&D and start year, C1 netting, horizon and derivative penalty, and the C6 split (scratch corrected.py): at 10.5% the base terms are +2.64 / +3.76, leaving gaps of -3.73 / -4.95, which closes 41-43% of the gap, not about 60%. The flip moves to about 8.6-8.7% (10-year) and 8.8-9.0% (7-year). At 8.1% the gaps are +1.89 / +3.51 (design +4.45 / +6.70). The 6.5% case uses GS's Airbus 9% WACC, while the game sets WACC_B 10.5% vs WACC_A 8.0% (combined_dash.py l.711-712). The ranking of the two fps plans also flips below about 9% (the 7-year becomes better).
problems.fix: Report flip rates after the fixes. For Boeing, use 10.5% (the game) or 8.1% (10.5% read as nominal), and label 6.5% as an Airbus-style sensitivity.

problems.parameter: C1 low case
problems.problem: The low case is not a lower bound. It sets kappa = 0, which raises value, and keeps the 25.64% margin through decades of collapsing demand. The design's own Mauboussin fade sensitivity roughly halves C1 and is not included in the low case.
problems.evidence: franchise_model.py c1(): no derivative when case == 'low'. Design: fading to the A320neo margin of 13.14% gives 10-year +0.90 and 7-year +1.39 at base.
problems.fix: Define the low case as the as-run tail plus the margin fade plus the base-case derivative.

problems.parameter: Applying the terms one-sidedly in the game
problems.problem: The same 20-year window applies to Airbus's NGSA, and Airbus's choices in the game carry no continuing value. Adding C1-C6 to Boeing's valuation alone changes the game's inputs on one side only.
problems.evidence: combined_dash.py l.1078: _a_nb_end_t = NGSA EIS - 2026 + 19. Airbus's columns (NGSA, Alt plan, A350 re-engine) are valued without any franchise term.
problems.fix: Either apply the analogous terms to Airbus (NGSA continuing value, A320 run-out), or state that rival columns are held fixed and the terms are an overlay on Boeing's valuation, not a change to the game.

problems.parameter: Evidence and parameter labels
problems.problem: Some evidence is mismatched to the claim and some labels are wrong.
problems.evidence: B-0222 is the 747-8 vs A380 very-large-aircraft case; the item's own finding: 'Boeing's 747-8 business case vs the A380 rested on taking about half of a roughly 740-aircraft very-large-aircraft market'. C1 cites it as a narrowbody '50% planning share'. BX-1033 is the KC-46 tanker. The share parameter's 'low 0.34 / base 0.345 / high 0.367' is not a case range: the code uses each plan's s60 in every case, and 0.367 is the 7-year plan. problems.fix: Drop B-0222 from C1, label BX-1033 as an analogy, relabel the share parameter by plan, correct the D_ref text and the line references.

problems.parameter: C1 base tail ('held' at the 2060 page value)
problems.problem: The base tail overrides the run's own demand input, and does so inconsistently. The artefact it corrects after 2060 also depresses demand inside the window, so the 'held' level is itself depressed. This makes the base conservative for the fps, but it is unlabelled.
problems.evidence: demand_page_n0.json 'about': 'replacement of today's fleet ... and as much again for growth, from 2038', so aircraft delivered after 2026 are never replaced. This drives both the fall after 2060 (1,166 to 364 by 2070) and the fall inside the window (2,038 in 2050 to 1,166 in 2060), which feeds the fps's 831 to 402. Do Nothing is capacity-bound in 2050-59, so a fix inside the window would raise only the fps plans.
problems.fix: Label the base tail as an override of the run's demand input. If the artefact is corrected, correct it inside the window too (re-run the game), not only after 2060.
